# INTRODUCTION

In his famous work, *The Old Regime and the Revolution* <note>original: "l'Ancien régime et la Révolution" (1856). In this influential book, Alexis de Tocqueville argued that the French Revolution was not a sudden break from the past but a continuation of trends already present in the monarchy.</note>, the main idea of which consists—as is well known—in the demonstration that one must learn to understand the great French Revolution not only in itself, but also through the history of the times that preceded it, Tocqueville points out that the true character of this great historical event can best be discovered in the writings of the economists or <term>physiocrats</term> <note>Physiocrats: A group of 18th-century French thinkers led by François Quesnay who believed that agriculture was the sole source of a nation's wealth and advocated for "natural laws" in governance.</note>. All the institutions that the Revolution was to abolish forever were the specific objects of their attacks; all those, on the contrary, which may be seen as the Revolution's own work, were announced by them in advance and advocated with passion. One could hardly cite a single institution whose seed was not deposited in some of their writings; one finds in them everything that is most substantial in the Revolution, including the revolutionary temperament itself.

Even if we admit that these remarks are debatable, it nonetheless follows that to understand this grandiose event, one must not neglect the study of the works of the party in question. On the eve of the centenary of the great French Revolution <note>This indicates the book was published around 1889, the 100th anniversary of the storming of the Bastille.</note>, the edition of all the economic writings of the founder of the physiocratic school <note>The founder refers to François Quesnay (1694–1774), who developed the famous "Economic Table" (*Tableau économique*).</note>, as well as the philosophical treatises by the same author, should not seem untimely.

Not only historical reasons in general, but also and especially reasons of <term>political economy</term> <note>Political economy: The historical term for the study of how nations manage production, trade, and wealth through government policy.</note> seem to make a publication of this kind desirable at the present moment; for our era applies even more strongly than Tocqueville's own time (1856) to what that writer added, namely:

> "Of all the people of that time, the economists are those who would appear the least out of place in ours. If I read the speeches and writings of the men who made the Revolution, I feel..." <note>The text breaks off here as the sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>The author introduces this collection of François Quesnay’s works by citing Alexis de Tocqueville’s argument that the Physiocrats' writings predicted and shaped the French Revolution. The preface highlights that studying these 18th-century economic theories is essential for understanding both history and modern political economy.</summary>

<keywords>Alexis de Tocqueville, French Revolution, Physiocracy, Political Economy, François Quesnay, 18th-century history, economic theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction, transitioning from Alexis de Tocqueville’s observations on the Physiocrats to the modern relevance of their theories in the late 19th century. "...suddenly transported to a place and into the midst of a society I do not know. But when I browse the books of the economists, it feels as if I have lived with these people and have just finished conversing with them."

In recent times, problems that were thought to have been forgotten and abandoned long ago have been brought back to light. Such is the case with the old <term>physiocratic</term> <note>Physiocratic: Relating to the "Physiocrats," a school of thought that believed land and agriculture were the only true sources of wealth.</note> principle according to which the power of the State must devote special care to domestic agriculture and strive, through its commercial policy, to obtain the best possible price for its products; this principle is currently inscribed on the banner of a party that has formed in almost all civilized countries, the agrarian party or the Agrarians. The struggle concerning the freedom of the grain trade and trade in general is, in our day, conducted with an ardor hardly less intense than in the time of <term>physiocracy</term>, and with few new arguments. And even the school's claim—a claim that was mocked for an entire century as a paradox—of establishing a <term>single tax</term> <note>Single Tax: An economic theory suggesting that the government should only tax the value of land, rather than labor or production.</note>, has recently found in the person of the American Henry George a defender as energetic as he is powerful by the number of his adherents. In his well-known book *Progress and Poverty*, he summarizes his ideas in the following manner, specifically calling upon the school of <term>Quesnay</term> <note>François Quesnay (1694–1774): The founder and leader of the Physiocrats and personal physician to King Louis XV.</note>: "The French economists of the last century proposed exactly what I have myself proposed, that is, that all taxation be abolished with the exception of a tax on the value of land." And this same author dedicated another work "to the memory of those illustrious Frenchmen of the eighteenth century, Quesnay, Turgot, Mirabeau, Dupont and their colleagues, who, in the night of despotism, foresaw the magnificence of the days to come."

Based on the above, one could almost speak of a current renaissance of the physiocratic system, if very noticeable differences did not stand out between the old and the new ideas.

The modern agrarian party seeks to revive agriculture by means completely opposite to those advocated in their time by the party of the economists. A high price for grain is to be obtained not through extreme freedom of trade, but through protectionism. Furthermore, absolute freedom of trade has now become the program of the economic party, against whose interests the physiocrats precisely wanted to rise—that is, the...

Finally, Henry George does not ask, as his predecessors did, for a <term>single tax</term> <note>original: "l'impôt unique"</note> to guarantee the private ownership of landed property and thereby demonstrate the rights of a specific class of landowners. On the contrary, he seeks to displace this class of owners through the "appropriation of <term>land rent</term> <note>Land Rent: In this context, the profit earned from land ownership itself, rather than from labor or improvements made to the land.</note> via taxation," and to achieve the <term>nationalization of the soil</term>.

It is not, therefore, the physiocratic system as such that is now celebrating its resurrection. Rather, it is the revival of several scattered ideas from this system—ideas that relate to the most diverse interests and some of which even strike us with a violent contrast. It should, therefore, be all the more interesting to look back at this ancient doctrine itself, from the time when the principles that are now independent of one another still moved in peaceful unity and were held in balance by a strictly logical discipline of ideas.

For this reason as well, the complete reproduction of the works of the author of this doctrine <note>Referring to François Quesnay (1694–1774), the French economist who served as the king's physician and founded the Physiocratic school.</note> must be considered a timely undertaking.

Indeed, the study of the doctrine of Quesnay—to whom certainly belongs the undisputed merit of having established the first strictly scientific system of <term>political economy</term>—has until now been neglected in a surprising manner. Henry George frankly admits to knowing the doctrine of Quesnay and his disciples only indirectly, that is to say, through the works of English writers. Consequently, he does not know if, from the phrase he approves of—"the land is the source of all wealth"—these men deduced other principles, whether true or false. Moreover, one quite frequently hears the complaint that, despite all good will, one cannot obtain any detailed knowledge of the physiocratic system, given that in the brief mentions made in textbooks of political economy, one encounters only paradoxes without being able to discover the idea that should link them. This complaint is justified. One can even speak of the discredit into which this ingenious system fell among economic theorists shortly after the death of its founder. How can this strange fact be explained?

->XII<-

practice during the two years of Turgot’s ministry, than in the unfavorable critique directed against Quesnay’s doctrine by Adam Smith in his famous work *An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations* (1776). The immense prestige this work enjoyed until well into our century—declining only relatively recently—led Smith's disciples to consider it a sacrilege to devote serious attention to a system their master had condemned.

It is true that this critique did not remain completely unanswered. For instance, putting the <term>physiocrats</term> <note>Physiocrats: A group of 18th-century French economists who believed that the wealth of nations was derived solely from the value of land development and agriculture, advocating for a "rule of nature."</note> aside, the Earl of Lauderdale (*An Inquiry into the Nature and Origin of Public Wealth*, 1804) describes the critique as a failure. He suggests that the defenders of the attacked doctrine did not "favor it as much with all their talent as the author of the *Wealth of Nations* did by the manner in which he believed he had refuted it." Furthermore, in the appendix of his German translation of J. B. Say’s *Treatise on Political Economy* (1807), L. J. Jakob, while approving of Smith, nonetheless added: "But if one examines the reasons by which Smith sought to support his thesis and demonstrate the falsity of Quesnay’s principles, one cannot deny that a great gap exists in his reasoning, and that much of what he says appears to confirm rather than refute the fundamental principle of the physiocrats" (that agricultural labor is the only kind that is productive).

Additionally, in a long note in his French translation of the *Wealth of Nations*, G. Garnier attempted to merge Smith's system with that of the physiocrats, declaring that Smith's counter-observations resulted from a simple misunderstanding. Be that as it may, the dominant opinion among other specialists has always been that which A. Blanqui expressed against G. Garnier with these words: "The system is judged without appeal" <note>original: "Le système est jugé sans appel." This implies the debate was considered closed and the Physiocrats' ideas definitively rejected.</note>.

Due to the great influence exercised for an entire century by Adam Smith's critique on the fate of the physiocratic system, it seemed impossible to remain silent on this fact in a work gathering the collected economic writings of Quesnay. We felt an even greater obligation to provide an explanation on this subject because a thorough examination reveals that the famous Scotsman's <note>Adam Smith (1723–1790), the Scottish philosopher often called the "Father of Economics."</note> objections are often highly arbitrary in nature and do not hold up against an objective counter-critique.

->XIII<-

During the two-and-a-half-year stay (March 1764 to October 1766) that the former professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow made on the continent with his illustrious pupil, the young Duke of Buccleuch, he spent about ten months in Paris. As we learn not only from his *biographer*, Dugald Stewart, but also from communications coming from Dupont de Nemours and the Abbé Morellet, Smith found himself in that city in quite intimate relations with Quesnay and his disciples, and especially with Turgot, to whom he had been particularly recommended by David Hume. > "was regarded there as a judicious and simple man, but one who had not yet proven himself."

Moreover, Morellet confirms to us that at that time Adam Smith had devoted himself in a special way to economic studies; in his *Memoirs*, he says (vol. I, p. 244):

> "I had known Smith during a trip he made to France. He spoke our language very poorly; but his *Theory of Moral Sentiments* had given me a great idea of his sagacity and depth, and truly I still regard him today as one of the men who have made the most complete observations and analyses in all the questions he treated. M. Turgot, who like me loved metaphysics, greatly esteemed his talent. We saw him several times; he was introduced at the home of Helvetius <note>Claude Adrien Helvétius (1715–1771) was a French philosopher and socialite whose salon was a center of Enlightenment thought.</note>: we spoke of commercial theory, banks, public credit, and several points of the great work he was meditating" etc.

His relations with the economists appear to have been so intimate that they considered him a fellow student. One can at least draw this conclusion from a passage of the "*Observations on the points in which Adam Smith agrees with the theory of M. Turgot, and those in which he has departed from it*" which Dupont attached to the *Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth* in his edition of Turgot's works; this passage, which is part of the polemical argument against Smith, is worded as follows:

> "Smith at liberty, Smith in his room or in that of a friend, as I saw him when we were fellow students <note>original: "condisciples"</note> at the home of M. Quesnay, would have been very careful not to deny it, etc."

It is true that Smith cloaked his critique in all the politeness imaginable. He praises the personal simplicity and modesty of "the ingenious and profound author of this system" <note>Referring to François Quesnay, the founder of Physiocracy.</note>. The followers of the system are men of "great knowledge and distinguished talent." He declares the system itself "noble and generous" and says that "with all its imperfections, nonetheless this system is perhaps, of everything that has yet been published on <term>political economy</term> <note>The study of how a country's laws, customs, and government interact with its production and trade.</note>, that which comes closest to the truth." Often these passages are cited to highlight the supposed high opinion that Smith must have had for the doctrine of the economists. But in reality, these remarks serve only to give even greater force to the objections formulated; for if, while speaking with such evident restraint, one ultimately reaches a judgment condemning the doctrine, this judgment must therefore be all the more just. Now, if Dugald Stewart says that Adam Smith—as he learned from Smith's own mouth—intended to dedicate his work *The Wealth of Nations* to Quesnay, and was only prevented from doing so by Quesnay's prior death, we are far from wishing to doubt this assertion. But this cannot prevent us from also pointing out the circumstances to the contrary.

Indeed, it must unfortunately be said that Adam Smith did not bring a great deal of good faith to his critique, as is noticeable from the very first words.

When, at the end of March 1776, the Scottish scholar released his long-awaited book to the public, Turgot had already occupied his ministerial post for nearly two years. The entire civilized world followed with deep attention the spectacle, appearing for the first time, of a great empire being governed and even reorganized according to the principles of science <note>This refers to Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot's attempt to implement liberal economic reforms in France as King Louis XVI's Controller-General of Finances.</note>. This event could not have interested anyone more than Adam Smith, whose mind was preparing a work on the same subject, and who had previously personally exchanged ideas with the author and guide of these political and administrative reforms in France. Now, is it possible that Smith—who at that time no longer lived in his retreat at Kirkcaldy, but was in London, where he was putting the finishing touches on his work—would have learned absolutely nothing of these events occurring in the neighboring country? ->XV<-

...begins the chapter on "Agricultural Systems" with the following surprising observation: "The system which represents the produce of land as the sole source of the revenue and wealth of every country, has never, so far as I know, been adopted by any nation, and it at present exists only in the speculations of a few men of great learning and ingenuity in France" <note>original: "Le système qui représente le produit de la terre comme la seule source du revenu et de la richesse d'un pays n'a jamais... été adopté par aucune nation..." This is a direct quote from Book IV, Chapter IX of Adam Smith's *The Wealth of Nations*.</note> etc. And he adds, to justify what he says, that he simply wishes to limit himself on this point to reproducing the fundamental principles of this system: "It can surely be no very long or very tedious task to examine the errors of a system which has never done, and probably never will do, any harm in any part of the world." <note>original: "Ce n'est sûrement pas la peine de discuter fort au long les erreurs d'une théorie qui n'a jamais fait et qui vraisemblablement ne fera jamais de mal en aucun lieu du monde."</note>

Now, setting aside the fact that this preceding explanation was false for that very period, it must also be seen as singular to make the scientific value of a system dependent on whether it has already been realized in practice or is expected to be. **Plato’s** theory of politics has never been applied either, and likely never will be; yet, its place in science has never been contested. Seeing, moreover, that in subsequent editions of his work, and even in the 3rd edition (1784)—which is distinguished by many additions and improvements—Smith did not modify this explanation at all, we can perfectly well assume that he did not see fit to make such a change because of the unfavorable position he chose to grant **Quesnay’s** system alongside his own doctrine. This impression is further strengthened when we closely examine Smith’s developments in detail.

That this author reproaches the doctrine he opposes with numerous paradoxes might still be acceptable. But what is already unjust is to continually apply the term "sect" to the disciples of this doctrine—a term to which the <term>Physiocrats</term> <note>The first organized school of economists, who believed that agriculture was the only source of wealth.</note> were very sensitive and against which they constantly protested as "an injurious expression" (see note 1, page 716). And what constitutes a distortion of the truth is when he says of them "that they affect to degrade (*sic*) the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants by designating them with the humiliating (*sic*) name of *sterile or unproductive class*," and that he repeats several times, insistently, that they instead bestowed upon agriculture the *honorable appellation* of *productive class*.

->XVI<-

It would be difficult to find a <term>Physiocratic</term><note>Physiocracy was an economic theory developed by 18th-century French thinkers who believed that land and agriculture were the only true sources of wealth.</note> work that, in discussing this point, did not reject the reproach that the label *non-productive* has something humiliating about it. "This epithet," says <term>Quesnay</term><note>François Quesnay (1694–1774) was the founder of the Physiocratic school and personal physician to King Louis XV.</note> himself, "has nothing shocking about it; there are many states more elevated than commerce that adopt it without reluctance. The ministers of the altars, the magistrates, the military carry out useful duties and belong to the *sterile class* regarding their functions . . . Physical distinctions do nothing to dignity; they should interest the self-esteem of men very little," etc. (see pages 521 and 522).

Now, this question formed exactly the central point of the passionate struggle in which the Physiocratic party was engaged at the time when <term>Adam Smith</term><note>The Scottish economist Adam Smith (1723–1790) lived in Paris from 1764 to 1766, where he frequently socialized with Quesnay’s circle.</note> lived in Paris among the members of this party. The quality of productivity applied simultaneously to the three classes of production—agriculture, industry, and commerce—was by no means established by Adam Smith alone. On the contrary, it was already claimed with energy by the defenders of the <term>mercantile system</term><note>The Mercantilists believed that national wealth was increased through trade and the accumulation of gold, opposing the Physiocratic focus on land.</note> against Quesnay, as one can be convinced by reading the part of the present work in which this subject falls. Smith was a personal witness in Paris to all the events and incidents linked to Quesnay's articles published by the *Journal of Agriculture, Commerce, and Finance* (1766). Instead, then, of taking up on his own account the reproach, refuted time and time again by the adversaries of that era, it would have been much more appropriate on his part to defend the school against the accusation that it had wanted to attach discredit to the designation of *non-productive*. And he would have had all the more reason to act this way because, in his own system, he maintains, as we know, the label *unproductive*—if not for industrial and commercial professions, at least for the classes of intellectual workers, such as state officials, the clergy, doctors, artists, etc.—and he does not intend to cast discredit on these latter classes either. Smith's reproach cannot, therefore, be viewed as entirely fair.

But also the positive objections directed against the classification established by the economists are of considerable weakness, and we find ourselves here in the presence of that part of the critique which, according to the judgment of <term>Lauderdale</term><note>James Maitland, 8th Earl of Lauderdale (1759–1839), was a Scottish peer and economist who criticized Smith's theories on wealth and value.</note> and <term>Jakob</term><note>Ludwig Heinrich von Jakob (1759–1827) was a German economist who helped disseminate and critique Smith's ideas in Germany.</note>, supports rather than overturns the principles for which Smith is bringing suit.

and re-ship existing materials and that they did not produce them themselves. But the cultivation of the land produces, in addition to the maintenance of the labor it requires, a surplus of materials first for the landowner, then for the professional classes, and it is for this purely physical reason that it receives the qualification of productive. The main argument that Smith advances against this “main error,” as he calls it, of the system under attack, is the following.

It is true, indeed, that independently of the yield required for their maintenance and the continuation of the operation, farmers and peasants still produce a <term>net product</term><note>The *produit net* is the surplus value produced by land after all costs of labor and capital have been paid; the Physiocrats believed only agriculture could yield this.</note> for the landowners, which is not the case for industrial professions. But he continues thus: “We would not call sterile or unproductive a marriage which reproduced only a son and a daughter to replace the father and the mother, although this marriage did not contribute at all to increasing the number of individuals of the human species and only continued the population as it was before. Thus, just as a marriage which yields three children is certainly more productive than one which yields only two, so the labor of farmers and rural workers is certainly more productive than that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. However, the superiority of the product of one of these classes does not make the other sterile and unproductive.” Thus speaks <term>Adam Smith</term><note>A reference to Smith’s *The Wealth of Nations* (1776), where he critiques the Physiocratic school of economics.</note>.

One wonders with astonishment how Smith could speak here of a “main error,” for it is nevertheless obvious that he is making a distinction less of the thing itself than of the terminology. Moreover, even today the question remains subject to discussion as to whether—admitting the same basis—the classification method of <term>Quesnay</term><note>François Quesnay, the leader of the Physiocrats, who categorized society into the productive class (farmers), the proprietary class (landowners), and the sterile class (artisans/merchants).</note> is not nevertheless preferable to that of Adam Smith. As is well known, the theory of **productive and unproductive labor** was precisely the point that Smith’s disciples did not maintain. Already his most fervent apostle, <term>J. B. Say</term><note>Jean-Baptiste Say (1767–1832), a French economist who popularized Smith's ideas but famously disagreed with him on the value of "immaterial" or intellectual labor.</note>, spoke out strongly against this theory, at least insofar as it opposes the productivity of intellectual labor.

->XVIII<-

of three means for the highest degree of well-being for all classes of people, namely: the establishment of 1° perfect justice, 2° perfect liberty, and 3° perfect equality <note>The original text includes the English phrase "perfectly equality," likely a direct citation of Smith’s own terminology.</note>. However, the fact that the <term>Physiocrats</term><note>A group of 18th-century French economists who believed that the wealth of nations derived solely from the value of "land agriculture" or "land development."</note> conversely derived the principle of social and economic inequality from the natural order contradicts this third point. This fact even constitutes one of the fundamental doctrines of their system.

Finally, when one reads—both as a chapter title and within the explanation itself—that the system “represents the *product* of the land as the sole source of the revenue and wealth of the country,” <note>The original includes the English word "produce" here.</note> one finds oneself in the presence of erroneous notions and opinions introduced into the system itself. In fact, <term>Quesnay</term><note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), the leading figure and founder of the Physiocratic school.</note> and his disciples always represented the land and, in a broader sense, agriculture as the source of public goods and prosperity, but *they never equated the products of the land with the source itself*. With Smith, it is different. The “annual produce of labor” in the primitive state of cultivation, and the “annual produce of land and labor” in the state of progressive cultivation, form—as is well known according to his terminology—the “fund” and, in an extended sense, the “source” of public wealth. It is the “source” because, according to his system, two torrents of goods flow from the annual fund: one for the immediate consumption of the population, the other, as <term>capital</term> in the proper sense of the word, for the operation of the enterprise which must produce new goods. But Quesnay was always a stranger to such a way of seeing things.

To conclude, let us add that Smith, in order to secure for his system the place he intended it to hold—as an intermediate theory between <term>mercantilism</term><note>An economic theory dominant from the 16th to 18th centuries that promoted government regulation of a nation’s economy for the purpose of augmenting state power at the expense of rival national powers, often focusing on accumulating gold and silver.</note> and <term>physiocratism</term>—represented the matter as if the principle of “natural liberty” had to be saved by him against these two systems. However, since Quesnay's theory rejected state intervention to an even higher degree and thus understood the notion of economic liberty from an infinitely more “natural” point of view than Smith himself, one can thus get an idea of the accuracy with which <term>Blanqui</term><note>Adolphe Blanqui (1798–1854), a French economist and historian of economic thought.</note>, basing himself directly on this critique of Physiocracy, could say: “The system is judged without appeal.”

->XIX<-

that the critique directed by him <note>Referring to Adam Smith.</note> against the system of the French economists is not at the level of what one was reasonably entitled to expect from him. This critique in no way proves what it intends to prove. Even today, the <term>physiocratic system</term><note>An 18th-century economic theory suggesting that land and agriculture are the true sources of wealth.</note> awaits its scientific refutation. The resulting consequence is that for a long century, <term>Quesnay’s</term><note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), the founder of the Physiocratic school.</note> doctrine has been treated unfairly, however erroneous it may otherwise be. It is high time to right this wrong through a new study of this master’s works.

The compatriots of Quesnay, it is true, have not neglected this study to the same extent as other nations, yet they have nevertheless done so in a quite noticeable way.

In general, however, one certainly cannot reproach the French for having shown no taste for historical literary studies in the matter of <term>political economy</term><note>The original study of production, trade, and their relations with law, custom, and government.</note>. On the contrary, they are much further advanced on this point than all other nations. Fortunately, they did not follow the advice of **J. B. Say**, their “most famous economist” according to **Blanqui**, who claimed that it mattered little to know what our predecessors dreamed on the subject, and that it was a matter of forgetting old errors rather than learning to know them. All the remarkable economists of France, since **Montchrétien de Vateville**, have been the subject of more or less detailed monographic works, prompted in part by competitions held by the ***Academy of Moral and Political Sciences***. In addition to a great quantity of essays on the history of economic literature, we possess a series of extensive and valuable works on the administrative activity of **Colbert** and the <term>mercantile principles</term><note>An economic policy (Mercantilism) designed to maximize exports and minimize imports through state intervention.</note> associated with it; we also have works on **Boisguillebert**, **Vauban**, **Law**, the **Abbé de St-Pierre**, etc., who have often been studied by several authors. Even several members of Quesnay’s school have, in our time, been the subject of specific literary studies. Let us recall among others the important work, *The Mirabeaus* <note>original title: "Les Mirabeau"</note> by **Loménie**, which goes hand-in-hand with the new edition of *The Friend of Mankind* <note>original title: "l'Ami des hommes"</note>, produced by **W. Rouxel**; let us also recall the book, published a short time ago, by **G. Schelle**, *Dupont de Nemours and the Physiocratic School*. Even a <term>Physiocrat</term> as secondary as **Ch. de Butré** had, not long ago, the honor of a detailed monographic study in the book by **R. Reuss**. But Quesnay himself, who is nevertheless the glory of French economists, has remained in the shadow. It is true that in the ***Collection of the Principal Economists***, published by **Guillaumin** a little over forty years ago, Quesnay has

But what might have satisfied the scientific needs of the first half of our century—and perhaps even exceeded those needs—is no longer sufficient for the requirements of the current era. It must be recognized that the edition produced by Daire of the principal writings of the founder of the <term>physiocratic system</term> <note>The first systematic school of political economy, which argued that the wealth of nations derived solely from the value of agriculture or land development.</note> was, for its time, a major scientific event. At a time when, as a result of the excessive praise directed specifically by a Frenchman, **J. B. Say** <note>Jean-Baptiste Say (1767–1832), a famous French economist who popularized Adam Smith's ideas in Europe but often dismissed earlier thinkers.</note>, toward **Adam Smith**, the Scottish master exercised unlimited authority in the field of <term>political economy</term>, there was merit in highlighting the fact that similar men had already lived and that the first theoretical system in this field was born in France.

In our day, by contrast, one can say that this Daire edition creates obstacles for historical literary research. People have become so accustomed to finding in this collection everything worth knowing about the physiocratic system that they have completely abandoned the study of the original works. Many things that could have been of great value for the understanding of the system's ideas, taken as a whole, have thus fallen into oblivion. From the perspective of the accuracy of historical accounts regarding these systems, it is no longer enough now to simply know an author's supposedly most important works: one must study the man in all his aspects; one must research not only his merits but also his flaws, which often appear as such only because of the time in which he lived, whereas later they may present themselves as true strengths. Today, we want to be able to trace the birth and development of ideas in order to know why they were formed and had to be formed in this way and not another. To this end, seemingly secondary circumstances and even unsuccessful attempts are often far more important than the principal works that show the man at his most perfect.

Frequently, the overall impression differs essentially from that which one acquires from just a few parts, which are always assembled in an arbitrary manner, at least to a certain extent. Often, too, an author has treated a main point of his doctrine with little vigor in certain prominent passages because elsewhere he expands upon the subject...

->XXI<-

with even more detail. In the works reproduced by **E. Daire**, no one, for example, will be able to find any information regarding **Quesnay's** opinion on the policy of interest rates for money. Given the character that permeates his theory, which tends to reject all State interference in economic relations, the reader would naturally suppose that on this point **Quesnay** also remained faithful to this principle. It is exactly the opposite that is true. In the present work (pages 399 and following), one can read an article titled *Observations on the Interest of Money*, which appeared under the pseudonym of **Mr. Nisaque** <note>An anagram of Quesnay.</note> in the January issue of the *Journal of Agriculture, Commerce, and Finance*, and in which **Quesnay** vigorously combats the opinion of merchants and financiers, according to which "the rate of interest on money lent for the establishment of perpetual annuities must rise or fall based on the competition of the greater or lesser number of lenders or borrowers; from which would result the ruin of the nation." And, a noteworthy thing, he expressly bases his arguments on <term>natural law</term> <note>The Physiocrats believed in a "Natural Order" of providential laws; here, Quesnay argues that natural justice requires state intervention to keep the economy balanced.</note> which must, in this case, be supported by <term>positive law</term> <note>Human-made statutes or government decrees.</note>. There is a need, he says, for a "positive law of the prince," an "authentic rule that would be renewed at least every ten years" to protect the borrower against the arbitrary interest rate of money fixed by the lender, and above all to maintain the rate of interest on capital in suitable proportions with the income from real estate; for nothing is as harmful to agriculture as an interest rate higher than the natural income of real estate and, moreover, continually variable; through this, mortgages would expel owners from their heritage, etc. One can remark that **Quesnay's** ideas already agree to a certain point with those of **Rodbertus** <note>Karl Johann Rodbertus (1805–1875), a German economist who later argued for state-regulated economic balances to protect the working and landed classes.</note>.

From the preceding, and indeed from other facts as well, one can see that **Quesnay** was quite far from pushing the economic freedom he demanded to an extreme. In this, he distinguishes himself essentially from his own school of followers. Thus, **Dupont** <note>Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours, a close disciple of Quesnay who often edited his master's work to make it seem more ideologically consistent.</note>, who was then the editor of the *Journal of Agriculture*, etc., allowed his diverging opinion to be glimpsed even at the moment the article was printed; indeed, he remarked in a note that the ideas in the article applied only to agriculture in the narrow sense of the word—which did not reflect **Quesnay's** true opinion—and he added that he "wished for a reply much more than he hoped for one." In the collection of **Quesnay's** economic writings, which he published

Other examples could still be given to demonstrate that, according to his complete economic works, **Quesnay** did not have exactly the same views as those attributed to him when taking as a basis his "most important" works known until now. But it follows, moreover, from the example cited, that it is an illusion to believe that one can learn to know **Quesnay's** system just as well through the works of his disciples as through those of the master himself.

On the contrary, the more one studies the countless writings of the physiocratic party, the more clearly one notices the essential divergences that exist between its members. In particular, nothing is less accurate than the statement by **Adam Smith** found in his critique reported above, consisting of saying "that the writers of this sect all follow, fundamentally and without any sensible variation, the doctrine of **Mr. Quesnay**;" and what further highlights **Smith's** carelessness is that he then describes as a "small book" the work *The Natural and Essential Order of Political Societies* by **Mercier de la Rivière**, a work in 2 volumes comprising a total of 900 duodecimo pages <note>original: "in-12"; a book size where each sheet is folded into 12 leaves, resulting in a portable but substantial volume.</note>, and to which he specifically refers the reader. It is true that the differences cited by **Dupont de Nemours** in his *Notice on the Economists*—which he placed at the head of the *Eulogy of Gournay* in his edition of the works of **Turgot**—are not accurate either. Regardless, one can only find **Quesnay’s** doctrine in its purity within the master himself, and it is also the master alone who can make known to us exactly the philosophical principles of his economic system. Several strictly logical consequences of certain fundamental principles, upon which the complete edifice stands or falls, are presented without connection by the disciples and consequently appear as paradoxes.

The study of the developments of the founder of the physiocratic system—which are only obscure if one has only a few parts before them—is made more attractive by the circumstance that one does not find there that tiresome enthusiasm of the disciples for the master. This was an enthusiasm that, for example, pushed the **Marquis de Mirabeau** to claim that the *Tableau économique* <note>original: *Tableau économique*; Quesnay's "Economic Table," a famous diagram showing how wealth flows through different classes of society.</note> is the third great invention of the human race after those of writing and money. And yet this enthusiasm generally only ma—

->XXIII<-

...appeared only when the writer’s own intellectual power began to decline.

Certainly, studying the economic works of **Quesnay** was no easy task, as some of them were difficult to find. The widespread error that the Versailles physician <note>François Quesnay (1694–1774) served as the consulting physician to King Louis XV at the Palace of Versailles before founding the "Physiocrat" school of economics.</note> wrote little on economic matters is clearly based on the fact that, in fields other than medicine, **Quesnay** produced no voluminous books. On economic questions, he only produced scattered studies and articles which, moreover, were not published under his own name. This explains, for example, why **Quesnay’s** contemporary disciple in Germany, **Mauvillon**, could state in his *Physiocratic Letters to Professor Dohm (1780)* <note>original German: *Physiokratische Briefe an den Herrn Professor Dohm*</note>:

> "In the physiocratic system, far from its inventor having written alone, it is precisely he who wrote the least."

**Blanqui**, in his *History of Political Economy (1838)*, expressed himself in the same vein, saying: "**Quesnay** wrote little and in a manner almost always sententious and obscure." And even in **Léonce de Lavergne’s** work on the *French Economists of the Eighteenth Century (1870)*, we find this surprising sentence: "Aside from his maxims, **Quesnay** wrote very little." We believe that thanks to the table of his works provided in the present volume, this claim will no longer be repeated. We hope at the same time to have contributed significantly to easing the study of the works of the founder of the first scientific system of political economy <note>The Physiocrats are often credited with creating the first rigorous "system" of economics, focusing on the circular flow of wealth and the primacy of agriculture.</note>.

It remains for us now to discuss the principles that guided us in the editing of this work.

Our first duty was to be complete. Indeed, there would have been no point in once again presenting the public with a simple selection of **Quesnay’s** works, since the edition by **E. Daire** <note>Eugène Daire's 1846 collection, *Physiocrates*, was the standard reference for decades but omitted many shorter or anonymous pieces.</note>, though meritorious for the time it appeared, is now considered insufficient precisely because it is incomplete. Consequently, we have searched fervently for every work written by **Quesnay** and have done our utmost to obtain them. We are certain that we have left no lead provided by physiocratic literature unexplored.

Another duty was accuracy. When it was not a matter of obvious printing errors, we reproduced the texts...

The present work appears at the moment when the most authoritative current representative of the history of economic literature in Germany, Wilhelm Roscher in Leipzig, celebrates the jubilee of his fiftieth year of a scientific career. By allowing ourselves to place upon the festive table this complete edition of the economic works of the man to whom the world owes the first scientific system of **political economy** <note>original: *économie politique*</note>, we express the hope that this jubilee—in which not only the scholars of Germany but also those from countries beyond its borders take part in spirit—may give a new impulse to historical literary studies in the field of political economy. It cannot be said that today these studies are devoted as much attention as they deserve. In Germany especially, it is practical questions of **social policy** <note>original: *politique sociale*</note> that now primarily attract the attention of young people working in the field of economic science. And, in the research so scholarly and meritorious being done on the past, the **history of economic conditions** is treated far more than the **history of theory**. At the same time, there is an effort to accomplish a revision of the fundamental principles of the science in accordance with the more advanced economic life of the present day. All of this is very heartening, but it does not exhaust the subject. If it is true that the theory transmitted to us no longer responds—and can no longer respond—to the requirements of the current time, because new elements of civilization have taken their place in the economic and social life of peoples, it is nonetheless true that we find no solid basis for establishing our own ideas except by connecting ourselves to the past and drawing from its intellectual treasures. <page-num>XVII</page-num>

questions that have long been at rest are suddenly reborn with a new vigor; and let us also observe, on the other hand, that ancient theories are often insufficient for our era only because they have been transmitted to us in an equally insufficient manner. Thus, alongside the necessity for a revision of fundamental principles, there arises the demand for a revision of **scientific tradition** <note>original: *tradition scientifique*; Oncken refers here to the historical record of scientific discovery and how past ideas are interpreted by later generations</note>. Tradition is and must likewise be in a state of continual movement; for as the necessities of the moment weigh heavily, sometimes upon one economic factor and sometimes upon another, there follows—for those **economic systems** <note>original: *systèmes économiques*</note> that have entered into history—a change in classification regarding their value in the present. Therefore, one must always rework the materials relating to them. No one would wish to claim that they have ever achieved something complete and conclusive in this regard; it can only be a matter of contributions to the general body of work. And by expressing the wish that the present volume be considered a modest contribution in this sense, we present it through these lines to the scholar whose jubilee we celebrate <note>Wilhelm Roscher, mentioned on the previous page</note>, as well as to the scientific public.

*Berne, October 1888.*

# FUNERAL ORATION
->OF<-
## MR. FRANÇOIS QUESNAY (¹),
->*delivered on the 20th of the same month, in the assembly of his disciples,*<-
->*by the Marquis* **DE MIRABEAU** *(²).*<-

->**GENTLEMEN,**<-

We have just lost our master: the true benefactor of men no longer belongs to the earth except through the memory and the forever-lasting effect of his benefits. It is for the common—

---

(1) Died December 16, 1774, at seven o’clock in the evening. (Original note.)
(2) This oration was, shortly thereafter, published in the first issue of the *New Economic Ephemerides* <note>original: *Nouvelles Ephémérides économiques*</note>, which appeared starting in January 1775. This monthly journal was the successor to the <term>Physiocratic</term> <note>Physiocracy was the first formal school of economics; its followers, like Quesnay, believed that a nation's wealth originated strictly from agriculture and land development.</note> organ *Ephemerides of the Citizen* <note>original: *Ephémérides du citoyen*</note>, which had ceased publication in 1772, and it was intended to support the administration of <term>Turgot</term> <note>Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot was a French economist and statesman who attempted to implement Physiocratic reforms as Controller-General of Finances.</note>. The editing had been resumed by the founder of the old *Ephemerides*, the Abbé Baudeau, and its publication was discontinued upon the fall of Turgot (July 1776). — One finds in the work *The Mirabeaus: New Studies on French Society in the 18th Century* <note>original: *Les Mirabeau. nouvelles études sur la société française au XVIIIᵉ siècle*</note>, by Louis de Loménie, Paris 1879, Vol. I, p. 335, a detailed account of the assembly in which the oration was read; here is that account:
> "On December 20, 1774, amidst the enthusiastic hopes born of a new reign, five months after Turgot entered the ministry, a fairly large number of people, in mourning attire, were gathered in the main salon of a mansion on the Rue Vaugirard. It was then, he added, “that Goliath's skull was split” (one can easily guess who is Goliath and who is David). From this second conversation, the doctor had conquered the first and most fanatical of his disciples. He had indeed conquered the doctor before having been conquered by him, since it will be remembered that it was Quesnay who, seduced by reading *The Friend of Men*, where he nevertheless recognized errors, had desired to confer with the author to correct and convert him.” A. ...said <note>Continuing the footnote from the previous page regarding the Physiocratic assemblies.</note>, sometimes turned into objects of ridicule by Bachaumont <note>Louis Petit de Bachaumont (1690–1771), a French writer known for his chronicles of Parisian life and gossip.</note> or Grimm <note>Friedrich Melchior, Baron von Grimm (1723–1807), a prominent journalist and diplomat in Enlightenment circles.</note>, and whose goal was to maintain the sacred fire among the followers of the science <note>In this context, "the science" refers to Physiocracy, often considered the first organized school of economic thought.</note>, to increase their number, and to attract distinguished foreigners traveling through Paris to the doctrine. That one is a habitual joke: they bring their own wine." — In the same year, he writes to one of his sons-in-law: "Our Tuesdays are becoming quite brilliant and are, consequently, very useful. You would have seen at the last one the Marshal de Broglie, the Duke de la Rochefaucauld, and many young notables." — The Marquis maintained these Tuesday assemblies for many years; he only gave them up under the influence of the discredit and ruin that weighed simultaneously upon his old age.... After dinner, they would read pieces intended for the *Ephemerides* <note>original: "Ephémérides du Citoyen," the official journal of the Physiocratic movement.</note> and discuss all the economic or political questions of the day."

Tears were forbidden in wise Egypt as soon as the judges had declared a man just and received into the bosom of the Gods. The public voice forbids us today from shedding them; a kind of joy concluded the ceremony of deification <note>original: "apothéose." The process of elevating a mortal to the rank of a god.</note>: antiquity would have placed our master above, far above Minos and Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, these were the legendary judges of the underworld, renowned for their absolute justice.</note>; and June 4th, the day of his birth, will be a day of celebration for posterity.

*If only that youth were now mine, which once was mine...* <note>original: "Si mihi quæ quondam fuerat .... si nunc foret illa juventa ...." A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* expressing a longing for the strength of one's younger years.</note> Why do I not have the same fire, the same ardor that he once did not disdain to inspire and guide! Why am I not what I once was, to render a worthy and just homage to him who wished, through constant and fatherly care, to devote me to some usefulness! How sweet it would be for me to show him to you at the head, not only of all philosophers, but also of all the benefactors of humanity; more studious, more industrious no doubt than Socrates, even more generous, for Socrates gave his disciples only his speeches, while our master enriched us with his own writings; wiser, finally, for Socrates made enemies: merit and truth find the seeds of enmity everywhere, but perfect merit yields to them in appearance and does not struggle against them; it feels that all contention is division and, consequently, a social disease.

Such were the ideas and character of our master. We may be told that his disciples hardly resemble him; it is for the future to show what society we might have disturbed, or rather which society will not owe to our master the homage of its own happiness. Socrates, they say, brought morality down from heaven; our master made it sprout upon the earth. The morality of heaven satisfies only privileged souls; that of the <term>net product</term> <note>original: "produit net." A central concept of Physiocracy referring to the surplus value produced by agriculture after all costs of production are deducted.</note> procures subsistence first for the children of men, prevents it from being snatched from them by violence and fraud, establishes its distribution, ensures its reproduction; and, shielding us from the constraints of imperious nature,

Everywhere he gathered the sparks from the torch of Prometheus; he reunited the scattered fragments in the hands of man, taught him how to illuminate his path on earth with them, and how to relate everything back to heaven, from whom alone he can hold everything. <meta>This page continues the Marquis de Mirabeau’s emotional tribute to François Quesnay. I will likely have little to say about his works, as mine are but the analysis of his own; but I will do justice to his memory: I will paint his moderation, his wisdom, his resignation, his virtues. I will show where he began, where he arrived, what use he made of his talents, his genius, and his favor; I will dispel the shadows that envy sought to cast over his career by making it a crime for him to have reassured a weak and frightened mind <note>This likely refers to Quesnay's role as the physician and advisor to King Louis XV, whom he attempted to guide toward reform.</note>, and thus blunted the murderous weapon that intrigue—hideous and ever active, the forerunner of calculated and prepared crimes—presents in all forms to any illegitimate authority. I will say what he was, what he could do, what he did for himself, for his own, for the unfortunate, for merit whether real or hoped for; what, above all, he abstained from doing, and in what a century, with such wit, perspicacity, and means; with what honest and concentrated firmness he suffered the sudden wind of a disgrace as audaciously stirred up as it was deeply meditated. (1) It is generally not known that the reversal which—through the appointment of Turgot <note>Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot (1727–1781), a reformist statesman and economist closely allied with the Physiocrats.</note> to the ministry—made Quesnay’s economic system dominant in France for some time, was fatal to the master’s personal position at court. Only the *Eulogy of Mirabeau* provides information on this subject, and it appears that the first ordinary physician <note>Quesnay’s official title at court.</note> was forced by a formal decree to retire and had thus fallen into complete disgrace. Was the cause due to an event that took place at the deathbed of Louis XV, as seems to be the case, or to another circumstance? This cannot be said with certainty. However, the profound aversion of Louis XVI <note>The grandson and successor of Louis XV, known for his more austere moral character.</note> for all persons who had a part in the intrigues of his grandfather’s mistresses is too well known for us to admit, with Mirabeau, that a powerful intrigue was necessary to bring about Quesnay's fall. One must suppose there is much truth in the expression used by the Bailli de Mirabeau <note>Jean-Antoine Riqueti, brother of the Marquis de Mirabeau.</note> to his elder brother: that Quesnay, "existing by the greatest of all abuses, cries out against abuses." Although we must pay tribute to the personal integrity of the King's physician at Versailles, and although we must even consider as exemplary in its kind the unalterable fidelity with which he remained attached to his benefactress, the Marquise de Pompadour <note>Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson (1721–1764), the powerful mistress of Louis XV who protected Quesnay and allowed the Physiocrats to meet in her apartments.</note> (see below for information on this subject drawn from the memoirs of Madame du Hausset and Marmontel), it is nonetheless indisputable that posterity does him no great honor for his liaison with the ill-famed mistress of Louis XV. It is understandable that Quesnay’s disciples sought to hide both his position regarding the Marquise de Pompadour and his final disgrace. If we did not possess the memoirs of Madame du Hausset, we would know almost nothing regarding this position. And as for Quesnay’s retirement, we find nothing on this subject in all Physiocratic literature besides the indication mentioned above. However, the fact itself was confirmed by a notice on July 26, 1774, published in the *Göttinger Gelehrten Anzeigen* <note>The "Göttingen Scholarly Announcements," one of the oldest and most prestigious academic journals in the German language.</note>, and composed in the following terms:

> "After the important service of a first personal physician had remained vacant for several years, the new King on May 7th (the death of Louis XV did not occur until May 10th) filled the same again with the famous Mr. Lieutaud, whose important works we have several times announced. Mr. Quesnay, who was personal physician *en survivance* <note>A legal term meaning he held the right to succeed to the position upon the death or retirement of the incumbent.</note>, was left in his rest as outdated, and in his place Mr. de la Sone, the Queen's personal physician, was promoted." <note>original: "Versailles. Nachdem seit verschiedenen Jahren die wichtige Bedienung eines ersten Leibarztes erledigt geblieben war, hat der neue König am 7. Mai... dieselbe mit dem berühmten Herrn Lieutaud wieder besetzt... Herr Quesnay, welcher Leibarzt en survivance war, ist als veraltet in seiner Ruhe gelassen, und an seine Stelle Herr de la Sone... befördert worden."</note>

(Compare, regarding Quesnay’s official position at court, note 2, page 15.) It is quite possible that this retirement—which, according to the words of Mirabeau, deeply wounded the man who was its object—also contributed to hastening his death, which took place a few months later. Whatever the case, it follows from the preceding that the sunset of the life of the creator of Physiocracy <note>The first modern school of economics, which argued that the wealth of nations was derived solely from the value of "land agriculture."</note> was by no means as serene as one might be inclined to believe given the appointment of Turgot (July 19) to a ministerial seat. A. O.

How, finally, his soul—always superior not only to human misfortunes but even to those of nature itself—was always peaceful, gentle, strong, steady, cheerful, active and, above all, wisely and profoundly resigned in the midst of suffering and the infirmity of old age <term>caducité: the state of being physically or mentally weakened by age</term>.

But sentiment and truth carry me away and compel me; and my master, who seems almost living still, sees and hears me. It is likewise for me to hear him; he says to me: "I have lived, but you have yet to live; it is through your works that you must honor my memory and justify my lessons." He repeats to me: *Get wisdom, acquire prudence; seize it and it will exalt you.* <note>Original Latin: "Posside sapientiam, acquire prudentiam; arripe illam et exaltabit te." A paraphrase of the biblical Book of Proverbs, 4:7-8.</note> O my master, your principles were within everyone's reach, but the same cannot be said for your lessons and your examples: your disciples will take from you only the wisdom of selflessness and the prudence of calculations. It is this—this constant and unflagging zeal—that they desire to achieve, that they hope to preserve: *seize it*. Let the common crowd of loudmouths denounce them as fiery and fanatical sectarians; let them add to the list of so-called factions a partisan name <note>Mirabeau is likely referring to the labels "Physiocrats" or "Economists," which were often used as slurs by critics in 18th-century France.</note> that custom attributes to them—factions which envy, opposition, restlessness, and idleness create and perpetuate, just as they brought them to life in the capital of disdain and glamour, of pretensions and ridicule, of pleasures and displeasures. Let that dwelling-place of false calculations, false judgments, false reports, false echoes, and false certainties declare them enthusiasts and dangerous. What does it matter, after all, to the earth, which has been so patient for so long in providing a field for all the delusions of our little species, and in restoring by night what our vertigo destroyed by day? What does it matter to the great order <note>Mirabeau refers to the "Natural Order," the Physiocratic belief that there is a divinely intended physical and moral system for society.</note> that opens its paternal bosom to us, ready to set us back on the path the moment our habitual suicide—now stripped of the rags and tatters of our own creation—reveals itself in all its deformity? What does it matter to that order, I say, that at the very time when all of Europe is waking up to the voice of truth, listening, believing, or at least doubting, and seeking to know and be instructed, a few "lost children" of frivolity and envy—and perhaps some emissaries of monopoly and corruption—attempt to ridicule or calumniate them?

Everything moves, everything obeys, sooner or later, the primitive impulse it received from nature. The first rays of sudden light,

[the light of his principles] provokes the cries and whistles of the sinister birds of darkness, especially when its radiance shows itself and rises in the midst of their habitual haunts. But in vain do these hideous enemies hurl clouds of filth and dust; in vain do some among them, more daring, seem to seek out the torch and defy it to the attack. The calculation and the distinction between investments <note>original: "avances," referring to capital invested in land and equipment</note> and the **net product** <term>produit net: the surplus value created by agricultural production after all costs and expenses are paid—a central concept of Quesnay’s system</term> are no longer a secret for the poor, fascinated human race; everything depended upon that. Then, and only then, will we no longer speak of **economists** <term>économistes: the original term for the Physiocrats, who were often criticized as a "sect" for their rigid devotion to Quesnay’s "Natural Order"</term>; and when man—instructed by man, restrained by man, aided by man, respected and cherished by man, who will see in him the useful and necessary agent of his own interest—walks in the way of the Lord God his creator and remains faithful to the law of the **natural order**, like the sun and the reptile, then, and only then, will the greatest possible number of dissidents return to the active crowd of men who have no concern but their own affairs, in the heart of concord and peace; and so too will those dangerous sectarians who call themselves the disciples of the **universal benefactor** of the entire earth. They shall pass away, but the memory of their respectable master shall remain forever. Man, despite himself, always imprinted with some remains of the seal of his origin—man, I say, is not ungrateful; he fills the registers of his memory only too much. In the vast collections of his frivolous or depraved annals, the page would be very light indeed if it admitted only the names of his benefactors; but that very discernment must be born from the knowledge of his true interests, and it is one more gift for which he will owe homage to our **teacher**.

May this happy time be accelerated by our labors and our vigils! But today, and at the very moment when our master leaves us, he belongs to future races, he takes possession of posterity . . . . ; but he leaves us. What function, My [Gentlemen]—

<meta>This page continues the funeral oration for François Quesnay, the founder of the Physiocratic school of economics. Having previously described the inevitable victory of Quesnay's "natural order" over ignorance, the Marquis de Mirabeau now turns to a personal and emotional appeal to his fellow disciples, urging them to turn their grief into a commitment to the school’s mission.</meta>

Gentlemen, what a duty it is for my heart to repeat to you that he is leaving us, and that his very soul forbids us from being discouraged by it. O my friend, both stern and steadfast, witness to my docility, guarantor of my honesty; O my counsel, O my guide, who from now on, in major circumstances, will organize my ideas and teach me, by his example, patience and resignation? O my Master, how much I have taken from you, and how poor and destitute I find myself; and yet you leave me as the leader, in a sense, or at least the elder of your grieving children: let the winds and storms come then to return to us, through necessity, the action and courage that it is impossible not to have lost . . . But where does a grief unworthy of its subject carry me; it is not with tears that one honors the memory of great men: all weakness is banished from their veneration; their heroic soul (and his especially) always disdained any homage other than the efforts one makes to imitate them. Let us occupy ourselves no longer, Gentlemen, with anything but this task—more meritorious even than it is painful—and let us renew, in this moment of anguish and tenderness, the internal oath we made to consecrate our labors to the instruction of our fellow men and to the development of the science <note>Mirabeau refers here to "the science" of Physiocracy, which held that social and economic laws were as fixed and discoverable as the laws of physics.</note>, which must one day render societies peaceful and prosperous, and men reasonable and virtuous.

Venerable bust which represents to us the features of our common master, the image of the vigilant and tender father whom we have all lost, it is before you, it is upon the altar raised to domestic charity <note>Mirabeau uses "domestic charity" to describe the intimate, familial bonds that united the inner circle of the Physiocratic school.</note> that we swear to be forever faithful to the vow of universal fraternity that our conscience—enlightened by the lessons of the excellent man whom you portray for us—made us pronounce. O my Master who hears us, if it were only necessary to extend and perpetuate your memory forever, our tender zeal would find nothing difficult, nothing rebuffing; but you would come back to life to repel praise if it were to be sterile. To will the good, to know the good, to do the good, to enlighten, to instruct, and to restore order: that is the only homage worthy of being offered to you; it shall be the worship of our entire lives. Deign to receive this solemn oath and offer it to the author of all good and all virtue <note>original: "l'auteur de tout bien," a common Enlightenment-era reference to God as the Creator.</note>, to whom you now return all the profit produced by the talents He gave you to develop during your career. Deign, deign, from the heights of heaven, to smile once more upon our labors and our tears, while my trembling hand offers you here on earth the first-fruits of the laurel which shall rise over your grave and which shall never perish!

# EULOGY
### OF
# QUESNAY

->BY<-

## JEAN-PAUL GRAND-JEAN DE FOUCHY

->*permanent secretary of the academy of sciences* ($^1$).<-

François Quesnay, esquire, counselor to the king, first ordinary physician, and first consulting physician ($^2$) to His Majesty; of <unclear>the</unclear> Acadé—

(1) This eulogy is reproduced in *The History of the Royal Academy of Sciences*, year 1774, published in Paris in 1778. — Grand-Jean de Fouchy, an astronomer, was a member since 1731 and the permanent secretary of the Academy since 1743. In this latter capacity and according to custom, he was responsible for delivering the eulogy for deceased members. Grand-Jean de Fouchy was by no means a physiocrat <note>Physiocracy was an economic theory developed by Quesnay suggesting that the wealth of nations derived solely from agriculture.</note>; this is why his remarks on Quesnay's economic studies are very brief, and are, moreover, not entirely accurate. Furthermore, almost all the data contained in the three following eulogies must be examined and weighed with care, given not only that they often contradict each other, but also that they are sometimes of a peculiar nature. **A. O.** <note>These initials refer to Auguste Oncken, the editor of this 1888 collection of Quesnay's works.</note>

(2) *The Royal Almanac*, a political yearbook of the Old Regime <term>Ancien Régime: the monarchic, aristocratic, social, and political system established in the Kingdom of France from the 15th century until the Revolution of 1789</term>, indicates, for this period, the following hierarchy of the king's physicians. At the head is the "first physician to the king," who is considered the actual doctor to the king in the event of illness. Next comes the "first ordinary physician to the king," who apparently had to supervise the king's daily regimen from a hygienic perspective (*a*). The third category consists of the "physicians serving by quarter at court." Their number averaged eight, and

(*a*) This conclusion can at least be drawn from information provided by Capefigue (*Madame de Pompadour*, Paris, 1858), regarding the king's suppers at Choisy. "Never was more than a single wine served for the king: chilled and iced champagne—that pleasant stimulant—and for cold and sickly stomachs, the wines of Volnay and Clos-Vougeot. Bordeaux, brought into fashion by the Marshal de Richelieu, was excluded from the king's suppers as nauseating and indigestible, according to the opinion of Quesnay." **A. O.**

<meta>This page continues the formal biographical eulogy of François Quesnay by Grand-Jean de Fouchy. It picks up mid-word from the previous page's mention of "Academies," moving from his official titles into the specific details of his birth and family origins. The editor, Auguste Oncken (A.O.), provides extensive commentary on the discrepancies found in historical records regarding Quesnay's official court status and his humble or professional ancestry.</meta>

...royal academies of sciences of France and England, that of Lyon, and former permanent secretary of the Royal Academy of Surgery, was born in Mérey (¹) near Montfort-l'Amaury, on June 4, 1694, to Nicolas Quesnay, a lawyer (²) in parliament <note>In the French Old Regime, a *parlement* was a powerful provincial appellate court rather than a legislative body.</note>, who practiced his profession at Montfort, and Louise Giroux.

A remark in the *Royal Almanac* <term>Almanach royal: An official annual directory of the French administration, listing the royal family, high officials, and court appointments.</term> says of them: "The ordinary physicians of the king, serving by quarter <note>Physicians at court often rotated their service in three-month shifts, or 'quarters.'</note>, hold free consultations at the Louvre every Tuesday of each week, except for feast days, from three o'clock in the afternoon until five." The majority of them resided in Paris. In the fourth category, there are the "consulting physicians of the king," some residing in Versailles, others in Paris. This section contained an average of four names. Finally, the list ends with the "other consulting physicians of the king." These are physicians whom the king charges with special missions either in Paris or in Versailles. The *Royal Almanac* indicates, in this section, the name of Quesnay for the first time in 1750, following changes that had already taken place during the course of the year 1749. Two other names also appear there, and while these are followed by various titles, Quesnay is simply listed as follows: "Quesnay at court." This is the period when Quesnay left the service of the Duke of Villeroi to enter that of the Marquise de Pompadour <note>Jeanne Antoinette Poisson, Madame de Pompadour, was the official chief mistress of King Louis XV and a highly influential patron of the Enlightenment.</note>. In 1752, his promotion to the title of "first ordinary physician" and "consulting physician to the king" took place. The *Royal Almanac* does not cite the dignity of "first consulting physician to the king" under a special title. Members of this category are mentioned in order of seniority. See also note 2, page 31.

As for the title of counselor to the king, Quesnay’s name is completely missing from the list of members of the Council of State published annually by the *Royal Almanac*. In other official lists, this title is also not given to him anywhere, which did, however, occur for some of his colleagues or predecessors. **A. O.**

(1) The uncertainties begin already concerning his place of birth. Whether the Count of Albon writes *Méré* (the now-accepted spelling) instead of *Mérey* is only a difference in orthography. On the other hand, Romance de Mesmon names the village of *Ecquevilly*—not explicitly as Quesnay's place of birth, but rather as his parents' place of residence. This author was then likely followed by Lord Crawford, the first editor of the *Memoirs of Madame du Hausset*, who in his biographical sketch of Quesnay formally designates Ecquevilly as the place of birth. **A. O.**

(2) There are also discrepancies regarding the father's profession. While de Fouchy and Albon agree that the father was a lawyer, but lived with his family in a small country village, Romance de Mesmon suggests that the father and mother were simple farmers. It appears, here too, that Lord Crawford only emphasized this more strongly by saying in his own words, "son of a laborer." Curiously, this indication is also found in the *Notice on the Economists* <term>Économistes: The name originally used for the Physiocrats, the first organized school of economic thought, which Quesnay founded.</term> that Dupont de Nemours added to the works of Turgot, which he edited (1808);

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, moving from the details of his birth and parentage into a description of his family life and early upbringing. The text explores the contrasting temperaments of his parents—his father, a selfless lawyer, and his mother, a practical farm manager—and how this environment shaped Quesnay's early connection to agriculture and his intellectual development.</meta>

Although Mr. and Mrs. Quesnay lived in the greatest harmony, their tastes were nevertheless quite different: the father, a man of law, devoted himself entirely to his profession, but he practiced it in a very singular way. He and the king’s prosecutor of Montfort, with whom he was bound in friendship, were on the lookout, so to speak, for any legal matters susceptible to a settlement. As long as they found the parties involved to be reasonable, they never failed to arrange an amicable resolution. One can easily judge that their goal was not self-interest <note>In this context, "interest" refers to the pursuit of legal fees or personal profit.</note>. To the shame of humanity, there is commonly much more to be demanded from passion than to be hoped for from gratitude.

These generous occupations absorbed Mr. Quesnay the father entirely, and he hardly meddled at all in the governance of his house, nor in the education of his children, for which he relied absolutely on his wife.

She, on the contrary, was lively and active, never losing sight for a single moment of the interior of her household or the administration of a country estate which belonged to them, and where a wise economy <note>In the 18th-century sense, "economy" (économie) referred to the careful management of a household or estate.</note> had established their home. The first objects that presented themselves to the eyes of the young Quesnay were thus the labors of agriculture; the first words he heard pronounced were terms of that art, in the tasks of which he employed his early years. His mother, believing she could do nothing better than to raise her son according to her own principles, destined him solely to replace her when she would no longer be in a state to hold the reins of the house. What a wrong she would have done to her son and to his fellow citizens if a poor education (¹) <note>The author uses "education" here to mean "upbringing" or "vocational direction."</note> could absolutely stifle genius!

Fortunately, nature had provided for it: the active and piercing mind of the young Quesnay enabled him to analyze everything he saw. He observed facts, he penetrated their relationships, and he knew how to draw sure rules from them. He had, without any assistance, put himself in a position to begin reading in the "great book of nature."

---

One reads there (before the eulogy of Gournay): "Mr. Quesnay, born on a farm, the son of a landowner and skilled cultivator," etc. But his pen was no doubt driven by the mania for making Quesnay appear as an accomplished cultivator from his youth. In this regard, one must also rely on the indications given by de Fouchy and d'Albon, for they agree with the other information provided about Quesnay's father, which comes in part from the son himself. — A. O. <note>Auguste Oncken, the editor of this volume.</note>
