<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, specifically following the account of his early childhood on a farm. The previous page ended by noting that his early environment was defined by the labors of agriculture, which provided the context for his unique path to literacy.</meta>

It was indeed the only book in which he could educate himself, for the truth of history does not allow us to hide that at eleven years old he did not yet know how to read; the first book that fell into his hands was the *Country House* <note>original: "Maison rustique". This was a famous 16th-century agricultural manual by Charles Estienne and Jean Liébault, which remained a standard reference for two centuries.</note> by Liébault. The desire to draw knowledge from it was almost his only teacher, and he managed to read it fluently with the little help he could get from the household gardener.

This first reading could not fail to make a mind as upright as his feel what fruit he could draw from the works of those who had preceded him. The desire to learn made him not only devour the books written in his language that were within his reach, but it also made him brave all the thorns of grammar: he learned, almost without a teacher, the Latin and Greek that were becoming necessary for him to draw from the treasures of antiquity.

One would have difficulty imagining how far his passion went: he was sometimes seen leaving Mérey at sunrise, during the long summer days, coming to Paris to buy a book, returning to Mérey while reading it, and arriving there in the evening, having walked twenty leagues <term>A "league" (lieue) was a measure of distance, roughly 4 kilometers; walking twenty leagues (80 km) in a single day while reading is an extraordinary feat emphasized by the biographer to show Quesnay's dedication.</term> on foot and read the book he had gone to get; the extreme desire to enlighten himself made the fatigues and inconveniences of a journey of this kind disappear in his eyes.

It is easy to judge how much such fortunate dispositions must have been pleasing to his father, who then saw in him all the hope of his family; thus he never ceased to encourage him: *the temple of virtue is*, he would say to him, *supported by four columns: honor and reward, shame and punishment*; it was not difficult to guess which one the young Quesnay would choose for support, and his conduct has left no doubt on this matter.

Despite the rapid progress he was making in the vast career of the sciences, his mind was already too mature not to perceive that it was impossible for a single man to—if I may speak thus—pursue all human knowledge simultaneously, and that it was absolutely necessary to choose a single science to the study of which he could devote himself entirely. The desire to be useful to his fellow countrymen determined him in favor of the **art of healing** <note>The "art of healing" (l'art de guérir) is a traditional term for medicine.</note>, which offered him both a vast field for acquiring useful and satisfying knowledge and—what touched his heart, truly a friend to humanity, even more deeply—provided him with countless opportunities to make this knowledge useful to his fellow citizens.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, following his self-taught mastery of Latin and Greek and his extraordinary dedication to obtaining books from Paris while still living in the countryside.</meta>

This laudable project, however, faced difficulties from his mother; she saw with regret her entire system overturned, and maternal love painted for her in the most vivid colors the dangers a young man of sixteen would face away from the paternal home: this fear, however, which would have been only too justified with many others, should not have alarmed her for her son; the young man’s zeal for acquiring the knowledge he lacked had become a violent passion that imperiously demanded the sacrifice of all others: it was therefore necessary to yield and let the young Quesnay depart.

As he had determined to begin with the profession of surgery, he placed himself with a surgeon established in his neighborhood to learn the first elements, believing him capable of teaching them; he was mistaken, for he was only able to learn how to perform bloodletting. But if this master was of little help to young Quesnay, the latter was in return very useful to him; this sort of master was not even "received" in Paris <note>meaning he was not officially licensed or admitted to the professional guild</note>, which had jurisdiction over his place of residence, and what is even worse, he was in no condition to be. The young Quesnay arrived quite opportunely; while the young man was away, the master found a way to seize the notebooks that Quesnay was writing for his own instruction and presented them in Paris to the lieutenant of the King's first surgeon as lessons he was giving to his student: the lieutenant found them excellent and, without any other examination, delivered his letters of mastership <term>lettres de maîtrise: formal documents granting the right to practice a trade as a master within the guild system</term> (1): it was Quesnay whom he was admitting, without knowing it, under the name of the other.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay. The previous page ended by describing how Quesnay’s first master in the countryside used Quesnay’s own notes to deceptively obtain his mastership from the King's first surgeon.</meta>

Although M. Quesnay was unaware of this deception, he soon noticed how little he could rely on the knowledge of this so-called master, and he left him to come to Paris to take advantage of all the resources that are found there in such abundance.

...two new provosts <note>administrative officers of the guild</note> each year, and that of the receiver <note>the treasurer</note> only every two years; all three by a majority of votes in the general assembly.

The 4th title is for the calling of assemblies, the order of sessions, and the manner of giving and collecting votes. The King's first surgeon is the natural-born president of the assemblies; his lieutenant presides in his absence; and in the absence of the lieutenant, the most senior of the provosts currently in office.

The 5th title speaks of those who must compose the general assemblies; the 6th, of those who compose the council assemblies; and the 7th, of the election of the latter.

The 8th title deals with the rights, immunities, prerogatives, and functions of the community <note>the guild or professional body of surgeons</note>. The art of surgery is declared there to be a liberal art <note>this was a major status shift, moving surgery from a manual "trade" to an intellectual "profession" alongside medicine and law</note>, with the granting of all the privileges of the liberal arts. The coat of arms of the community—which is azure with three gold boxes, two at the top and the other at the base, with a gold fleur-de-lis in the center—are confirmed to it; and the masters of Paris are given the right to be admitted as associates in all the communities of the kingdom without new examination and without paying anything, with seniority dating from the day of their reception in the Paris guild.

The 9th title specifies those who may practice surgery in the city and suburbs of Paris; which is only permitted to masters or to associates admitted into the community, either through the "grand masterpiece" or through the "minor experience" <term>légère expérience: a simplified qualification process for certain practitioners</term>.

The 10th title speaks of apprentices, those aspiring to mastership, and the qualities one must have to be admitted to the grand masterpiece <term>grand chef-d'œuvre: the final technical project and series of exams required to become a Master Surgeon</term>. No master may have more than one apprentice at a time; the apprenticeship cannot be less than two years without interruption; no one can be an aspirant for the grand masterpiece unless he is the son of a master, or a master's apprentice, or if he has served one of the masters for six consecutive years, or several masters for seven years. In case of competition, the sons of masters take the first place, following the seniority of their father; then the apprentices, and then the assistants and servants of the masters.

In the 11th title, the acts that compose the grand masterpiece are explained: these acts are the matriculation, the trial, the first examination, the four weeks, the final examination, and the taking of the oath. The matriculation is the registration of the aspirant’s name in the community register as admitted to the masterpiece, which is only granted to him after he has been judged sufficient and capable by a summary examination. The questions of the first examination are conducted by nine masters chosen by the first surgeon, and those of the last by at least twelve, drawn by lot. The "four weeks" are: the first on osteology <note>the study of bones</note>, the second on anatomy, the third on bloodletting <note>the surgical practice of withdrawing blood to treat illness</note>, and the fourth and last on medicines—during which the aspirant sustains various acts, performs several demonstrations, and composes various medica...

ments, and responds to several questions put to him by the four provosts in office. Finally, in the last act, called the reception, or taking of the oath, the applicant is questioned by the first surgeon, or his lieutenant, regarding some disease or surgical operation, about which he is required to provide a written report on the spot; once his report is read and approved, he is received and takes the oath.

The 12th title deals with the minor examination <note>original: "légère expérience," a specific tier of testing for professional qualification</note>, which consists of two examinations held on two different days: one on theory and the other on operations.

The 13th title concerns the aggregated members <note>associates</note> of the community <note>the professional guild</note>, and the manner of aggregating and receiving them. Those who may be aggregated are the King’s surgeons, those of the royal family, the four barber-surgeons who follow the court at the nomination of the Grand Provost; the eight surgeons serving in the Great Artillery; the principal surgeons of the Royal Hospital of the Invalides who have served there for six years, etc. After being received, all of these form a single body with the community, enjoying the same privileges, subject to the same policing, governed by the same statutes, and ruled by the same regulations.

Talk of the experts for hernia bandages is found in the 14th title, and of the reception of master midwives in the 15th. Regarding the former, they are forbidden from performing any operation or incision under any pretext whatsoever; they are permitted only to apply their bandages. No applicant can be admitted to the status of expert for bandages without the consent of the King’s first physician, and unless he has served two years under one of the master surgeons or one of the experts then established in Paris. In the examination he must undergo, the questioning is conducted by the first surgeon, or his lieutenant, and by the four provosts in office. Finally, he must pay the fees set by article 126 of the statutes. Concerning the reception of midwives, they can only be received if they are daughters of mistresses <note>master-midwives</note> or apprentices—specifically, having served three years under the mistresses or three months at the Hôtel-Dieu <note>the primary hospital of Paris</note>. Their examination is conducted by the first surgeon, or his lieutenant, the four provosts in office, and the four sworn midwives of the Châtelet <note>the royal administrative and judicial headquarters of Paris</note>, in the presence of the Dean of the Faculty of Medicine, the two physicians of the Châtelet, the Dean of the community, and eight masters. The fees they must pay are set by article 127 of the statutes.

The fees that must be paid for receptions and aggregations are set by the eight articles of the 16th title.

Finally, the 17th and last title establishes the general police <note>regulatory oversight and public order</note> that must be observed in the city and suburbs of Paris by all those who practice surgery, or who are bound by the execution of the statutes and regulations; and to ensure enforcement, inspections by the provosts in office are mandated, even in privileged places <note>districts normally exempt from certain royal or guild jurisdictions</note>. This new work served as recreation for him, and he made such progress in it that portraits by his hand have been seen that were very life-like, and he had drawn and engraved most of the human bones in a manner perfect enough that these works could be acknowledged by the most skilled experts in this genre.

His courses being completely finished, it was now only a matter of putting the enlightenment he had just acquired to the service of his fellow citizens. With this in view, he formed the project of establishing himself at Mantes <note>A town on the Seine, west of Paris, known today as Mantes-la-Jolie</note> and, to achieve this, he presented himself to the surgeons of that city to be admitted to the ordinary examinations. His reputation, which had preceded him there, ought to have smoothed away all difficulties; it had quite the opposite effect. The surgeons of Mantes thought they saw a dangerous competitor in this candidate and refused him absolutely. Armed with the formal record of their refusal, Mr. Quesnay came to Paris to be received for the city of Mantes; he was received with the highest praise and obtained his letters <note>Professional certification or license</note> on August 9, 1718. It was also during this same time that he married Jeanne-Catherine Dauphin, daughter of a merchant of the "Six Corps" <note>The "Six Corps" were the most powerful and elite merchant guilds of Paris, representing trades such as clothiers, grocers, and jewelers.</note> of Paris.

The celebrated Mr. Silva published a book on bloodletting <note>original: "saignée"; a common medical practice of the time involving the withdrawal of blood to cure illness.</note> in 1727; this book was received with all the applause due to the reputation of the author. Mr. Quesnay dared to notice errors in it and wrote a critique based on the laws of hydrostatics <note>The branch of physics dealing with fluids at rest and the pressure they exert.</note>. Several of his friends, to whom he entrusted his plan to publish it—among others the celebrated Father Bougeant—did their best to discourage him. The latter specifically, being a friend to both parties, represented to Mr. Quesnay how disadvantageous it would be for a simple provincial surgeon to struggle against one of the "coryphées" <note>A term borrowed from Greek drama, here meaning a leader or preeminent figure in the field.</note> of Parisian medicine, almost unanimously recognized as the lawgiver in this area. Mr. Quesnay responded to this imposing picture only by praying Father Bougeant to be so kind as to read his manuscript. Mr. Silva, relying perhaps a bit too much on the superiority of his own enlightenment <note>A reference to Silva's high standing in the intellectual and medical circles of the Enlightenment.</note>, was content to return the manuscript with a kind of disdain. However, barely had Father Bougeant <note>Guillaume-Hyacinthe Bougeant (1690–1743), a Jesuit historian and author who acted as an intermediary.</note> departed when he wished to renew negotiations; but it was no longer the right time, as the manuscript had been returned to Mr. Quesnay. Nevertheless, Mr. Silva found a way to persuade the Marshal de Noailles to arrange a meeting at his home between the two contenders in the presence of several people capable of judging this dispute. Mr. Silva, always stiffened by his reputation and his alleged superiority, thought he could overawe Mr. Quesnay with a magisterial tone and a sort of ironic mockery; but the "surgeon from Mantes" was not swayed by brilliant rhetoric. He soon won the support of all those present, and it was necessary to grant Mr. Quesnay the freedom to publish his work. We will pass over in silence the delay caused by the royal censor, a friend of Mr. Silva, who held the manuscript for nearly a year; but finally, Mr. Quesnay obtained express orders from the Chancellor d'Aguesseau <note>Henri François d'Aguesseau (1668–1751), a legendary Chancellor of France known for his judicial reforms.</note>, and the manuscript was finally recovered, approved, and printed (1).

Mr. Silva, irritated by this publication which he regarded as a kind of assault, wanted to overwhelm his adversary with a thunderous response. With this view, he several times gathered at his home the most famous mathematicians <note>original: "géomètres"; at the time, this term often referred to mathematicians and scientists in general.</note> of this Academy who had assisted him in the calculations upon which his first work was based. But after having carefully read and examined Mr. Quesnay's critique, it was decided that it should remain unanswered. Apparently, Mr. Silva adopted this decision in good faith, for at his death many years after this event, no trace of a projected response was found in his papers. It was around this same time that he was admitted into the Society of Arts, which then existed in Paris with the King's permission and under the protection of the late Count of Clermont, a prince of the blood <note>A "prince of the blood" (prince du sang) was a person legitimately descended in the male line from a sovereign.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of François Quesnay’s relocation from Mantes to Paris. Having secured Quesnay’s willingness to move, his patron, the King’s first surgeon M. de la Peyronie, now works to overcome the legal and institutional hurdles required to integrate a provincial surgeon into the elite Parisian medical establishment.</meta>

Mr. de la Peyronie still had one difficulty to overcome. Mr. Quesnay, however worthy he might be, was not a member of the Paris College of Surgery <note>The *Collège de Chirurgie* was the professional guild that regulated surgical practice in the capital; membership was strictly controlled.</note>. He could not decently propose that Quesnay enter through the ordinary route; to remove this final obstacle, on August 3, 1737, he had him appointed to a post as an **ordinary surgeon to the king**, within the Provostry of the Household <note>The *prévôté de l’hôtel* was a judicial and administrative department of the King's court; this appointment was a legal "shortcut" to grant Quesnay elite status.</note>. This office gave him the legal right of *aggregation* <note>The formal process of being admitted into a professional body or guild.</note> to the College of Surgery, and shortly thereafter led to him obtaining the patent of <term>royal professor of the schools</term> <note>A prestigious teaching title within the surgical faculty.</note>, specifically for the branch of surgical medications (¹).

The desires of the first surgeon were thus satisfied: Mr. Quesnay was named secretary of the Academy of Surgery, and he did not delay in justifying the choice that had been made, by publishing the first volume of the *Memoirs* (²) of this company, at the head—

We can even assert that the utility of this work is not limited to instructing those destined for surgery; there is no amateur of any other science who could not find profit in it.

After some general reflections on the obstacles that seem most to oppose the advancement of the sciences, he enters more specifically into the subject matter and develops the principal rules that must guide those who apply themselves to the art of healing. Observation and experience <note>In the 18th century, "experience" often referred specifically to experimental testing and clinical trials.</note> are the two guides he offers them; through the former, one unravels the often obscure progress of nature; through the latter, one interrogates it and succeeds in wresting away its secrets; neither should ever be separated from the other. Observation without experience can only produce an uncertain theory; experience without observation yields only a confused heap of disconnected facts, more likely to lead to error than to the truth. Joined together, they lead there surely, and without them there is neither science nor art. Applying this principle then to surgery, he carefully discards arbitrary and unfounded opinions, mere likelihoods, and possibilities; he admits only knowledge supported by causes and the signs that allow them to be recognized. In a word, he traces in this work the plan for a luminous theory and a safe, enlightened practice; he highlights the merit of the great men who distinguished themselves in this useful and brilliant career, among whose number it would be too unjust to refuse him, after his death, a distinguished place. The limits prescribed for our eulogies have forced us to extremely shorten the notice we have just given of this piece, which is interesting for all those who love or cultivate the sciences.

This same volume contains, besides several separate observations, four memoirs by Mr. Quesnay.

In a second memoir, he investigates, based on his observations, the different cases in which it is necessary to increase the number of trepan crowns, and shows, through remarkable examples, that the skull can be successfully opened across a large area whenever the case requires it.

These four memoirs are, as we can see, a continuous dissertation on head wounds (¹); it would seem that Mr. Quesnay wished to give, in this same volume, an example of the application of the rules he had provided in his preface.

The lawsuit that arose almost immediately after the publication of this volume, between the Faculty of Medicine and the College of Surgeons, put Mr. Quesnay’s capacity to a new test; the latter believed they had a sure resource in his talents, and they were not mistaken; he took the greatest part not only in the polemical works, but also in the legal briefs <note>original: "mémoires juridiques"</note> that appeared during the seven-year interval that this great affair lasted; the surgeon became an antiquarian, a legal consultant, and a historian, and in all these capacities rendered the most essential services to his company <note>In this context, his "company" refers to the professional guild or corporation of surgeons.</note>. In the conclusions of the memoir, we read: "The public has its very life to defend in the disputes between physicians and surgeons; the latter, on the contrary, are fighting for very important interests.... Public interest is therefore truly the sole object of the decision in the disputes between physicians and surgeons; and this interest is of the utmost importance." The article *Surgeon* <note>original: "Chirurgien"</note> in the *Encyclopedia* <note>The famous *Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers*, edited by Diderot and d’Alembert.</note> of d'Alembert and Diderot provides detailed information on the specific subject of this struggle. According to this article, the royal patent of 1731, by which the Royal Academy of Surgery was founded, had granted the community of Saint-Côme <term>Saint-Côme</term> <note>The professional guild of surgeons in Paris, named after Saint Cosmas, one of the patron saints of surgeons.</note> various rights that brought the members of this community closer to the status of physicians.

"This law," expresses the article in question, "washed them of the ignominy <note>This refers to the historically low status of surgeons, who were previously grouped with barbers because they performed manual procedures.</note> that covered them: by breaking the contract of union with the barbers, it restored surgeons to the primitive state of their art, and to all the rights, privileges, and prerogatives they enjoyed by the authority of the laws before this union. The Faculty of Medicine disputed the prerogatives the surgeons wished to claim for themselves, and it sought to portray the re-establishment of letters <note>Meaning academic or scholarly study.</note> within the field of surgery as an innovation detrimental to the public good and even to the progress of surgery. The university rose up against the surgeons, claiming the exclusive right to teach. The surgeons responded to all the objections made against them. They proved against the university that a profession founded on consistent legislation authorized them to give, wherever they saw fit, public lessons on the art and science of surgery; that they had always fully enjoyed the right to teach publicly within the university; that surgery being a profound and most essential science, it could only be taught fully and safely by surgeons; and that since surgeons had always been part of the university, the teaching of this science had always belonged to the university. From this, the surgeons concluded that the university, to preserve this right which they did not contest, was wrong to oppose the King's declaration. This declaration, by maintaining the surgeons—who were henceforth required to be Masters of Arts <note>original: "maîtres-ès-arts"; an academic degree required for higher professional status.</note>—in the possession of reading and teaching publicly within the university, entirely preserved the university's own rights. They added that if the university refused to recognize the college and the Faculty of Surgery as part of itself, it still could not forbid surgeons the right to teach this science, they being the only ones recognized as capable of teaching it fully; and that the university would in this case vainly oppose the laws, custom, and reason with its alleged exclusive right to teach, since it cannot ignore that this right, which it holds from the popes, has been given by our Kings—the sole arbiters of the fate of the sciences—to various colleges that teach, outside the university, sciences that the university itself teaches. These disputes, which were long and heated, and during the course of which the two main parties undoubtedly engaged in proceedings that were hardly worthy..."

**All those who knew Mr. Quesnay know how much his desire**

...[claims], to support their respective pretensions, were finally ended by a decree of the Council of State on July 4, 1750. „The King, wishing to prevent or end all new difficulties between two professions (medicine and surgery) which are so closely related, and to ensure that good understanding reigns between them—which is no less necessary for their perfection and honor than for the preservation of the health and lives of His Majesty's subjects—has resolved to explain his intentions on this subject.“ The King prescribes by this decree: 1st, a complete course of studies in all parts of the art and science of surgery, which shall last three consecutive years; 2nd, that to make the courses more useful to students in the art and science of surgery, and to enable them to combine practice with theory, there shall immediately be established in the College of St. Cosmas <term>St-Côme</term> <note>The College of Saint-Côme was the historic seat of the surgeons' guild in Paris, long at odds with the University's Faculty of Medicine.</note> in Paris, a practical school of anatomy and surgical operations, where all parts of anatomy will be demonstrated free of charge, and where the students themselves will perform the dissections and operations they have been taught; 3rd, His Majesty orders that students shall enroll at the beginning of each year of the course of study, and that they cannot be admitted to the rank of master without providing proper certificates of their period of study. The King regulates, through several articles, how the Faculty of Medicine shall be invited by the graduate students to the public act they sustain at the end of their licensing for their reception into the College of Surgery; and His Majesty wills that the candidate give the Dean of the Faculty the title of *Dean of the most healthy faculty* <note>original Latin: "decanus saluberrimæ facultatis"</note>, and to each of the two assisting doctors, that of *most wise doctor* <note>original Latin: "sapientissimus doctor"</note>, following the custom observed in the schools of the University of Paris. These three doctors have only the first hour to raise objections to the candidate; the other three hours that the act lasts are given to the masters in surgery, who alone have the deliberative voice regarding the candidate's admission. By Article XIX of this decree, His Majesty clarifies the rights and prerogatives that the masters in surgery are to enjoy; consequently, he orders that in accordance with the declaration of April 23, 1743, they shall enjoy the prerogatives, honors, and rights attributed to the other liberal arts, as well as the rights and privileges enjoyed by the notable citizens <note>original: "notables bourgeois"</note> of Paris; and His Majesty, by Article XX, declares that he does not intend for the titles of school and college to set a precedent, or that under the pretext of these titles, surgeons may claim any of the rights of members and subordinates of the University of Paris. This restriction places the College of Surgery at the same level as the Royal College <note>Now known as the Collège de France.</note> and that of Louis-le-Grand.“

At the time of the final resolution of the dispute, which ended in victory for the surgeons, Quesnay had already been in an influential position at court for a year. He undoubtedly made great efforts in favor of the decree of July 4, 1750, and it is perhaps on this that Fouchy’s <note>Jean-Paul Grandjean de Fouchy (1707–1788), a French astronomer and perpetual secretary of the Academy of Sciences.</note> assertion rests, stating that in this affair Quesnay also proved himself a "legal expert" <note>original: "jurisconsulte"</note> and drafted various "legal briefs." A. O.

Nor did Quesnay purchase the succession to this important post "to enable himself to practice medicine without anxiety," but rather it was a specific event that brought about this change in Quesnay's position (see on this subject note 1, page 32). In 1762, the *Royal Almanac* gives a second name alongside that of Quesnay, namely Le Monnier, physician of the Paris faculty, *in succession*. In 1773 and 1774, the office of "First Physician" remained vacant. It is quite possible that Quesnay performed the duties without being the legal title-holder, and this fact may have given rise, during the illness of Louis XV, to those frictions which provoked the disgrace with which Louis XVI struck Quesnay. The *Almanac* of the year 1775 (Quesnay died December 16, 1774) nevertheless still indicates him in his former office.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, following the discussion of his ennoblement and his nickname "the thinker" given by King Louis XV. Having established his status at court, the text now backtracks slightly to detail his formal recognition by the era's great scientific institutions and the publication history of his foundational medical works.</meta>

33
Oncken, Works of Quesnay.
3

A man such as Mr. Quesnay was destined to be sought after by all literary societies; as early as 1735, he was a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences, Humanities, and Arts of Lyon; the Royal Society of London had long since admitted him among its members; the Academy <note>The Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris.</note> also desired to acquire him. It took advantage of the first opportunity that arose, and on May 12, 1751, he obtained the position of **free associate**, vacant due to the death of the Marquis d'Albert.

Mr. Quesnay had long since proven his worth through the excellent works he had published. Independently of the book he published in 1730 regarding his dispute with Mr. Silva <note>Jean-Baptiste Silva was a prominent physician to the King; he and Quesnay famously disagreed over the mechanics and efficacy of bloodletting.</note>, titled *Observations on the Effects of Bloodletting* <note>original: "Observations sur les effets de la saignée"</note>, he had published as early as 1736 his *Physical Essay on the Animal Economy* <note>original: "Essai physique sur l'économie animale." In the 18th century, "economy" referred to the organized system or functional arrangement of a living body.</note>, to which he added another small work titled: *The Art of Healing by Bloodletting* <note>original: "l'Art de guérir par la saignée"</note>.

It is astonishing to see with what precision and brevity he was able to treat these two important subjects, while nevertheless delving into everything most interesting regarding these matters; for the two works combined comprise only a single <term>duodecimo</term> <note>A book size where the printed sheet is folded to create 12 leaves (24 pages), resulting in a small, portable volume.</note> volume. Throughout, facts form the principles and the evidence that serve as his foundation; they are presented with such brevity and placed in such a clear light that, although they only pass rapidly before the eyes, they are no less striking. Furthermore, the order in which they are presented is so natural that the result is a system filled with novelty without being "new." These are merely the true principles of this branch of medicine, supported by more decisive observations than had been employed until then, from which a full conviction arises.

Reasoning takes up little space in this work; one finds only those arguments necessary to present and prove with precision the doctrine that must spring from the experiments and observations stated by the author. He is so persuaded that beyond facts nothing is certain, that the "first causes" he admits are usually only the first general effects, which he does not attempt to explain, but which serve him in explaining an infinity of others. 

He subsequently produced a second edition of his *Animal Economy*, considerably expanded and notably including many tables; it appeared in 1747 in three <term>duodecimo</term> volumes. The second edition of the *Treatise on the Effects and Usage of Bloodletting* <note>original: "Traité des effets et de l'usage de la saignée"</note> also appeared in 1750 with additions; it had been preceded in 1749 by two treatises, one on *suppuration* <note>The formation or discharge of pus.</note> and the other on *gangrene*.

<meta>This page continues the biographical sketch of François Quesnay, moving from his early medical publications and academic appointments to his major 1753 work on fevers and his transition into the "royal" printing phase under King Louis XV. In 1753, Mr. Quesnay published his *Treatise on Continuous Fevers* <note>original: "Traité des fièvres continues"</note>, in which he gathered and examined the principal knowledge that the ancients had acquired on this subject through observation and practice, particularly regarding prognostics, <term>coction<gloss>An archaic medical concept referring to the "ripening" or digestion of a disease within the body before it can be expelled.</gloss></term>, crises, and the cure of these illnesses. We shall not repeat here what we said at that time in the *History of the Academy* (1753, p. 143); but we cannot refrain from adding a singular anecdote: this work, perhaps the most interesting to come from his pen, was composed entirely while with the army, amidst the tumult of a camp and in a barn that served as housing for him and all his people, and where he had entrenched himself upon a heap of straw. One may judge by this the ease with which he worked and the faithfulness of his memory; one should not, however, be surprised by it; he who knew how to read and meditate on a high road during the burning heat of the <term>dog days<gloss>The hottest period of the summer, traditionally associated with the star Sirius.</gloss></term> must have been quite at ease composing a book in a barn and on the pile of straw where we have just depicted him.

The last works of Mr. Quesnay were printed at Versailles by express order of the late King, who himself pulled several proofs; they consisted of observations on the *Preservation of Sight* <note>original: "conservation de la vue"</note>, in quarto format; a work on *Psychology, or the Science of the Soul* <note>original: "psychologie ou science de l'âme"</note>, in the same format; and a fairly extensive extract of the *Royal Economies of Mr. de Sully* <note>original: "économies royales de M. de Sully"</note>. These works have been so carefully sequestered that not even a single copy remains with his family (¹).

The last was the beginning of the work that occupied Mr. Quesnay during the greater part of his final years; he possessed, to the highest degree, the spirit of patriotism; he knew—

He was in a position to see, more closely than any other, the inner workings of the government; he devoted himself entirely to the **economic system**; he composed on this subject a treatise entitled *Physiocracy, or the Natural Constitution of Government* <note>original: "La Physiocratie ou Constitution naturelle du gouvernement"</note>, and this book was published in 1758 through the care of Mr. Dupont, Inspector General of Commerce; he provided a very large number of interesting memoirs on this subject which are scattered throughout agricultural journals and in the *Ephemerides of the Citizen* <note>original: "Ephémérides du citoyen"</note>; he favored, with all his power, those who applied themselves to this work, and communicated to them, without reservation, the insights he had acquired therein. This passion remained with him until the last moment, and in the month preceding his death, he still composed three memoirs on this object which led a man of high office (1) to say that *Mr. Quesnay had the head of a thirty-year-old on the body of an eighty-year-old*.

We shall not follow him any further into this new career; it is too far removed from the occupations of the Academy, which would rashly exceed its boundaries by treating here matters that are not its object, which have not been submitted to its examination, and which it is well aware the government is essentially concerned with; but what we are permitted to highlight is Mr. Quesnay’s love for his fellow citizens—a love so pure and so detached from all self-interest. It was the multitude of works on this matter that placed him, in a sense, at the head and made him like the <term>oracle<gloss>A source of wise counsel or prophetic opinion; here, it refers to Quesnay’s role as the intellectual leader of the Physiocrats.</gloss></term> of all those who ran the same course. It is a fine thing to be, in some way, the legislator of those very people who work to impose laws on other men.

The calculations inseparable from the combinations necessary for this work often made him regret having neglected the study of mathematics, and as he knew difficulties only to conquer them, he believed he could overcome these by devoting himself to that study; but he was forgetting his age; the vigor of his organs no longer responded to the activity of his soul, and his head was no longer in a state to sustain, as before, long and painful work on...

The National Library of Paris still possesses a pamphlet titled *Polygonometry* <note>original: "Polygonométrie"</note> in which one easily recognizes the author of the *Philosophical Researches*. It is probable that he often had such proofs run off at the printing house of the royal castle, and that the cost of this work was then charged to the King's account. This is likely how the fable arose that these memoirs were printed by the King’s express order. — Compare note 1, page 125. A. O.

Despite the multiplicity of Mr. <term>Quesnay's</term><note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), the primary subject of this text, was a French surgeon and economist who founded the "Physiocratic" school of thought.</note> knowledge and the vivacity of his mind, he had felt that freedom of thought must have limits; he had made a sustained study of religious matters <gloss>(¹)</gloss>, and all his writings bear the mark of the respect he had for religion; justice has always been done to him on this point; his morals and his conduct were, so to speak, the image and living expression of his feelings in this regard. He reaped the fruit of this through the tranquility that accompanied his final moments; he died on December 16, 1774, having watched death approach with the same serenity with which he would have contemplated the end of a beautiful day—a precious calm that accompanies only the death of the virtuous, and which flees far from those who have strayed from the paths of virtue.

Mr. Quesnay was neither of an advantageous height nor figure; he had, however, a witty countenance, and his conversation did not contradict this appearance; it was equally instructive and amusing; he possessed the precious art of bringing himself to the level of all those with whom he had to deal, and of letting only as much of his ability appear as was necessary to instruct them, without wounding their <term>self-esteem</term><note>original: "amour-propre"</note> by making them feel an unnecessary superiority.

He possessed to the highest degree the art of knowing men; he forced them, so to speak, without them noticing, to show themselves to his eyes as they truly were; thus he granted his confidence unreservedly to those who deserved it, and his long experience at court had enabled him to speak without saying anything to others; he only managed them to this point, however, when they had not yet fully unmasked themselves; those who revealed an open soul to him—

<meta>This page concludes the biographical sketch of François Quesnay, following the description of his moral character and his peaceful death in 1774. It transitions from his personal integrity to his intellectual habits and his legacy within the Academy.</meta>

vile and corrupt could be certain, regardless of their status, of being treated as they deserved.

The amount of knowledge of every kind he had amassed was immense and seems incredible, if one considers the little time that an always very active life had left him; but he knew how to make use of even the smallest moments. A fortunate memory and an excellent mind gave him the means to join these detached pieces so perfectly that they formed a continuous whole within him; he could almost have found the elements of a science in a dictionary. This erudition, moreover, was held by him only in reserve for when it was needed; it served him only to always be at the level of any conversation. All the sciences and all the arts were familiar to him; he was far from using all this knowledge to spare himself from research. The opinions of the greatest men became <term>authorities</term><note>In this context, "authorities" refers to established scholarly or scientific precedents that were typically accepted without question.</note> for him only after he had submitted them to examination and experience; and in this sense, one can say that even the ideas he had borrowed from others were his own, and that his works were absolutely original. All these qualities were crowned in him by an unaffected simplicity, which made his company extremely pleasant, even in domestic life where he was always found to be even-tempered and where the serenity of his soul was reflected in even his smallest actions.

Although he had been at court for a long time and enjoyed considerable influence there, he never even had the thought of employing it for himself or for his own family; and if he did sometimes make use of it, it was never except in favor of those he believed capable of serving the public. The French nation was his family, and he believed himself a debtor to anyone who could serve it. In a word, one can say that if the enthusiasm of <term>patriotism</term><note>In the 18th century, "patriotism" referred to a selfless dedication to the "common good" and the welfare of the state, rather than just nationalistic pride.</note>, a very long career, and the most precious talents—employed relentlessly and to their full extent for the good of society—give any right to the gratitude of men, no one has ever had more right to it than Mr. Quesnay. From his marriage, he left only a son and a daughter; the latter had been married to Mr. <term>Hévin</term><note>Prudent Hévin (1715–1789) was a prominent French surgeon and a close associate of Quesnay.</note>, first surgeon to <term>Madame</term><note>In the French court, "Madame" usually referred to the eldest daughter of the King or the wife of the King's brother.</note>, to whom at her death she left four children. The position of <term>free associate</term><note>A member of the Academy who was not required to perform the regular duties of the professional members, often chosen from among distinguished figures or patrons of the sciences.</note> held by Mr. Quesnay in this Academy has been filled by Mr. Menard de Chousy, Councilor of State, Comptroller General of the King's Household, Knight of the royal, military, and hospital orders of Our Lady of Mount Carmel and of Saint Lazarus of Jerusalem, who was already a <term>supernumerary</term><note>An extra member of a society or organization beyond the usual required number.</note> in this class.

# HISTORICAL EULOGY
## OF
### MR. QUESNAY,

->*containing the analysis of his works, by the Count of A\*\*\** ($^1$)->

> ->He was a citizen who could speak the free<-
> ->words of his mind, and devote his life to the truth<-
> ->*Juvenal*, IV. Sat.<-
<note>original: "Civis erat qui libera posset / Verba animi proferre, et vitam impendere vero." This quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal emphasizes Quesnay’s commitment to speaking truth to power, a significant trait for a man living at the heart of the French royal court.</note>

To relieve suffering humanity; to perfect the <term>useful arts</term><note>The "useful arts" (arts utiles) refers to practical sciences and skills, particularly agriculture and manufacturing, which the Physiocrats believed were the foundation of national wealth.</note>; to enlighten peoples on their true interests; to establish in an invariable manner the principles of administration; to show the fatal effects of a bad <term>public regime</term><note>Refers to the system of governance and economic management of a state.</note>, and to indicate its causes and remedies; to instruct men of all ages, all ranks, all nations, and all centuries to come: this is to deserve from the entire universe the acclaim that it grants only to a few, even among those whom we regard as great men. Who was more worthy of this glory than the famous Quesnay, whom death has taken from us? A friend to his fellow men, he dedicated his labors to prolonging their days: everything that concerned them was dear to him. His zeal for the public good, sustained by a powerful and vigorous genius, led him to combat prejudices contrary to the progress of truth and to create a system that suggests in its author new and profound views, as well as noble, generous, and grand sentiments. Supported by the sacred principles of nature and the immutable rules of <term>order</term><note>In Physiocratic thought, "Order" (l'ordre naturel) refers to the providential laws governing society and the economy, which humans should discover and follow rather than try to invent.</note>, it will last as long as nature and order exist. Let us portray his talents, his character, his manners, his conduct, and his writings with the simplicity that was so natural to him, and which serves as the most beautiful ornament of truth. The lights of his genius will enlighten us, and the qualities of his soul will excite us to virtue.

François Quesnay, <term>squire</term><note>French: *écuyer*. In the 18th century, this was a title of nobility or a status designation for a gentleman of the court.</note>, counselor, first ordinary physician and consultant to the King, was born in *Méré*, near Montfort-l'Amaury, on June 4, 1694, to a very respectable family; his father was a lawyer of universally recognized integrity. The love he had for agriculture—the first of all the arts because it is the most necessary—led him to retire to the countryside on a property he owned. He placed his fondest hopes in young Quesnay: he took pleasure in forming his heart and instilling in him the principles of a healthy morality; he said to him what Quesnay loved to repeat when recalling the memory of his father:

Quesnay’s scientific education was not as hurried as his moral education; he was an example of the advantage later claimed by <term>Jean-Jacques Rousseau</term><note>A reference to the educational philosophy in Rousseau's *Emile* (1762), which argued that children should be allowed to develop physically and naturally before being subjected to rigorous intellectual schooling.</note>, of allowing the body to strengthen before fatiguing the intelligence. Under the eyes of a very active mother, he followed the rural labors in which she delighted. It was there that he began to study the operations of a benevolent nature; that he came to know the richness and variety of its productions. From then on, he felt a keen taste and a decided inclination for agriculture, which he maintained forever.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, following the description of his birth in Méré and his father's decision to retire to the countryside. It explores how his rural upbringing shaped his later economic theories.</meta>

It is likely this study, this dominant love of the countryside, which since turned his philosophy toward objects of public utility; it was these influences that led him to the first principles of his politics, and to that demonstration—which he rendered so striking—that cultivation is the *unique* source of wealth, and that its progress is the sole foundation of the prosperity of empires and the success of all other human labors. If Quesnay had been raised in a city, perhaps we would never have had a Quesnay.

At eleven years old, he had not yet learned to read; he consequently knew very few words, but he already knew "things": this loss of time had been merely apparent. Like those steeds whose youth has been carefully managed, his first steps were firm, his pace rapid and sustained. Scarcely was the path of the sciences opened to him than he was seen to cross it, leaving all his competitors far behind.

The first book that chance put into his hands was *The New Rural Household* <note>original: *Nouvelle Maison rustique*, a highly influential 18th-century manual on farming and estate management by Louis Liger</note>; he read it with greed; the connections between the theories he found there and the practices he saw every day interested his curiosity. Man only learns easily what he understands; and when his first studies are supported by the experience of the things they treat, they form the judgment along with the memory; this is an advantage that is never lost and which decides the course of an entire life.

Quesnay soon had the opportunity to prove this. Greedy for knowledge, impatient to dig into the treasures of antiquity, he learned Latin and Greek almost without a master. The vigorous health he owed to his rural education nourished his ardor for work. He was often seen on a summer day leaving Méré at sunrise, coming to Paris to buy a book, returning while reading it, and by evening having traveled twenty leagues <note>approximately 50-60 miles</note> on foot, having devoured the author he wished to know. It was in this way that the works of Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero became familiar to him in a short time. At sixteen and a half years old, he had finished the course of study ordinarily called the <term>humanities</term><note>The traditional curriculum of grammar, rhetoric, and classical literature.</note>.

It was then that his mother, a woman of strong reason and a vigorous character, gave him Montaigne to read, saying to him: "Here, this is to tear the afterbirth off your head." <note>original: "Tiens, voilà pour t’arracher l’arrière-faix de dessus la tête." A vivid midwifery metaphor; she suggests that his formal schooling was merely the labor, and Montaigne’s skepticism and wisdom would finally clear his mind of the "clutter" of birth.</note> This interesting anecdote, which I felt I should report, is enough to

Quesnay already possessed a judgment too solid not to understand that to embrace all sciences equally is to renounce the glory of mastering any of them deeply. He remained uncertain for some time on the specific choice he should make; finally, an eager desire to make himself useful to society fixed his focus on medicine.

Convinced that surgery, botany, and experimental physics <note>The term "physics" here encompasses the general study of natural laws and properties of matter.</note> are linked to this science by the most immediate relationships, he studied them with the same ardor under the greatest masters of the capital <note>The "capital" refers to Paris, then the center of European scientific education.</note>. He then went to settle in a village called Orgeru, in order to apply himself more easily to the knowledge of plants (³); from there, he moved to Mantes to practice surgery.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, describing his early surgical practice in Mantes and the beginnings of his intellectual transition from medicine to economic theory, sparked by a medical controversy.</meta>

It was there that he began to display his zeal, and where he showed all its selflessness. Quesnay was endowed with that generous sensitivity that one must possess to feel all its charms. The misery of the people in whose midst he lived constantly offered to his eyes a touching spectacle to which he never refused his tears. This brotherhood <note>Quesnay’s concept of "fraternity" or social bonds would later become a cornerstone of his economic theories.</note>, the solid and principal link of the economic system of which he was later the inventor and father <note>Quesnay is known as the founder of the "Physiocratic" school of economics, the first organized school of economic thought, which emphasized that the wealth of nations derived solely from the value of "land agriculture."</note>, this love for the well-being of his fellow men without distinction, naturally led him toward the most arduous and difficult undertakings. The aids of his art were lavished upon all who implored them, in all places, at all times, despite the harshness of every season. Always happy in the happiness of others, his sleepless nights, his labors, and his continuous research never had any other goal. Far from chasing after glory—that brilliant phantom which constantly dazzles ordinary men—Quesnay intended to lead a retired and obscure life. If he was eager to perfect himself in his art, it was with no other view than to practice it with greater safety for those who had recourse to him.

However, the many successes under his hand extended his reputation and earned him the position of surgeon at the Hôtel-Dieu <note>An "Hôtel-Dieu" (literally "Hostel of God") was the traditional name for the principal hospital in French towns, typically providing care for the poor and run by religious orders.</note> of Mantes. Called from all sides for the most serious illnesses, he could barely keep up with the confidence the public showed in him.

Quesnay was as yet known only upon this small stage; and satisfied with the good he did there every day, he was not more ambitious, until an unexpected event provided him with the opportunity to bring even more brilliant talents to light, and fixed the eyes of learned Europe upon him... In 1727, Mr. Silva <note>Jean-Baptiste Silva (1682–1742) was a highly celebrated French physician of Jewish descent who served the French royalty and was a leading medical authority of the Enlightenment.</note>, who was then considered the most skillful doctor known, published a treatise on <term>bloodletting<note>Original French: *saignée*. This was a common medical practice of the time based on the theory of balancing the "humors" of the body by withdrawing blood.</note></term>. This work, adorned with a fine style, enriched with seemingly profound calculations and ingenious observations on a subject unfamiliar to the public, enjoyed the most brilliant success. Quesnay read it and found that its principles were totally contrary to those he had formed through his studies and which his experience had confirmed. He judged that the consequences could be dangerous for the art of healing, and resolved to combat it. However, at the moment of struggling against a man of the highest reputation who held the premier positions, he could not ward off some anxieties: he reviewed, with the greatest severity, all the principles of his knowledge regarding the ma-

This critique appeared in 1730 under the title *Observations on the effects of bloodletting, founded on the laws of hydrostatics, with critical remarks on the treatise on the use of different kinds of bloodletting by Mr. Silva.* <note>Hydrostatics is the study of fluids at rest. Quesnay's hope was not disappointed. Hardly had his book appeared than its great superiority over that of Mr. Silva was decided by all competent judges.

His fame then carried him into the most distinguished circles of society, where he made himself loved through the charms of his character and his wit; the liveliness and gaiety of the latter provided him with pleasant witticisms in social gatherings, yet without ever offending anyone. His manners were gentle and honest, his kindness thoughtful, and his erudition varied and stripped of pedantry; thus, as soon as he became known, he was sought after by everyone. The late Marshal de Noailles <note>Adrien Maurice de Noailles, a prominent French nobleman and military leader.</note> made him his friend, and it was at his home that Quesnay had the opportunity to make the acquaintance of Mr. de la Peyronie <note>François de la Peyronie (1678–1747), the king’s premier surgeon, who was instrumental in professionalizing surgery as a discipline distinct from barber-surgery.</note>; the conversations these two famous men had on objects relating to their art gave the latter the highest idea of Quesnay’s merit. Around this same time, Mr. de la Peyronie had just obtained the foundation of the Royal Academy of Surgery; he believed that no one was more capable than Quesnay of filling the position of <term>perpetual secretary</term> <note>A prestigious, lifelong appointment as the primary administrator and intellectual editor of an academic institution.</note>, and he tasked him with editing the first volume of the memoirs of this nascent company.

The preface to this work, written by Quesnay, is a masterpiece of genius and taste, which alone could have earned him an everlasting reputation; indeed, what intelligence in the plan, what justice in the arrangement, what truth in the principles, what connection in the consequences, what depth in the thoughts, what elegance in the expression, what harmony, what clarity, what precision in the style; in a word, what perfection in the whole! And let no one imagine that its reading should be reserved only for those who devote themselves to the...

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay. The previous page ended mid-word with "eruditi...", likely referring to his "erudition" or scholarship. The author, after showing that the sciences remain long shrouded in obscurity, and that the rays of light cast upon them at intervals by a few great men are not sufficient for their glory; that their progress is slow; and that their perfection seems to flee from them the closer they approach it, gives the principal rules that must be put into practice if one wishes to become skilled in the **art of healing**. <note>The "art of healing" (*l'art de guérir*) was a standard 18th-century term encompassing both internal medicine and external surgery.</note>

***Observation and experience*** are, according to Quesnay, the two sources from which flow the truths that can enrich this art. Through observation, one follows nature in its obscure path and examines it attentively; through experience, one questions nature and wrests its secrets from it. Observation and experience must remain closely linked and provide mutual assistance to one another. The former, left to its own strength, can lead into error; it is uncertain. Self-interest, prejudice, and personal ways of perceiving are often reefs upon which truth is shipwrecked. The latter, without the help of observation, can likewise lead astray; it must be brought back to the testimony of reason. It is upon the mutual agreement of both that the science of nature prints its seal. Without theory, there is neither science nor art; Quesnay correctly defines the theory of surgery as ***practice reduced to precepts***. He rejects from it arbitrary applications, opinions dictated by imagination alone, simple likelihoods, and pure possibilities. Knowledge based on the causes of our ailments, on the observation of their signs, on the laws of the <term>animal economy</term> <note>The "animal economy" refers to the organization and living functions of a body, treated as a complex system.</note>, on the operation of remedies, on physics, and on nature, compose the theory of the art of healing. Everything our author says about it is true, judicious, wise, methodical, well-reasoned, and well-connected, and can be applied to an infinite number of other sciences.

But although the theory of surgery is luminous and profound, the precepts of which it is formed are nevertheless circumscribed within narrow limits. Where the torch of certainty is extinguished, one has no other guides to lead oneself than ***conjecture and analogy***. In the works of the mind, these often contribute to the discovery of truth; but it belongs only to learned men, to geniuses, to make use of them, and even then...

The favors showered upon Quesnay were not begged for; although he was at court—that is to say, in the midst of incessant solicitations—he never adopted its ways; he had a soul too sincere and too beautiful to bend to flattery. The use he made of his influence made him respectable even to those most accustomed to respecting nothing. The most illustrious titles are those provided by personal merit. Boerhaave <note>Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738) was a world-renowned Dutch physician often considered the father of modern physiology.</note> had produced a physiology in which he shed light on the structure of the body’s organs and their specific functions; but he had omitted to explain the primary physical causes that give them action, or at least had spoken of them only very briefly. Quesnay understood the full importance of this part of physiology; it was new: he believed he should treat it for the public good.

The plan of his work is to establish the principles necessary for the knowledge of the general causes which concur with the organs of the body in the operations of nature and can occasion other advantageous or harmful effects, independently of the action of these same organs. To fulfill this plan according to his views, Quesnay treats the principles of bodies in general, which he divides into two kinds: principles of simple bodies, which are called constitutive principles—by this he means matter and form; and principles or elements of <term>mixts</term><note>In early modern chemistry and physics, a "mixt" referred to a compound substance made of simpler elements.</note>, that is to say, bodies composed of simple bodies. The details into which he enters on these objects, which he treats separately, are as varied as they are interesting and useful. I will not speak of the constitutive and elementary principles which relate only to physics or <term>physico-medical science</term><note>The study of how physical laws and mechanics apply to the human body and medical treatment.</note>. I will focus only on the sensitive and intellectual faculties that these latter principles contain.

What Quesnay puts forward regarding sensations, perceptions, discernment, and memory, imagination, and science, should place him alongside that great man (¹), whose opinion on the extent and the system of <term>vision in God</term><note>A philosophical doctrine (original: "vision en Dieu") suggesting that human knowledge occurs through a direct union with the divine mind.</note> he contested; so well did he manage to make his metaphysics precise and luminous. <meta>This page continues the analysis of François Quesnay’s philosophical and physiological writings, moving from his study of physical matter to his exploration of the human mind, morality, and the search for truth.</meta>

...to act like a broken and harmful machine. This is a thoughtful portrait of morality, which heralds a man of both wisdom and religious faith.

The chapters on instinct, the <term>internal senses</term><note>In 18th-century philosophy, these were the mental faculties—such as imagination and memory—that process information received from the physical senses.</note>, conception, and <term>common sense</term><note>The author distinguishes "common sense" (the basic, shared ability to perceive) from formal reasoning and judgment.</note> (as distinguished from reason and judgment), as well as <term>bias</term><note>The original French term is *prévention*, referring specifically to ideas or "pre-conceptions" adopted from others before one examines them for oneself.</note> (which differs from prejudice), ideas, thought, the imaginative faculty, the certainty of the knowledge our ideas provide us, the will, reason, attention, intellectual memory, reflection, examination or contemplation, reasoning, and judgment, are written with a sagacity that leaves the reader wanting for nothing. Quesnay delves deeply into human liberty; he defines it as the power to deliberate in order to determine, through reason, whether to act or not to act. He speaks with equal truth about the principles of exercising this freedom, the functions of the soul in this exercise, the proper use one must make of it, the advantages and disadvantages of habit, and the duties to be fulfilled toward society—which he expanded upon more extensively in other works I shall mention below. What he says regarding the immortality of the soul is further proof of his knowledge of his religion.

He then outlines the sources of our errors in the search for truth; according to him, they stem from three causes: *bias*, *prejudice*, and *supposition*.

*Bias*, which we follow through communication and which is a common result of the unsuccessful research of those who pass it on to us, arises from the very ideas shared with us, or from errors in reasoning capable of seducing us, since they seduced the authors themselves. To these <term>captious</term><note>Deceptive or fallacious, especially in an argument intended to confuse.</note> reasonings are added the terms used to represent these shared ideas—terms that are sometimes imprecise, vague, or shrouded in obscurity. Philosophy has accepted many expressions that depict only indeterminate and confused ideas. Later, through extension, these same expressions were given a more specific meaning; from this springs the infinite number of false ideas that the mind embraces. Quesnay does not enter into an examination of these terms because it is safer and easier, in the pursuit of truth, to consider ideas attentively and to dispel error by expressing oneself clearly, rather than trying to abolish the false meanings of certain expressions that tyrannize minds through the <term>despotism of usage</term><note>The "despotism of usage" refers to how the established, common way of using words—even if incorrect—becomes almost impossible to change because everyone is used to it.</note>.

The errors of *prejudice* are easy to destroy when one moves toward truth with the intention of reaching it and with the necessary disposition. The desire to find it is the greatest step one...

<meta>The previous page appears to have been discussing the early stages of intellectual inquiry and the initial efforts to reach the truth. ...can do toward it. New insights, more thoughtful observations, and a more sustained and combined examination complete the triumph and make us grasp truths that had escaped us.

Supposition is the most common source of our errors; it is the work of curiosity and the insatiable desire we have to expand the sphere of our knowledge. In all objects, there are properties that hide from our weak sight. The relationships they have with one another are likewise veiled from us. We even believe we perceive contradictions within them, which only appear so to us because of the lack of connection found in our ideas. The darkness of our ignorance torments us. We agitate ourselves within the narrow circle of our thoughts, where the mind is as if imprisoned; we break the barrier that constricts it; and to satisfy our curiosity, we abandon ourselves to likelihood. For vague and incomplete ideas, we substitute determined and complete ones. The illusion is pleasant; it seduces us. The more we consider these artificial ideas, the more the shadows hiding the natural ones thicken; the more properties we seem to see in objects, the more of them we adopt, and the more our errors increase. From this come those brilliant and ingenious systems that the imagination produces in pleasant transports; from this come those hypothetical sentiments that strip the sciences of their certainty and evidence.

To protect oneself from the dangerous effects of supposition, one must distrust oneself, study the limits of one's knowledge, and allow oneself to be seduced neither by one's own fictions nor those of others. One must adopt only those opinions established on reason and nature—sure and invariable rules that Quesnay <note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), a French physician and economist who founded the Physiocratic school, emphasizing the laws of nature.</note> followed constantly in the course of his studies and that all men should embrace for the progress of truth.

After this, our author speaks of taste. He relies on experience to prove that there is a general taste and another that is particular. These true and judicious observations, concerning flavors, smells, sounds, and the objects of sight and touch, apply equally to music, painting, architecture, engraving, poetry, eloquence, and the sentiments of the soul.

Genius is the father and the preserver of all these arts; it belonged to Quesnay to sketch their portrait. Genius alone must paint genius. With what richness of imagination our author represents its effects! His brush is by turns noble

One is astonished that so few geniuses have been endowed with a sure taste. One will cease to be so if one reflects on the difference Quesnay places between the causes that form the one and the other. Taste is produced by an exquisite feeling, and genius by a prompt intelligence, by an ardent imagination, and by vivid and elevated feelings. Taste requires much knowledge, especially that of rules; genius can exist without them. Witness Racan <note>Honorat de Bueil, Seigneur de Racan (1589–1670), a French poet and original member of the Académie Française.</note> and the carpenter of Nevers (²), called the Virgil of the Plane <note>original: "Virgile à rabot." A "rabot" is a carpenter's plane. This refers to Adam Billaut, a carpenter who became a celebrated poet.</note>. Both men of genius, the first lived in ignorance, and the second had not the slightest tincture of the sciences or the fine arts (³). The Abbé Desfontaines, who became so formidable in the literary empire through his critiques—most of which were satires—had acquired much knowledge; he possessed taste, despite the partiality and the falsehood of his judgments: yet he was born without genius. Nature and art together form taste; genius is owed entirely to nature. But what nature provides for taste is infinitely less rare and less precious than what she gives to genius. Let us admit, nevertheless, that it is very difficult to judge works of the mind soundly.

The disruption of the faculties of the soul, which influences the body, engenders several diseases, and the disruption of the faculties of the body, which influences the soul, alters its functions. This subject can therefore only be useful to discuss; it is even necessary and forms a part of physiology; Quesnay treated it like a master. After having finished his work on *Animal Economy* <note>The "Animal Economy" was an 18th-century term for the branch of physiology that studied the laws governing the life and functions of living organisms.</note>, Quesnay found himself naturally led to occupy himself with *Political Economy*. By reflecting on the influences of the soul's affections on the body, one is not long in becoming convinced that men cannot have true health if they are not happy, and cannot be happy if they do not live under a good government.

Quesnay is perhaps the only physician who thought of this kind of *hygiene* (¹); when he wished to understand the principles of the science of government, the first that struck him was that men are sensitive beings, powerfully excited by needs to seek enjoyments and to flee privations and pain. To know how to multiply these enjoyments so necessary to the human species, it was necessary to return to the source of the goods that provide them. It was then that Quesnay remembered the first occupations of his childhood and that agriculture fixed his attention with an even more vivid interest.

The politicians who had written before him counted several sources of wealth: cultivation, commerce, and industry. Quesnay recognized and demonstrated that agriculture, fishing, and the exploitation of mines and quarries were the only sources of wealth, and that the labors of commerce and industry consisted only of services, transport, and manufacturing, which give only new forms to raw materials and through the consumption of pre-existing subsistence; that the wages for these labors were only the necessary reimbursement of their costs, the interest on the advances they require, the indemnity for the risks they entail, and that the whole offered only exchanges of wealth for other wealth of equal value, whereas in agriculture there is a real production of wealth—of raw materials and subsistence that did not exist before—whose value surpasses that of the

<meta>The text continues from the previous page, completing the sentence about the source of goods. The transition moves from the origins of human needs to the specific economic "advances" identified by François Quesnay as necessary for agricultural production.</meta>

expenses that were required to carry out this reproduction <note>In Physiocratic theory, "reproduction" refers to the annual renewal of wealth through agriculture.</note>, primarily due to the fertile property with which heaven has endowed nature, and which it has allowed man to direct for his own profit through powerful activity. This was his first discovery in political economy.

This insight gave birth to several developments that could themselves be considered further discoveries. Quesnay remarked that cultivation does not only consist of labor, but that it requires "advances" <note>The term "advances" (avances) in this context refers to the capital or initial investments required before any harvest or profit can be realized.</note>, because all work entails costly consumption.

These advances of cultivation are of several kinds.

There are those that are inseparable from the land upon which they were made, and which, when joined to the land's productive quality, constitute the very value of that land. Such are the expenses for draining marshes, clearing away harmful woods, planting necessary ones, constructing buildings, directing water flow, digging wells, etc. These expenses make land that was initially wild fit for cultivation: they establish the dominion of man over what was previously only the temporary lair of a few fleeting animals. Once these expenses have been made, there are no other means of recovery than the enjoyment and cultivation of the land they have prepared. One cannot transport them elsewhere; they form, so to speak, but one and the same thing with the ground that received them and which owes them its useful existence. Quesnay, after having detailed the nature of this species of advances, named them ***land advances*** <note>original: *avances foncières*; these are essentially permanent land improvements.</note>.

There are others whose existence must precede the cultivation of the land; of this nature are the livestock, herds of different species, and the instruments and tools of rural labor. A farmer who proposes to develop the heritage prepared by the landowner must bring a complete set of equipment for rural operation to this land. To form this set, a mass of wealth is required, proportional to the extent of the soil and the nature of the operation. In addition to the draft animals, plowing instruments, and farm furniture, one must have the first seeds and all the provisional subsistence needed until the harvest. It is this block of preliminary and indispensable expenses that Quesnay designated by the name of ***primitive advances of cultivation*** <note>original: *avances primitives*; these represent the initial capital investment in equipment and livestock.</note>.

Finally, there is a third kind: those of the perpetual tasks of cultivation, such as plowing, sowing, harvesting, the wages of the men employed, the food for the necessary animals, etc., etc. These advances must be renewed <note>The text cuts off here; these are known in Physiocracy as "annual advances" (*avances annuelles*).</note>
