<meta>The text continues from the previous page, finishing the description of land advances (permanent improvements) and transitioning into the cyclic nature of agricultural investment as defined by François Quesnay.</meta>

every year, for the cycle of the same tasks must begin again each year. Quesnay gave these the name *annual advances* <note>original: "avances annuelles"; these refer to recurring costs like seeds and seasonal wages.</note>, and he included the three types of advances under the general name of *productive advances*.

*Land advances* <note>original: "avances foncières"; permanent improvements like drainage or buildings mentioned on the previous page.</note> do not need to be frequently renewed; a slight maintenance is enough for them. But it is the use of *original* and *annual* advances <note>original: "avances primitives" (durable capital like tools and livestock) and "avances annuelles" (operating costs).</note>, directed by the farmer's intelligence, which gives birth to the *annual* harvest or the total reproduction of the territory. To perpetuate this, it is necessary to take from each harvest the reimbursement of the annual advances—which must be restarted to prepare the following year's harvest—and the maintenance of the original advances, as well as a sort of interest for the capital employed in these advances. This ensures that the profession of the farmer is no less profitable to the one who practices it than any other profession could have been.

The farmer, subject to these original and annual advances, could not lose the value of these advances—a value that is necessary and inviolable—without agriculture languishing; otherwise the land, being progressively abandoned, would become as if struck with sterility.

The interest on the sum that the farmer has advanced, the habitual maintenance of the capital <note>original: "fonds"; the stock or assets used to generate value.</note> he makes productive, and the compensation for losses and risks are due to him by the same right. Without this, what would become of justice? What would become of the funds necessary for the exploitation of lands? What would become of cultivation, the harvests, and the men they must sustain?

These various sums which must be set aside annually from the harvests so that cultivation continues without decay have been called by our rural policy the *returns of cultivation* <note>original: "reprises de la culture"; the portion of the harvest that must be reinvested to keep the farm running.</note>; he gave the name *net product* <term>net product: "produit net"; the true surplus or profit remaining after all expenses are paid, which the Physiocrats believed only land could produce.</term> to what remains of the value of the harvests once the *returns of cultivation* have been fulfilled. This is the price of the productive capacity of the land, just as the returns themselves are the wages of the labor that stimulated this capacity. This expression, which designates the profit remaining for the entire proprietary class when all the costs of its operation have been deducted, presents an idea that is simple, just, clear, and consistent with the logic of language; one day it will be difficult to conceive that there could have been people frivolous enough to attempt to turn it into ridicule.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of agricultural investment, moving from private capital (land advances) to the role of the state (sovereign advances) and the definition of the "net product" as the foundation of economic science according to François Quesnay.</meta>

...of land advances, but also the sovereignty <note>Meaning the state or the ruling authority.</note> charged with public expenses for education, civil, military, and political protection, and public administration; that is to say, the responsibility to build and maintain the great common properties—roads, bridges, canals, and others—which give value to private holdings.

These large and useful expenses, which may be called **sovereign advances**, are the title <note>The legal or moral justification.</note> by virtue of which the sovereignty can and must take its share of the **net product** <term>net product: the surplus value or profit remaining after all costs of production and maintenance have been paid.</term> of cultivated lands.

These ideas and expressions belong to Quesnay; and posterity—which is moved by no passion and knows neither enthusiasm nor envy—just and grateful posterity will surely feel that a man who has detailed every part of a science, who has seen and fixed its internal logic, and who has created its nomenclature, is the true inventor of that science, even if he shared some common ideas with certain illustrious contemporaries. But those ideas of which we have spoken until now are claimed by none of them.

We shall remark, with the justice we owe to the memory of Quesnay—who was so little jealous of his own glory that he was far from wanting to appropriate that of others—we shall remark on the points where his thoughts met with those of other great men whose names, like his own, will be recommended to future generations.

Moreover, one must agree that this simple distinction between *the recoveries of cultivation and its net product* <note>original: "les reprises de la culture et son produit net"; 'recoveries' refers to the portion of the harvest used to pay back the farmer's operating costs.</note> is the key to the science of political economy.

The *net product* is the reward for land advances; it is the portion of the harvest belonging to the owner of the soil and the sovereignty. It follows that, for equal harvests, the more *net product* there is to be expected, the more advantageous it is to possess lands, to expand them, or to improve them through land advances. From this, it results that the increase of the *net product* brings about natural increases in cultivation and, consequently, in food supply and population. This happens necessarily through the irresistible movement of self-interest, which leads people to seek out, create, and improve land properties in proportion to the greater profit they offer their owners.

But what is the sure means of obtaining, for equal harvests, the greatest possible *net product*? It is to restrict, as much as possible, the costs of labor, transport, and manufacturing of every kind. This cannot be achieved without degradation and without in—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of economic justice, transitioning from the state's role in infrastructure to the shared principles of François Quesnay and his contemporary, Vincent de Gournay, regarding free trade and the removal of market restrictions.</meta>

justice except through the greatest freedom of competition and the most absolute immunity <note>Meaning exemption from taxes or legal restrictions.</note> for all types of labor.

Prohibitions restrict labor, taxes make it more expensive and overburden it, and exclusive privileges cause it to degenerate into a costly and destructive monopoly; therefore, there should be neither prohibitions, nor taxes, nor exclusive privileges on this labor.

It is here that Quesnay found common ground with the wise Mr. de Gournay, Intendant of Commerce and his contemporary, whom he esteemed and loved, and upon whose person and disciples he took pleasure in basing part of his hope for his homeland. Mr. de Gournay had reached this practical result by a different path: no one, he said, does what is useful to commerce as well as those who engage in it; therefore, no regulations should be imposed on them. No one is as interested in knowing whether a commercial enterprise, a factory establishment, or the exercise of a profession will be profitable as the one who wishes to attempt it; therefore, there should be neither corporations, nor guilds <term>jurandes: the administrative bodies of trade guilds in pre-Revolutionary France that controlled entry into professions.</term>, nor exclusive privileges. No one can be sure of deriving the greatest profit from their labor if they are not free to do it as they see fit and if they are subject to an inquisition and troublesome formalities. Every tax on labor or transport <note>original: "voiturage"</note> brings about inquisitions and hindrances that disrupt trade, and discourage and ruin merchants; it is therefore necessary to free their work from these taxes that block their success: *let them do as they will and let them pass.* <note>original: "laissez-les faire et laissez-les passer," the famous maxim that gave rise to the economic term "laissez-faire."</note>

It is to this point that Mr. de Gournay had been led by contemplating the interest men have in liberty, and Mr. Quesnay by calculating the interest they have in an abundant reproduction of subsistence and wealth (1).

<meta>This page continues the discussion of François Quesnay’s life and his influential economic theories, specifically how his proximity to the French royal court provided a platform for his ideas on free trade and social structure.</meta>

...palace of the late king (¹) where he enjoyed powerful protection (²). How rare it is to make such a use of favor, and to make no other use of it!

Regarding the trade of products, and specifically that of grain, it was Quesnay who observed that the liberty which equalizes prices—by calling to the aid of regions in the grip of famine the productions of those in abundance, and by allowing the surplus of the latter to be preserved for lean years—it was he, I say, who observed that this beneficial liberty ensures a great profit for the sellers of products, for the farmers, and for the landowners, without causing any loss to the consumers, and even while lowering the average price of their subsistence. This truth, which at first seems paradoxical, is based on the fact that consumers need an equal quantity of products every year, which they pay for at unequal prices according to local abundance or scarcity; whereas producers have little to sell in years of high prices and much in those where the price is debased by the excess of a reproduction <note>the annual harvest yield</note> that surpasses possible or profitable sales. Such is the basis of an ingenious and profound calculation, which presents one of the strongest arguments in favor of <term>free trade</term> <note>the policy of not restricting imports or exports</note> and which is another of Quesnay’s discoveries.

But let us continue the examination of his progress in the science of political economy and the <term>nomenclature</term> <note>the system of naming and classification</note> he provided as he advanced toward all objects.

After the farmers who perform the productive labor and the landowners who receive the *net product* <note>original: "produit net"; the surplus value generated by agriculture after all costs are paid</note>, one cannot help but recognize another order of labor which facilitates enjoyment without multiplying the materials that provide the basic stock and the wealth that pays for them. Such are those tasks necessary for products, both natural and manufactured, to reach their final destination, which is consumption. They must be transported, shaped, and traded; this is what constitutes commerce and manufacturing; this is what gives existence to the merchants, artisans, and artists who form a remarkable class among men united in society.

The men within a state are therefore divided into three classes.

<meta>This page continues the explanation of François Quesnay’s social and economic classification system, following the introduction of the concept of the "net product" as the surplus wealth generated by land.</meta>

The first is the *productive* class; this is that of the cultivators, a beneficent class whose wealth constitutes the strength and glory of empires, since it is from them that the happiness or misfortune of the other two flows. To degrade them, to torment them, or to overwhelm them under the weight of taxes—which cannot impede the <term>reinvestments</term> <note>original: "reprises"; the portion of the harvest a farmer must keep to cover costs and seed for the following year</note> without destroying the regenerating wealth—is to crush the nation that rests upon them. Sovereigns, ministers, and administrators: protect, reward, and increase the number of cultivators if you wish for the State, whose reins you hold in your hands, to shine with a lasting brilliance.

The second class is that of the *landowners*, that is to say, the private possessors who establish the land investments, maintain them, and receive and spend their portion of the product; as well as the agents of sovereignty, who fulfill all the functions of public authority and who are paid by another portion of the same net product.

The third is that which contains the merchants, the <term>artisans</term> <note>original: "artistes"; in the 18th century, this referred to skilled craftsmen and technicians</note>, and their employees. This class occupies itself with useful, interesting, and ingenious works, but these are paid for by the wealth that the soil or the waters have brought into being: this class exchanges, it arranges, but it produces nothing. To call it "non-productive" would be a compound expression poorly suited to the simplicity of the language. Quesnay named it the *class of sterile expenses* . . . . Here, what a rumor arises, what cries are heard! "What? The class of those who, by their talents, their industry, and their profession, animate commerce, maintain the movement of its gears, attract the gold of foreign nations, and spread abundance everywhere—must it be called a sterile class because, instead of dedicating its labor to the plow to furrow the fields, it employs it in manufactures or trades?" . . No, I shall reply to these honest citizens, who are too quick to take offense. The class of industrial wage-earners has never been regarded as useless to the State; but it is "sterile" because it differs from the productive class, because it creates nothing, because it does nothing but give a new form to what has already been produced, and because its labors are paid for and do not themselves pay; whereas the labors of cultivation pay for themselves and, moreover, pay for all other human labors. This sterility, which is not an insult but a quality derived from the nature of things, is the most certain guarantee of the immunity that enlightened governments must ensure for the agents of commerce and the arts. If they produced wealth, how could one justify exempting them <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the author is arguing that because the "sterile class" only transforms wealth rather than creating it, taxing them would only result in higher prices for the other classes, thus justifying their tax-exempt status in Physiocratic theory.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the three economic classes, specifically addressing the misconception that the "sterile class" (merchants and artisans) should be taxed, and beginning a detailed explanation of how wealth circulates between these groups according to the Physiocratic "Tableau Économique."</meta>

...of a contribution for the authority that protects property; if they produce no such surplus, their exemption is a matter of natural right. A strange misunderstanding! Men demand that commerce and the arts be subjected to taxes, and they are seen as their defenders. Others maintain that no one has the right to demand contributions from either merchants or <term>artisans</term> <note>original: "artistes"; in the 18th century, this referred to skilled craftsmen, manufacturers, and technicians rather than fine artists</note>, and they are passed off as their enemies (¹).

Do not believe that these prejudices can be lasting. It will soon be understood that tax must only be taken where nature herself has provided the means to satisfy it—at the source of revenue—and that it is the common interest of the three classes that forms society.

It is between these three classes that food supplies and raw materials are distributed. The productive class, which first gathers the totality of the harvest, keeps for itself its <term>reinvestments</term> <note>original: "reprises"; the portion of the crop or funds a farmer must retain to cover operating costs, seeds, and his own subsistence for the following year</note> and pays the <term>net product</term> <note>original: "produit net"; the surplus wealth or rent remaining after all production costs are paid</note> to the landowner. By this first sharing of the harvests, the landowners acquire the means to spend; they spend part with the productive class by purchasing food, and part with the sterile class by purchasing manufactured goods. The productive class itself spends the reinvestments it had reserved: it consumes the largest portion in kind for its own subsistence and passes the remainder to the sterile class to pay for the goods, clothing, and tools that the cultivators require. The sterile class thus receives the wages of the other two; but as it must be fed and must continue the work that sustains it, it spends the entirety of its receipts with the productive class—partly on food and partly on the purchase of raw materials, which are the object of its labors and industry and the replacement of its advances.

It is in this way that the totality of the harvest is divided among three classes. The first part is for the one who produced it through his labor; the second is sold to the landowner class for that portion of its net product which it consumes as food; and the third to the sterile class, which consumes a portion and—

(1) I hope that the errors I may have made regarding the nature of taxation, in my *Observations on the New Plan of Taxation* printed last year, have led to no ill consequence. I confess them and abjure them with all my heart. At my age, it is said, one is permitted to be mistaken. If that is so, my fault is light. <meta>This page continues the explanation of the circulation of wealth between the three economic classes (productive, sterile, and proprietary), specifically detailing how the "sterile class" (artisans and merchants) must replenish their materials. It introduces François Quesnay’s famous "Tableau Économique" as a vital tool for understanding these flows, defending it against critics who dismissed it as overly complex or absurd.</meta>

...uses the other portion to replenish the stock of its works and workshops. For warehouses and factories could not sustain themselves or would collapse under their own weight from a lack of merchandise (which various sales would deplete), if the <term>sterile class</term> <note>In Physiocratic theory, the "sterile class" included merchants and artisans; they were considered "sterile" not because they were useless, but because they only transformed existing materials rather than creating new "net" wealth from the earth like farmers do.</note> did not buy back new raw materials in proportion to its output to continue its labors.

It is through minted money that the greater part of the distribution and consumption of the products forming the annual harvests is carried out. It circulates between the three classes; the farmer gives the first impetus to this circulation; he pays the <term>net product</term> <note>original: "produit net"; the surplus wealth or rent remaining after all production costs are paid</note> to the landowner and buys manufactured goods from the sterile class. The second circulation is that produced by the landowner who, with his net product, purchases food, craftsmanship, and labor. The sterile class carries out the third circulation by buying, in its turn, food and raw materials. 

Of these three distributions, two are incomplete and do not pass successively through all three classes. The first is the portion that the farmer gives to the sterile class to pay for the works it has done for him; the second is that which the landowner gives to the farmer as the price for his food. But there is also a portion circulating through all three classes: it is that employed in the purchase of manufactured goods. It passes from the hands of the landowner into those of the sterile class, only to return afterwards to its source: I mean, to the <term>productive class</term> <note>Those who work the land (farmers, fishermen, miners) and are seen as the only group capable of creating new wealth.</note> which provides the food and the raw materials necessary for the works of craft.

To make this distribution of produce and wealth, its effects, and its consequences more easily understood, <term>Quesnay</term> <note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), the leading figure of the Physiocrats and personal physician to King Louis XV.</note> devised a way to depict it by establishing the three classes in three columns and marking the different items of expenditure, purchase, and sale they conduct with one another using dotted lines that cross over.

This is what has been called the <term>Economic Table</term> <note>original: "Tableau économique"; a groundbreaking diagram published in 1758 that visualized the flow of money and goods in an economy, often considered the first precise mathematical model in economics.</note>, a precious formula that greatly simplifies the work of political calculators who are already trained and enlightened. Yet, there is nothing amusing about it, and it only allows for the ridicule of those who have preferred to make it an object of mockery rather than taking the trouble to study it. This habit of lampooning subjects of such high importance instead of reflecting upon them seems to suggest a certain pettiness in the political writers who have indulged in it. It seems to me that it is not

<meta>This page continues the defense of François Quesnay’s economic theories, transitioning from a description of the circulation of money to the utility of his "Economic Table" as a mathematical tool for national accounting.</meta>

...not unlike the way geometers handle the profound theories by which they simplify the efforts of the human mind within their learned research.

One may consult, in the work *Physiocracy* <note>original: "physiocratie"; referring to the 1767 collection of François Quesnay's writings edited by Dupont de Nemours</note>, this ***Economic Table*** <note>original: "Tableau économique"; a famous diagram representing the flow of money and goods in an economy</note>, reduced by its author himself to the greatest simplicity. There, one will see that it can accept very diverse data and also present very different results. A society may be in a state of stability, of increasing prosperity, or of decadence: the tables that depict it in these different states are not the same; for if they were, they would no longer truly represent it. One must collect the data upon which they wish to construct the table of a state. If the data are false, the table will yield a misleading result. And such are all rules of arithmetic when they are employed upon inaccurate data.

But the fact remains that with a certain number of assured facts and the help of the ***Economic Table***, one can very promptly calculate the state of a nation.

For example, if the total harvest, the sum of the **net product** <note>The surplus wealth remaining after all production costs—wages, seeds, and maintenance—have been paid</note>, and the habitual order of expenses are given, one will know perfectly what the population is in each of the three classes and their respective levels of wealth.

If, on the contrary, it is the population that is given along with the order of expenses and the sum of the **net product**, one will know what the total harvest is, what the <term>cultivator’s returns</term> <note>original: "reprises du cultivateur"; the portion of the harvest the farmer must keep to cover the costs of the next planting season</note> amount to, and how the population is divided among the various classes.

If it is the <term>cultivator’s returns</term>, the order of expenses, and the population that are given, one will know what the **net product** is, and again how the population is divided between the different types of <term>sterile or productive labor</term> <note>In this system, "productive" labor (farming) creates new wealth, while "sterile" labor (industry/trade) only transforms existing wealth</note>.

Given the order of expenses, the population, and the type of culture, one will know what the **total reproduction** <note>The total annual output of the nation's land</note> is, what the <term>cultivator’s returns</term> are, and what the **net product** is.

One would need a truly marvelous talent to persuade those who wish to reflect upon it for a moment that all of this is merely trivial and contemptible, and that humanity does not owe the greatest obligations to the sublime genius who made these discoveries. For our part, we shall bless this respectable and beneficent man who has shown us, through a simple calculation, all men in their places, holding one another by the hand, convinced of the need they have for each other, bound by their interests which touch and merge together.

The text concludes by praising the Physiocratic vision of a society where all classes are harmoniously linked by mutual economic interest.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the mathematical application of the Economic Table to the fundamental philosophical and political principles of the "science of economics" (Physiocracy). It completes the thought from the previous page regarding the calculation of a nation's wealth and begins a systematic list of maxims for good governance.</meta>

The foundations of public wealth are built upon those of the science of *economics*; religion, customs, laws, politics, finances, agriculture, trade, arts, education, mutual duties—everything that contributes to the happiness of sovereigns and subjects falls within the circle that composes it.

The monarch is the head of the nation; as the guardian of public force, he must maintain justice and watch over the rights of his subjects; his authority must therefore be "unique and superior to all
« individuals of society." <note>This reflects the Physiocratic ideal of "legal despotism," where a single sovereign enforces the natural laws of property and heightens efficiency.</note>

The best laws form the best governments. To establish these laws, one must know them. "The nation must therefore be
« instructed in the general laws of the natural order, which constitute the
« government that is evidently the most perfect." <note>The "natural order" (ordre naturel) was the core Physiocratic belief that human societies are governed by providential, physical laws as certain as those of geometry.</note>

Everything comes originally from the land. "Let the sovereign and the
« nation therefore never lose sight of the fact that the land is the sole
« source of wealth and that it is agriculture that multiplies it."

The fear of being stripped of one's property stifles competition, casts one into despondency, and prevents the making of the necessary advances <note>In this context, "advances" (avances) refers to the capital investment—seeds, tools, and labor—required before a harvest can be produced.</note> and labors necessary to increase its value: "Let the ownership of
« landed property and movable wealth therefore be secured to those
« who are their legitimate possessors."

The advances of agriculture are sacred because of their necessity for annual reproduction. Commodities must be regarded as the fundamental basis of trade; to burden them with taxes is to wish to destroy this basis and, with it, the building it supports:
"Taxation, if it is not to be destructive, must therefore be established on the
« net product <note>original: "produit net"; the surplus value remaining after all production costs have been paid</note> of landed property; justice demands that it be pro-
« portional to the mass of the nation's income; let its increase,
« therefore, follow that of the income."

Men and lands are useful to the state only when the advances made to agriculture come to their aid; it is upon these that the *net product* of the owner depends: "Let the advances
« of the cultivator therefore be sufficient to regenerate an-
« nually, through the expenses of land cultivation, the
« greatest possible product."

Every sterile fortune—that is, one which is employed neither in agriculture nor in trade—gnaws at the nation: "Let the total
« sum of income therefore return into annual circulation and
« travel through its entire extent."

<meta>This page continues the systematic presentation of economic maxims following the foundational principles established on the previous page. It shifts focus from the source of wealth (the land) to the mechanics of trade, pricing, and the circulation of money.</meta>

The increase in land revenue is found to be in proportion to the reduction that occurs in trade costs.
> “Let us therefore facilitate markets and the transport of products and manufactured goods through the repair of roads and the navigation of canals, rivers, and the sea.”

The low price of natural products is unfavorable to the nation's trade in an exchange of commodities for commodities. In such cases, the foreigner always gains.
> “Let there be no effort, then, to lower the price of food supplies and goods within the kingdom. As is the market value, so is the income; abundance and lack of value is not wealth; scarcity and high prices are misery; abundance and high prices are opulence.” <note>The Physiocrats argued that "abundance and high prices" (*abondance et cherté*) was the ideal state, as it indicated a high "net product" or surplus wealth that benefited the entire economy, whereas low prices for crops would bankrupt the farmers who were the engine of the nation.</note>

Experience demonstrates that the price of food is the thermometer for the day laborer's wages. These wages rise or fall according to the changes occurring in those prices.
> “Let it not be believed, then, that cheap food is profitable to the common people.” <note>The author argues that if food prices drop, employers simply lower wages accordingly, meaning the poor gain nothing while the agricultural sector—the source of all wealth—is weakened.</note>

Wealth is the most powerful goad for labor.
> “Let the comfort of the lowest classes of citizens, therefore, not be diminished.”

Sterile savings make circulation less vibrant.
> “Let landowners and those who practice lucrative professions not indulge in them, then.” <note>"Sterile savings" (*épargnes stériles*) refers to the hoarding of money. In this economic model, wealth must circulate—being spent on consumption or reinvested in the land—to keep the "body politic" healthy.</note>

Foreign trade must result in an increase in wealth for the nation.
> “Let the nation not suffer loss in this reciprocal trade, and let it not be deceived by an apparent advantage.”

Prohibitions, exclusive privileges, and injunctions place shackles on trade, diminish its activity, restrict its scope, and discourage the merchant; they harm landowners and even prejudice the common people.
> “Let complete freedom of trade be maintained; for the safest, most exact, and most profitable commercial policy for the state and the nation, both internally and externally, consists in the full freedom of competition.” <note>This is the famous *laissez-faire* doctrine: the belief that the economy regulates itself best when the government removes monopolies and trade barriers.</note>

Population is only useful to the state because it multiplies its wealth: it cannot multiply wealth without possessing some. Wealth is born from wealth.
> “Let us therefore be less attentive to the increase of population than to the growth of income.” <note>This challenges the older "Populationist" view that a large population was a good in itself. For the Physiocrats, a large, starving population was a liability; the priority was increasing the wealth of the land to support the people.</note>

Government expenditures are greater or smaller according to public wealth. It is from national prosperity...

<meta>This page continues the list of economic maxims by François Quesnay, the founder of the Physiocratic school. It transitions from general principles to a bibliography of Quesnay's major works and a critique of previous legal philosophers regarding the nature of the social contract.</meta>

...that one must judge if there are excesses in government spending. “Let it therefore be less occupied with the care of saving, than with the operations necessary for the prosperity of the kingdom.”

Pecuniary fortunes <note>In Physiocratic thought, "pecuniary fortunes" refers to wealth held in money or financial paper. The Physiocrats viewed this as "sterile" wealth because, unlike agriculture, it did not create a "net product" or new value.</note> always rise to the detriment of the public good. “Let the administration of finance, whether in the collection of taxes or in government spending, therefore occasion none of them.”

The misfortune of the state does not stir pecuniary fortunes. They exist clandestinely and exist only for themselves: they have neither **COUNTRY** nor **KING**. “Let us then hope for resources for the extraordinary needs of the state only from the prosperity of the nation, and not from the credit of financiers.”

Financial annuities <note>Interest payments on government debt.</note> are destructive to public wealth. In addition to the debt they imply, they result in a trade that further swells sterile pecuniary fortunes, which causes land cultivation to suffer. “Let the state therefore avoid the loans that form these financial annuities.”

It is according to these maxims—inspired in Quesnay by reason, nature, justice, and the common and reciprocal interest of nations—that this great man composed all his economic works. The articles *Grains* and *Farmers*, with which he enriched the *Encyclopedic Dictionary* <note>The *Encyclopédie* edited by Diderot and d’Alembert, a cornerstone of the Enlightenment.</note>, the *Extract from the Royal Economies of Sully*, the *Dialogue on Commerce* and on the *Labor of Artisans*, the *Problems on the Revolutions* that would occur in prices through the effect of the suppression of restrictions on trade; that on the advantages of establishing a <term>direct tax|The Physiocratic proposal to replace all indirect taxes with a single tax on the "net product" of land, which they believed was the only truly taxable surplus.</term>, and his excellent *Treatise on Natural Right*, which is still one of the works in which he most showed his observant genius, discovering, with as much simplicity as accuracy, the most unknown truths. 

Until Quesnay, all writers—Grotius, Pufendorf, Burlamaqui, Cumberland, Vattel and so many others—had confused <term>natural right|The inherent, universal laws of justice and nature that exist prior to any human-made laws.</term> and jurisprudence, which has more or less regulated or restricted its use; they spoke only of the latter while announcing discussions on the former. He dispelled this confusion; it had been said, written, and maintained (it was a sentiment universally adopted among philosophers) that men, by uniting in society, sacrificed a part of their liberty to make the use of the other part more peaceful; Quesnay proved that men in society had never sacrificed the slightest part of their liberty and neither could nor should have done so; that the extent of their rights was precisely the same as in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of François Quesnay’s intellectual contributions and the reception of his Physiocratic system. I will not dwell upon several other writings with which he enriched the *Citizen’s Ephemerides* <note>The *Éphémérides du citoyen*, founded in 1765, became the official journal of the Physiocratic school (the "Economists"), serving as a platform for their theories on agriculture and natural law.</note> and the *Journal of Agriculture*. If one looks back through the chain of even the most remote centuries, one will see no man who worked more solidly than Quesnay for public happiness. Like his students, he experienced strange contradictions, maintained with a doggedness that shows very little enlightenment. It is not only today that people take pleasure in launching the bolts of anathema against those who preach a new doctrine. But neither will it be the first time that the most contested truths have triumphed over the most established prejudices and preconceptions.

The cradle of the high sciences has always been tossed by the storm. Their creators, as a reward for the light they spread upon the earth, found only chains and executioners. Confucius was threatened with death and Socrates suffered it, both for having taught a morality that posterity has admired. Ramus <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a French humanist and logician who challenged traditional Aristotelian philosophy and was murdered during the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre.</note> rose up against the chimeras of Aristotle and was slaughtered. Galileo published a proven truth and was loaded with irons. Did this marvelous art, which perpetuates from age to age the errors and truths birthed by the human mind (1), not bring persecutions upon its inventor in the capital of France? Thanks to philosophy, our century is not a century of barbarism: but is it for all that any less opposed to the progress of political truths? If it does not arm itself with daggers to fight them, it employs weapons just as treacherous, sharp, and biting: those of calumny and sarcasm. The virtuous man is not discouraged by them; he responds only with silence. His enemies may well congratulate themselves, but he despises them, pities them, and continues to do good by spreading instruction through his writings. How many such examples did Quesnay provide for us?

<meta>This page continues the eulogy of François Quesnay. one cannot speak the name without being moved, and who was the honorable victim of his zeal for the useful truths discovered by Quesnay, and to the dissemination of which he was the first to devote himself? <note>This refers to Victor de Riqueti, Marquis de Mirabeau (1715–1789), Quesnay’s first major convert to Physiocracy. There is yet a glory more precious than that of the mind, and which one could not refuse Quesnay without extreme injustice. It is that which takes its source from the qualities of the heart; he possessed manners so simple, morals so gentle, a character so steady, and conversation so agreeable until the end of his long career, that he always brought happiness to those around him. If he differed in opinion from certain scholars and if he engaged with them in disputes, he never mixed in the slightest bitterness; he knew too well that polemical works should not be libels, that reason is not expressed through insults, and that one usually resorts to personal attacks when one lacks evidence.

Quesnay had the rare talent for knowing men at first sight; he saw into their interior, read into the depths of their soul, grasped their tastes and their talents, and analyzed the whole of their being, if I may put it that way. From this talent came that prodigious variety of tones he adopted to put himself in harmony with the character of others.

The spirit of society is to make those who compose it shine. Quesnay possessed this spirit. In the circles where he was present, who ever left without being satisfied with himself and having a favorable opinion of his own merit? To find the means to make everyone speak with success, he feigned ignorance of many things and requested instruction in a manner always suited to the knowledge of those he addressed; he prompted thought and bestowed wit, in a sense, without it being noticed, so as not to wound self-esteem <note>The original term is *amour-propre*, a central concept in 18th-century French philosophy referring to a type of self-love based on the opinion of others.</note>. Despite his most brilliant reputation, he possessed a modesty that gave a new luster to merit; the base passion of jealousy never infected his soul. Being all things to all men, he enlightened with his knowledge the men who consulted him; he aided them with his advice and encouraged them with the hope of glory or the lure of rewards.

<meta>This page continues the eulogy of François Quesnay, following the description of his remarkable ability to read human character. It shifts from his intellectual talents to his personal charitable acts, his tireless work ethic in old age, and his deep religious convictions, which the author contrasts with the radical atheism of some contemporary Enlightenment thinkers.</meta>

Despite his modest fortune, he was the support of those he saw overwhelmed by the burden of poverty. His selflessness was unique, and this is why he left his descendants no other heritage than his virtues. When he used his influence <note>The original term "crédit" refers to his social and political standing at court as the King's physician, which gave him access to powerful officials.</note>, it was with the discernment and fairness required by delicate and scrupulous integrity. Let us not forget one of the most beautiful episodes of his life, since it represents so well the integrity and sensitivity of his heart. Someone was involved in a lawsuit; convinced of success if he could manage to bring Quesnay to his side—so well known were the doctor’s insights, impartiality, and justice—he pressed him to petition the judges in his favor. Quesnay fulfilled his wishes and helped him win his case. Shortly after, he was informed of the defeated party’s deplorable fate; he was deeply moved by it. His sensitivity gave rise to doubts that alarmed his conscience. To free himself from them, he sent the unfortunate man bank notes for the sum he had lost. How rare are the men who join a strict sense of equity with tender compassion!

Work was a necessity for Quesnay, which he fulfilled constantly through inclination and taste. Shortly before his death, he composed three memoirs on political economy <term>political economy</term> <note>In the 18th century, this term referred to the "Physiocratic" science of managing a nation’s net product and agricultural wealth to ensure social order.</note>, commissioned by a person in high office. Upon reading them, this person was so astonished that they could not help saying:

> "that the author had managed to preserve both
> "all the vigor of youth and the solidity of maturity in 
> "an octogenarian body."

It was unlikely that so many combined virtues did not take their source in religion. Quesnay possessed a great deal of it; he was not one of those impious authors who are indignant at the mysteries <note>original: "ténèbres" (darkness/shadows). The author refers to the aspects of faith that cannot be explained by reason alone.</note> covering one side of religion; who wish to calculate everything geometrically and subject the most sublime objects to the weak light of their own intelligence; who believe they can only acquire celebrity through their monstrous audacity in rising against heaven. Proud and haughty giants, they do not fear that in scaling the heavens they approach the lightning! They brave it even when it rumbles and they feel themselves struck by it. Quesnay, quite different from them, took religion as the foundation stone of his system; he respected it in all his writings and paid it the tribute it is due. His heart was filled with it, and his heart always guided his genius.

<meta>This page concludes the eulogy of François Quesnay, following the discussion of his deep integrity and his final intellectual works on political economy. It focuses on his stoic death in December 1774 and the lasting honors bestowed upon him by the medical community.</meta>

at last it must come to an end; and that terrible moment when, upon the brink of the grave, truth appears before us to reveal all the illusions that have seduced us, became for Quesnay the triumph of his heroism.

A few hours before his death, there is no longer any hope for him. The alarm spreads; his family already mourns him as the best of fathers, and the servant who attends him as the best of masters. Quesnay sees the tears of the latter falling and wishes to know the cause; he learns it without distress, with that intrepidity and that steadfast assurance given by a conscience sheltered from reproach and remorse. He replies to him: “Console yourself; I was not born never to die. Look at this portrait before me; read the year of my birth at the bottom, and judge for yourself if I have not lived long enough. . . . . .” Yes, great man, you had lived long enough for yourself, for your glory, but not long enough for the human race.

His virtuous life preserved him from the horrors of death; his final moments were without fear; he placed himself in the hands of religion and died peacefully on December 16, 1774.

The College of Surgery <note>The *Académie Royale de Chirurgie*, established in 1731. Quesnay served as its perpetual secretary and was instrumental in raising the status of surgeons in France.</note> has demonstrated, in a flattering manner, the high regard it held for Quesnay’s merit; it has kept his name at the head of the list of its members and placed his portrait in the council chamber among the portraits of its celebrated members: an honor it granted, during their lifetimes, only to Quesnay and to one other man endowed with the same genius as he in the <term>art of healing</term> <note>A traditional 18th-century way of referring to the practice of medicine and surgery.</note>. (¹)

How many titles capable of ensuring immortality are united in favor of Quesnay! Great by his writings, great by his conduct, great by the services he rendered to his fellow men, his glory will be eternal and unalterable. No longer is he among us, this benevolent man to whom antiquity would have raised altars—this legislator, this philosopher, this moralist, this universal genius, the light of his century, the oracle of truth, the interpreter of virtue. **QUESNAY** is no more . . . . Let criticism blunt its arrows; let malice be silenced, and let us at least learn to respect the ashes of great men, whom injustice spares so little while they live.

(1) Mr. Petit. <note>original: "M. Petit." Jean-Louis Petit (1674–1750) was a famous surgeon, inventor of the screw-tourniquet, and the first director of the Royal Academy of Surgery.</note> (Original note.)

<meta>This page continues the "Eulogy of François Quesnay," following the introduction of the Egyptian tradition of judging a man's life after death. It transitions from the ancient concept of merit to a philosophical reflection on how nature produces genius and how modern society often corrupts the original character of an individual.</meta>

With the swiftness of their spread, the ancient nations awarded only small prizes for great virtues; nobler palms, but a judgment more fearsome still, today await the man driven by the desire for glory. His judge is the general society of enlightened nations and impartial posterity. It is this severe tribunal which, weighing the actions and thoughts of men, devotes them to oblivion or to fame according to whether they were useless or virtuous; it is before this imposing tribunal that we are going to conduct the examination of a life that was full. Historians, if we seem to fall into the genre of <note>panegyrists: authors of speeches or texts written in high praise of someone</note>, we will not defend ourselves against it; it is the quality of a good man that his history is his own praise.

One of the most beautiful and perhaps least observed sights is the progress of nature in the formation of men of genius: lavish in her magnificence, she sows the seeds of talent as profusely as the seeds of plants, and both only grow in a small number of circumstances. The crowd of a large city, its distractions, its duties, perhaps even the luxury of knowledge and the multitude of study materials stifle these delicate seeds, just as the shadow of forests withers and dries the young stems that spring in abundance from the acorns the oak has shaken from its proud head. Our gardens produce only useless and adulterated flowers; it is in the mountains and on the rocks that fragrant <term>vulneraries: plants used for healing wounds</term> are born. The man whom nature raises in silence and solitude grows like her under the benign influence of the eye of the world.

In society, preceded by a multitude of effects that succeed and multiply without leaving time to seek their causes, the mind grows accustomed to a kind of laziness; it enjoys everything and knows nothing; it assumes and does not observe; the progress of nature is hidden from it, the simplest processes of the arts are foreign to it; its sensitivity is dulled, and in the clash of passions and interests it contracts only a vain politeness—a true lie of social customs, a seductive mask of universal benevolence. Each day alters the type that nature imprints on the individual; the result for the whole species is a uniform character; we are born originals and we die copies. (¹)

<meta>This page continues the "Eulogy of François Quesnay." But in the countryside, man, left to himself, belongs entirely to nature; his ideas, being less crowded, are less confused; they have the time to develop. Forced to question himself, he grows accustomed to reflection; a spectator of the great cycle of natural revolutions, of nature’s ends and her means, he unconsciously adopts the habit of order and proportions which, in every art, seem to be the secret of nature and her unique means of achieving universal harmony. Far from great interests, he is exempt from great passions; his undisturbed heart opens to natural sentiments—to that love for mankind which perhaps can only be preserved in its integrity when far away from them. If he carries within himself the spark of genius, gentle contemplation will enrapture his heart, and his mind, tormented by an insatiable curiosity, will constantly make him feel the need to perceive and to know.

Ignorance is the natural state of man; restlessness or tranquility within this passive state is the only difference between the common man and the man of genius: the latter is nature's masterpiece, and she does not produce him lavishly. Breadth of conception, sagacity, keenness of perception—in a word, the gift of the mind—is the first present she bestows upon those she favors; a fragile gift that circumstances can either develop or destroy. The mind is an instrument applicable to everything; chance—that sequence of causes and effects that we have not arranged ourselves—decides its direction and fixes its talent by placing it in certain circumstances. Taste, almost always determined by early habits (to which a tender feeling of memory attaches itself despite our efforts), confines the mind to a specific field, making it more familiar and preparing it for superior success. From this comes that almost general opinion of natural dispositions and of that sort of "particular vocation" <note>The author argues here against the idea of "innate talent" or a "calling" from birth, suggesting instead that interests are shaped by early environment and nostalgia.</note> which nature never actually gave. Even a man of intellect is in the hands of nature like a block of stone in those of the sculptor.

If circumstances favor him, if science—enriched by the spoils of time—opens its immense book before him, he will shine with immortal talents: at the bar <note>referring to a career in law</note>, on the stage, or in the solitary study of the learned and sensitive man, whose laborious leisure <note>original: "oisiveté laborieuse" — a common 18th-century term for the productive, intellectual work performed in private study</note> he will charm. But if nature acts as a stepmother <note>original: "nature marâtre" — a literary trope describing nature as cruel or withholding rather than nurturing</note>, or rather as a blind force, giving him the seeds of talent but refusing him the proper circumstances to make them bloom, he remains unknown to the entire world and to himself,

It is not so with the man of genius; to whatever class he may belong, in whatever rank chance has seen him born—upon a throne like Charlemagne or among the lowest of artisans like Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet." The ordinary man bustles painfully through the details of life; an ungrateful and inactive heir to the actions and opinions of those who preceded him, he enjoys the benefits of their discoveries without thinking of increasing them, and the favorable circumstances in which he finds himself without daring to conceive the possibility of expanding them. Nature, for him, is motionless, and the human spirit is without action: he is like that ephemeral insect which, destined for an existence of a few hours, is equally ignorant of the path of the sun that lights its way and the nourishment of the tree upon which it rests. But the man of genius cannot confine himself to these details that absorb other men: an immense horizon offers itself to his eyes; the origin, the progress, and the current state of opinions and circumstances occupy his gaze, and, in the distance, his eagle eye discovers what he can still add to the sum of the most <term>sublime</term><note>In this context, "sublime" refers to the highest, most transcendent forms of knowledge or beauty.</note> knowledge or boldest enterprises.

Genius is the spirit that generalizes and brings order; restlessness in ignorance and method in knowledge form its distinct character. Forced by its very nature to embrace a vast career, it seizes the most distant connections, compares them, and, making itself master of every detailed truth, leads them back to a common trunk—to a <term>mother truth</term><note>original: "vérité mère." A fundamental or generative principle from which other truths are derived.</note>, that unique and necessary principle of every science: for the universal genius who governs the world, nature itself is undoubtedly nothing but one great truth.

The chance of circumstances only holds power over him by determining the subject of his meditations; thus the apple that fell before Newton’s eyes (1) gave birth to the system of universal gravitation, and perhaps we owe the system of political economy <note>Political economy is the study of production and trade and their relations with law, custom, and government.</note> to the chance that placed Quesnay’s childhood in the fields (let us speak the language of posterity, for we are already that to him).

Nature paid the initial costs of his education, and if he always maintained a firm reason and a healthy, vigorous judgment, he undoubtedly owed it to the advantage of having formed his understanding slowly, admitting nothing that he had not first presented to the touchstone of examination; this path of the mind is quite contrary to common education which, piling the opinions of men into the memories of students rather than into their judgment through the sanction of authority, accustoms them to receive truth or falsehood indifferently and without discussion.

Nature had placed him at the point where Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French philosopher who famously advocated for "methodological doubt"—stripping away all preconceived notions to rebuild knowledge on certain foundations.</note> struggled to place himself when he wished to forget everything in order to relearn everything.

However, an immense curiosity wore upon his soul; already, aided by a surgeon from the village of Ecquevilly and the few books he could obtain, he had taught himself almost entirely alone both Latin and Greek, and searched through that obscure chaos of ancient and modern opinions that we call philosophy; a sterile study for one who was not already a philosopher. He who was reasonable enough to ask God for wisdom had undoubtedly obtained it in advance.

His own reflection had raised him to those few abstract truths that are within the reach of men; it only remained for Quesnay to confront nature with society and take his place in the world. His parents would have liked to concentrate his desires and views within the narrow circle of their fortune and habits: it is the misfortune of men who usually enter society prematurely to accept its burdens without knowing either what they are taking on or what they are capable of. Authority, pride, or caprice dictate to experience a choice whose least inconveniences are the distastes of incapacity; bitter and dangerous fruits of the double prejudice which, classifying men and jobs without regard for talent and respective utility, leaves to fortune the freedom to make the most bizarre and false pairings. Quesnay was spared from this danger; his soul was formed before his professional status, and prejudice allowed him to follow a profession that he was one day to make so noble. <meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, following his self-taught beginnings in the village of Ecquevilly. He had glimpsed the connections between surgery and all branches of physics <note>In the 18th century, "physics" referred broadly to the study of the laws of nature and the material world.</note>; in the study of sciences, it is the measure of one’s own mind that each person finds, and never that of nature. He thus triumphed over the opposition of his family, but soon the surgeon of Ecquevilly no longer found himself in a position to keep up with his pupil; the latter had composed several notebooks based on his readings, which his master—who had come to petition for admission to the College of Saint-Côme <note>The prestigious professional guild and school for surgeons in Paris, named after the patron saint of surgeons.</note>—dared to present as his own and was received with applause. At this signal of encouragement, Quesnay finally did himself justice; he came to Paris to finish the profound studies to which he had devoted himself and to receive his master’s degree. (1)

Several years passed for him in the practice of his art and in the rare, painful, and little-appreciated labor of digesting his ideas and observations to form theories from them; a laborious but enchanting occupation of the wise man, which tears him away from everything and leaves him with no regrets for anything. Perhaps the peaceful pleasure of this meditative state would have hidden him for a long time in Mantes, where he had established his practice, had not a rare and fortunate combination of circumstances come to snatch him from his obscurity to put him in his rightful place.

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, following his move to Mantes and the "fortunate combination of circumstances" that led him to professional recognition. ...a project useful to the public, advantageous to the art, and glorious for its author; this was the establishment of the Academy of Surgery. <note>The Royal Academy of Surgery was founded in 1731 by Georges Mareschal and François Gigot de la Peyronie.</note> He needed collaborators, and he sought them everywhere. He discovered Quesnay, and it was to this stroke of luck that the latter owed a celebrity that his modesty and his aversion to all intrigue would have undoubtedly denied him, or at least would have made him wait a long time to achieve. When so many conditions are required to form superior talent, so many conditions to bring it to light, and so many others to preserve it from intrigue and envy, should we be so surprised to see it in practice so rarely? Thus, when nature forms the diamond, it is not enough for her to have chosen a *matrix* <note>In mineralogy, the "matrix" is the surrounding rock or earth in which a gem is formed.</note> of sand or clay; she must slowly filter her crystalline juices and carefully push aside the metallic veins from which the stone might receive a distorting tint.

Urged by Garengeot to write about the art <note>The "art" here refers to the practice of surgery and medicine.</note>—to justify the testimony of this just and generous man—Quesnay willingly complied; a natural opportunity had presented itself. The physician Silva <note>Jean-Baptiste Silva (1682–1742), a prominent physician of the era.</note> had just released a treatise on bloodletting, whose principles were due to be challenged. Quesnay attacked it with a critique that was itself a complete treatise. His theory, absolutely opposed to that of Silva (¹),

---

(1) Silva, paying no attention to the **contractility** <term>contractility: the ability of living tissue, like muscles or blood vessels, to shrink or tighten</term> of the arterial membrane, considered blood to be like ordinary fluids that flow through absolutely passive channels. He believed he was able to divert it from one part of the body by opening a vein in an opposite part; he attributed this to **derivation** <term>derivation: drawing blood from a vessel near the affected area</term>, which he believed to be much more significant than **revulsion** <term>revulsion: drawing blood from a distant part of the body to redirect the flow away from an inflamed area</term>. This was an error, since derivation and revulsion must be equal to one another, both being proportional to the evacuation.

The effects of bloodletting are limited to evacuation, spoliation, and dimotion. <note>In 18th-century medicine, "spoliation" referred to the thinning or depletion of the blood, and "dimotion" referred to the movement or change in the flow of bodily fluids.</note>

At the moment of evacuation, a tightening occurs in the arterial membrane, always proportional to the decrease in liquid, so that after the bloodletting, the vessels remain as full as before; these are the effects of the contractility of the membrane and of air pressure.

Until then, the effects of bloodletting had only been explained by the "void" that people believed it left in the vessels; but how can a bloodletting, which does not remove even a one-hundred-and-fiftieth part of the fluid, cause such noticeable and lasting effects? Why do nine or ten bloodlettings discolor all the flesh, as seen in the dissection of such a subject, even though there is only a very small loss of the mass of the **humors**? <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that ancient and early modern medicine believed controlled health</term> why does the...

<meta>This page continues the biography of François Quesnay, detailing how his intellectual disputes brought him to the attention of La Peyronie. It transitions from his personal career to a detailed explanation of his revolutionary medical theories regarding bloodletting, specifically his concepts of "spoliation" and "dimotion," and how these apply to different biological temperaments.</meta>

...gave rise to disputes whose effect was to spread his reputation and serve his fortune. La Peyronie, now convinced, saw in him the man necessary for the establishment of his Academy. <note>François Gigot de la Peyronie (1678–1747) was the King's premier surgeon and a key figure in elevating surgery to a professional science.</note>

Does bloodletting weaken one more than other forms of bodily evacuation, and can it not be replaced by them? All of this is explained by what he calls <term>spoliation</term> <note>From the Latin *spoliatio*, meaning "plundering" or "stripping." Quesnay used this to describe how bloodletting specifically strips the body of red blood cells.</note>, a new term that expressed an even newer idea; that is to say, by the reduction of the red part of the blood which, in relative proportion, is removed in a greater quantity than the other humors. <note>In traditional medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note> This assertion is proven by calculations which show that by drawing a twenty-seventh of the blood mass, one does not even draw a hundredth of the total mass of all humors. This proportion increases progressively if bloodlettings are repeated, because the "white juices" <note>Referring to lymph and chyle, the colorless fluids of the body.</note> are incessantly reproduced, while nature only slowly forms that red blood which the hand of man spills so casually.

The <term>spoliation</term> facilitates the action of the arterial membranes, dissipates their contraction—which is the most common cause of the blood flow being cut off in the capillaries—and restores to this fluid all its circulatory movement: this is what he calls <term>dimotion</term> <note>A term coined by Quesnay to describe the "un-stopping" or movement of blood out of congested areas.</note>, an effect previously attributed to a "void" that was merely supposed to exist. The momentary weakening caused by bloodletting is another cause of <term>dimotion</term>; in that instant, the blood is carried from the arterial capillaries into the veins and the heart, whose action has just been interrupted and which no longer sends much blood into the arteries; the action of these vessels is very languid, they do not refill their capillaries, the blood remains as if stopped in the large arterial and venous vessels, and the capillaries of both remain very empty, from which arises the paleness of the skin.

From this theory is naturally deduced this small number of principles for practice: that bloodletting, while favorable to temperaments in which this red part abounds <note>The "sanguine" temperament.</note>, can be useful to a certain extent for bilious temperaments, in that it moderates the activity of the arteries which are easily irritated; but that it must be employed very soberly in melancholic temperaments, where blood is scarce, arterial movement is much slowed, and the humors are poorly processed; finally, it is extremely rare that it is suitable for <term>phlegmatic temperaments</term> <note>Original: *tempéraments pituiteux*. Characterized by an excess of "pituite" or phlegm, leading to sluggishness.</note>, where the humors are raw and glutinous, the strength is languishing, and bile is slow to form.

Women and children who, by reason of their weakness, share much with the phlegmatic temperament, have the same reasons to avoid bloodletting (a). The same is true for the elderly; in them, organic action is slowed; if it is further relaxed, the retained excrementitious juices will become more acrid. See the *Treatise on Bloodletting by Quesnay. Year 1730.* (Original note).

---

(a) One would be wrong to infer from periodic evacuation <note>Menstruation.</note> that women are more "sanguine" than men. They lose a large part of their blood through this process, and it regenerates more slowly than in our own bodies. A consequence of this same bias led people to regard the cessation of menses as the cause of uterine ulcers; there is reason to believe that they instead come from the acrimony <note>In 18th-century medicine, "acrimony" referred to a perceived chemical harshness or "sharpness" in bodily fluids that caused irritation or erosion.</note> of the humor, and that if they only manifest at the cessation of menses, it is because until then a portion of the tainted humor was rejected every month, so it did not have time to cause havoc. Bloodletting does not substitute for this advantage; it is likewise insufficient against hemorrhages because these come from a particular acrimony: neither can it be used to restore menses in the case of blood dissolution; in such cases, one must only use <term>iron-based remedies</term> <note>Original: *martiaux*, referring to "Mars," the alchemical name for iron.</note>, restoratives, stomachics, and milk. (Original note.)

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the professionalization of surgery in 18th-century France, shifting focus from Quesnay’s specific medical theories to the institutional vision of his patron, François Gigot de la Peyronie. This man, eternally famous in the history of the arts for the revolution he brought to surgery, was occupied solely by this project—the sublimity of which can only be felt by transporting oneself back to the time when he first conceived the idea. The goal was to gather surgeons into a single body that would serve as a repository of knowledge and a hearth of enlightenment. He understood that by uniting its scattered members, emulation—the mother of success—would animate every academician; he saw that when the isolated experience of each practitioner (which, even over a long career, can only produce a small number of often inaccurate and poorly observed facts) was compared and mutually critiqued, a more reliable theory would result, serving as an infallible guide for practice. 

This idea, which receives universal approval today now that it has been consecrated by the success of five volumes of memoirs—where every branch of <term>physics</term> <note>In the 18th century, "physics" often referred broadly to natural science and the study of the laws of the human body.</note> concurs to ennoble and enlighten an art which was then nothing more than a trade—this idea must have seemed bizarre and perhaps even extravagant in its time. How could surgery be pulled from the degradation in which it found itself? Lumped together with a lowly class of artisans, how could one hope to raise to the status of "academicians" a group of people, some of whom did not even know how to read? <note>Until the mid-1700s, surgeons were often part of the same guild as barbers ("barber-surgeons") and were considered manual laborers rather than educated professionals like physicians.</note> This is what La Peyronie dared to conceive, and what he executed. 

In less than twenty years, he raised his art to the highest point of perfection it could reach; superior talents were formed there, and by a rare stroke of luck, he seems to have left to his successor, along with his position, his paternal views for the advancement and perfection of surgery (¹); a rare example in our modern times of two men who devoted their lives and their fortunes to the public good and the progress of knowledge. If one must measure admiration for human enterprises by the grandeur rather than the celebrity of their plan—if one considers the resistance he must have faced from public prejudices (so quick to form and so slow to be destroyed), from the ignorance of the subjects he wished to employ, from the ill will of some, and in short, from the combination of moral obstacles, often more invincible than physical resistance—doubtless La Peyronie...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of François Quesnay’s indispensable role in the Royal Academy of Surgery, shifting from his editorial leadership to his specific scientific contributions and his transition from surgeon to physician due to health concerns.</meta>

If Quesnay was less original in the other memoirs, the facts of which had been presented to the Academy, he at least demonstrated the power of a methodical and analytical mind in their composition. He showed how wisdom knows how to link new observations to already accepted principles, and the resources of genius required to draw from them new doctrines applicable to a large number of cases that previously seemed hardly capable of such application. So much work secretly undermined an already delicate state of health; gout, from which he suffered frequent attacks, made him fear that his hand would eventually fail him in the practice of surgery. He therefore determined to take up the status of a physician; this was not a change of profession, for he had combined all branches of medical study in his training.

---

The stagnation of humors <note>In traditional medicine, "humors" were the vital bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health.</note> is born of stagnation when arterial movement is suspended: then, left to their own spontaneous movement, they fall into fermentation or putrefaction. In the first case, they become vinous, sour, or rancid; in the second, they become foul-smelling, their essential salt becomes a volatile alkali, their components separate, and they fall into dissolution. These two movements differ in that substances containing an acidic salt are alone subject to fermentation; it is rot that commonly attacks those containing an alkaline salt.

The imperfections of humors poorly formed by the action of the vessels <note>Referring to the blood vessels and their role in circulating and "processing" fluids.</note> are reduced to crudity, perversion, and faults of consistency.

Crudity <term>crudity: in historical medicine, this refers to "raw" or undigested bodily fluids that have not yet been properly matured or "cooked" by the body's internal heat</term> comes from the weakness of organs that are insufficient to process the chylous juices <note>Chyle is a milky bodily fluid containing fat droplets, formed in the small intestine during digestion.</note>, to disentangle the different substances from which humors are formed, to excite the heat necessary for their coction <term>coction: the "cooking" or ripening of humors within the body through natural heat</term>, and to expel excrementitious juices. This type of imperfection does not make them entirely harmful to the animal economy <note>A common 18th-century term for the functional system of a living body.</note>: these humors can still be brought to their perfection. It is not the same for those humors that the excessive action of the vessels has altered: fats, albuminous juices, and saline excrements are more exposed than others to this type of perversion. The consistency of humors fails through either excess or deficiency, but more often through the latter.

In the four following Memoirs, he undertakes to illuminate *practice* in one of the most difficult and important branches of surgery: head wounds. There, he determines the reasons for resorting to the trepan <term>trepan: a cylindrical saw used to remove a circular piece of bone from the skull</term> or for avoiding it; the cases where the skull must be opened across a large area; the exfoliations <note>The process by which dead bone separates from living bone.</note> of the skull and the means to hasten or avoid them. Finally, in treating wounds of the brain, he demonstrates this assertion—equally new and bold—that this organ itself is susceptible to operations which, in a great number of cases, can save the patient's life. He determines at the same time the remedies that are best suited for the cure of wounds involving this part. A discovery for which we must also give credit to Mr. Quesnay is his opposition to the long-held opinion regarding fractures that extend from one part of the skull to another across the sutures <note>The fibrous joints where the bones of the skull meet.</note>: he demonstrates that if one suspects any displacement in the bony parts, one must trepan directly on the sutures themselves. See *Memoirs of the Academy of Surgery.* (Note from the original text).
