...had shared with M. de Choiseul <note>Étienne-François de Choiseul, a powerful minister under Louis XV</note> the secret of the post, that is to say, the extracts of the letters that were opened; a privilege that M. d’Argenson had not enjoyed, despite all his favor. I heard it said that M. de Choiseul abused this and told his friends the amusing stories and romantic intrigues often contained in the letters that were unsealed. The method, as I heard it told, was very simple. Six or seven clerks at the General Post Office sorted the letters they were ordered to unseal and took an impression of the seal with a ball of mercury; then, they placed the letter, seal-side down, over a cup of hot water which melted the wax without damaging anything; they opened it, made an extract, and then resealed it using the impression. This is how I heard the matter described. The superintendent of posts brought the extracts to the king on Sundays. One would see him enter and pass through like the ministers, for this dreaded task. Doctor Quesnay, several times in my presence, flew into a rage over this *infamous ministry*, as he called it, to such an extent that he would foam at the mouth. "I would no more willingly dine with the superintendent of posts than with the executioner," the doctor would say. It must be admitted that, in the apartment of the king's mistress <note>Madame de Pompadour, in whose service the author, Madame du Hausset, was employed</note>, it is astonishing to hear such remarks; and this lasted for twenty years without anyone speaking of it. "It was honesty speaking with *vivacity*," said M. de Marigny <note>Abel-François Poisson de Vandières, Marquis de Marigny and brother of Madame de Pompadour. See page 122. — Note by A. An enchanter appeared and said to me: 'I am touched by your predicament: here, take this little packet of *perlimpinpin* <note>A term for a quack's magic powder or "snake oil," used here by Quesnay as an allegory for money</note> powder; everyone to whom you give some will house you, feed you, and show you all kinds of politeness.' But he who asks him for that beautiful ribbon, if he dared to say what he thought, would say: 'I am vain and I would very much like, when I pass by, to see the people look at me with a stupidly admiring eye, to stand aside for me; I would like, when I enter a room, to produce an effect and capture the attention of people who will perhaps mock me when I leave; I would like to be called *My Lord* by the multitude.' Is all that not just hot air? That ribbon will be of no use to him in almost any other country; it gives him no power. But my coins give me the means to help the unfortunate everywhere. Long live the all-powerful *perlimpinpin* powder!" — At these last words, a burst of laughter was heard in the next room, which was separated only by a curtain. The door being opened, the King entered with *Madame* <note>Madame de Pompadour, the King's official mistress.</note> and *M. de Gontaut*. He said: "Long live the *perlimpinpin* powder! Madame showed great friendship to the doctor, and the King, laughing and praising the powder, went out. I left, and the doctor did too. I set about writing down this conversation immediately. *Page 82.* An event that made me tremble, as well as Madame <note>Madame de Pompadour, the official mistress of King Louis XV.</note>, gained me the King’s familiarity. In the middle of the night, Madame entered my room, which was right next to hers, in her chemise and in despair. “Come,” she said, “the King is dying.” One can imagine my terror. I put on a petticoat and found the King in his bed, gasping for breath. What was to be done? It was a bout of indigestion. We threw some water on him; he came to. I made him swallow some Hoffman's drops <term>Hoffman's drops: A popular 18th-century remedy consisting of a mixture of alcohol and ether, used to treat fainting, stomach aches, and "vapors."</term>, and he said to me: “Let us not make any noise; just go to Quesnay’s <note>François Quesnay (1694–1774), the King's physician and a famous economist of the Physiocrat school.</note> and tell him that it is your mistress who is unwell, and tell his servants not to speak of it.” Quesnay lived right next door; he came immediately and was very astonished to see the King in such a state. He felt his pulse and said: “The crisis is over; but if the King were sixty years old, this could have been serious.” He went to his rooms to fetch some drug; he returned soon after and began to drench the King with scented water. I have forgotten the remedy that Doctor Quesnay made him take; but the effect was marvelous: it seems to me they were ***General La Motte’s drops*** <term>General La Motte’s drops: Also known as "Gold Drops," a prestigious and expensive proprietary medicine containing gold salts, believed to cure various ailments.</term>. I woke a wardrobe maid to make some tea, as if for myself; the King took three cups, put on his dressing gown and stockings, and reached his apartments leaning on the doctor. What a sight to see us all three half-naked! Madame put on a robe as quickly as possible, as did I, and the King changed behind his curtains, closed quite decently. He talked about his brief illness and showed great sensitivity for the care we had given him. More than an hour later, I still felt the greatest terror, thinking that the King could have died in our midst. Fortunately, he recovered at once, and no one among the servants noticed what had happened. I simply told the wardrobe maid to put everything back in order, and she believed that Madame had been ill. The next day, the King secretly gave Quesnay a little note for Madame, in which he said: *My dear friend must have been very afraid; but let her be calm; I am well, and the doctor will confirm it to you.* From that moment on, the King grew accustomed to me; and touched by the devotion I had shown him, he often made gracious faces at me, in his own way, and gave me small presents; every New Year’s Day, he would give me about twenty louis <note>Gold coins named after the King; twenty louis was a substantial sum, worth roughly 480 livres.</note> worth of porcelain. (1) We are dealing here with what is certainly Madame du Hausset’s most important communication for the history of political economy, for these Memoirs clearly concern the first draft—shrouded in a mysterious obscurity—of the **Economic Table** <note>original: *Tableau économique*, a landmark economic model representing the flow of wealth in an economy.</note>. Permit us to insert here some research that we have already published elsewhere (<note>original German title: *Die Maxime: Laissez-faire et laissez-passer, ihr Ursprung, ihr Werden*, Berne 1886; translated as: *The Maxim: Laissez-faire and laissez-passer, its origin and development*</note>, pages 100 and following), which can be reproduced here with a few additions. — In the earliest form in which it appeared, the **Economic Table** is lost to posterity. The first edition intended for the public was not made by the author himself, but by the Marquis de Mirabeau as an appendix to his *Friend of Mankind* <note>original: *L'Ami des hommes*</note>, 1760, and he presented it to the public after having reworked it. The **Table** appeared in a more extended form in the same author's *Rural Philosophy* <note>original: *Philosophie rurale*</note>, 1763, and it is only in the June 1766 issue of the *Journal of Agriculture, Commerce, and Finance*, then edited by Dupont de Nemours, that we find an *Analysis* written by the master’s own hand. This *Analysis* is reproduced in Dupont’s collection: **Physiocracy** <note>original: *Physiocratie*</note>, etc. (vol. I, 1768). Accounts even differ on the exact timing of its birth. The author, who is, as we know, Mr. Quesnay, has told us several times that this edition was from the month of December 1758 and that he had certain dates for it; the *Friend of Men* <note>Mirabeau's nickname, taken from the title of his most famous book, "L'Ami des hommes."</note>, his first disciple, who was then entirely connected with him, assures us that it is only from the year 1759 and even that it is not from the beginning of that year, and that he also has certain dates for it.”

Dupont adds that he only reports this difference in account regarding such a modern fact, and on the part of two men who should be so well informed of it, to show in passing how difficult it is to write history and how much one must generally rely on the dates it presents and on the small circumstances it reports. One may well admit, and it has always been admitted, that Quesnay’s indication is the correct one.

Now, what was happening at the court of Versailles in this month of December that gave life to the *Economic Table*? Never, during all the time that preceded the French Revolution, had such great disorder reigned there as at that moment. "...did not love the king, and with good reason," said Mirabeau, "and I love him too; but I have never seen you so passionate." — "Ah!" said Quesnay, "I am thinking of what would follow." — "Well! the Dauphin <note>The title given to the heir apparent to the French throne.</note> is virtuous." — "Yes, and full of good intentions, and he has wit;"

> "...some proofs." And Dupont de Nemours <note>Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours (1739–1817), a French economist and close associate of Quesnay who later moved to America.</note> later said (*Notice on the Economists*, in the works of Turgot published by him in 1808) in specific terms: "He (Quesnay) created this maxim: **Poor peasants, poor kingdom; poor kingdom, poor king.** And he had the good fortune to succeed in *having it printed at Versailles by the hand of Louis XV*." Others, for example Léonce de Lavergne (*The French Economists of the Eighteenth Century*, Paris 1870, page 66), then added that these proofs, pulled by the king himself, were intended for "the personal use of the king." Since then, this fact has generally been admitted in the literature of political economy. But recently Loménie, in *The Mirabeaus*, Vol. II, p. 194, has presented an objection on this point, certainly with reason, saying that all those who know the <term>Economic Table <note>Original: "Tableau économique." This was the first systematic attempt to model the workings of a national economy, visualizing the circulation of wealth between farmers, landowners, and artisans.</note></term> "have some right to doubt that the most indolent and careless of kings took the trouble to seriously apply his attention to it." And this doubt is confirmed if the preceding account by Madame du Hausset <note>The lady-in-waiting to Madame de Pompadour whose memoirs provide intimate details of court life.</note> can be related to the *Economic Table*.

It is important first of all to know when this memorandum, through which Quesnay had wanted to become prime minister, was placed before the King's eyes. Madame du Hausset gives no precise indication on this subject. However, the fact that the account begins with a note concerning both the disgrace and the cardinal's hat of Minister de Bernis (to which the obvious allusion "is he not going to be a cardinal" refers), leaves no doubt that the event the chambermaid would learn "a few months later" from Quesnay's own mouth occurred in December 1758. This was the month during which both the minister's promotion to the cardinalate took place (to speak exactly, *already on November 30*), as did the fall of the cardinal, and then the creation of the *Economic Table* (as Quesnay says). If this is the case, and it concerns the memorandum mentioned by Madame du Hausset, accompanied by the first draft of the *Economic Table*, it results in the remarkable circumstance that it aimed at nothing less than placing its author—and with him his economic system—at the head of the government. This was an attempt that Madame de Pompadour herself considered dangerous and which, despite her protective support, failed due to the refusal of the King, who had no sympathy for the economic dreams of his physician, as other communications also inform us (see page 130). It was Choiseul, as we know, who was chosen in his place, and it is perhaps for this reason that Quesnay always had an aversion to this minister, an aversion that Choiseul returned in full measure. To facilitate the reading of the memorandums for the King and perhaps the ministers, they already at that time, as is the custom now, had a limited number of proofs pulled by the printing press of the Chateau of Versailles. This took place regularly "by order of the king." Often such proofs arrived in the King's hands while still damp, which is to say, as if he had just taken them out of the press himself. The small

---

The number of copies that Quesnay had made of his Memoir and which, as is clear from all the indications on this subject, were intended not for the general public, but for the king and for people of his immediate entourage, may subsequently have been lost, or suppressed by Quesnay himself in order to make the traces of this unfortunate candidacy for the post of prime minister disappear once and for all; at least, we only know of this attempt through the communications of Madame du Hausset <note>The lady-in-waiting to Madame de Pompadour, whose memoirs provide intimate details of the French court.</note>. The "school" <note>The Physiocratic school of economic thought led by Quesnay.</note> itself said nothing on this matter. But the author naturally had to seek to preserve the theoretical quintessence of the *Table*. This was later delivered to the public, partly by the Marquis de Mirabeau, in various reworked forms, and partly in the form of an *Analysis* by Quesnay himself, but never—it is important to note—in its original draft. If, therefore, in these reworked forms of the Memoir, one does not find the expression "central point" referring to the post of prime minister, this changes nothing. Subsequently, Quesnay had to abandon the practical organizational proposals as no longer relevant to the matter and because they might have been considered treasonous. From all this emerges the error of those fanciful claims regarding the origin of the <term>Economic Table <note>The "Tableau économique," a diagram created by Quesnay to demonstrate how wealth circulated between different classes in society.</note></term> cited in the history of political economy.

Moreover, we have from this same Dupont de Nemours <note>A close disciple of Quesnay and a key figure in the Physiocratic movement.</note>, upon whom these singular claims are primarily based, an assertion which generally agrees with the information from Madame du Hausset; and as it dates from 44 years prior to his later claim mentioned above, it can command greater confidence than the others. Indeed, a few years after the creation of the *Table*, Dupont, who had only just joined Quesnay’s movement, drafted a treatise: *On the Export and Import of Grains*. At the instigation, no doubt, of his master, the author of this work dedicated it to the Marquise de Pompadour <note>The official mistress of Louis XV and a patron of the arts and sciences.</note>, and one reads in the dedication: *"It is to you that the public owes its first knowledge of it, through the printing that you had done in your home and under your own eyes of the Economic Table and its explanation."* There is, therefore, no mention of the king here. It was only later, when the <term>physiocrats <note>From the Greek for "government of nature," these were the first systematic economists.</note></term> found it unpleasant to recall their master's relationship with the royal mistress <note>Original: "courtisane."</note>, that they placed the king's name everywhere the Marquise de Pompadour's name should have been. Quesnay cannot be held responsible for this; he always declared himself openly and loyally a grateful servant of his benefactress, and it is obviously being faithful to his spirit to expose the real situation in its true light.

Are you not the master of the parliaments as you are of all your kingdom? — That is true, said the King; but without these councilors and these presidents, I would not have been struck by that *gentleman* (he always called his assassin by this name <note>The King is referring to Robert-François Damiens, who attempted to stab him to death in 1757.</note>). — Oh! Sire, cried Madame de Pompadour. — Read the trial, he said; it is the talk of these gentlemen whom he names that turned his head. — But, said Madame, I have often thought that if one could send the Archbishop (2) <note>original: "M. de Beaumont." Christophe de Beaumont, the Archbishop of Paris, whose religious rigor often fueled the conflicts between the King and the Parlements.</note> to Rome. — Find someone who can handle that business, he said, and I will give him what...

*Page 181.* M. du Verney (1) was Madame’s <note>Madame de Pompadour.</note> trusted man regarding everything concerning war, which they say he understood perfectly well despite not being a soldier. The old Marshal de Noailles called him, with contempt, the "general of the flour," <note>original: "général des farines." It was he who saw to the appointment of M. de Richelieu to command the army in place of Marshal d’Estrées. He came to see Quesnay two days later, and I was at his house. The doctor began to speak of war, and I remember he said: "Military men make a great mystery of their art, but why do young princes all have great success? It is because they have activity and audacity. Why do sovereigns who command their own troops do great things? It is because they are masters of taking risks." This speech made an impression on me.

"It can only be regenerated," said la Rivière, "by a conquest like that of China, or by some great internal upheaval; but woe to those who find themselves there: the French people do not go about things with a light hand." These words made me tremble, and I hurried to leave. M. de Marigni did the same, without appearing to be affected by what was being said. "You heard," he said to me; "but have no fear, nothing is repeated of what is said at the doctor’s house: these are honest people, though a bit chimerical; <note>Fanciful or visionary; living in a world of theoretical ideas.</note> they do not know how to stop themselves, however they are, I believe,

*Page 195.* M. Duclos <note>Charles Pinot Duclos (1704–1772), a French author and historian known for his social commentary.</note> used to visit the doctor <note>François Quesnay, physician to the King and leader of the "Physiocrat" economists.</note> and would hold forth with his usual passion. I heard him say to two or three people: "We are unjust toward the great, the ministers, and the princes; nothing is more common, for example, than to speak ill of their intelligence. A few days ago, I quite surprised one of those little gentlemen from the 'brigade of the infallibles' by telling him that I would prove to him that there have been more people of intellect in the House of Bourbon, over the last hundred years, than in any other."

"You proved that?" someone said with a sneer.

"Yes," said Duclos, "and I shall repeat it for you. The Great Condé <note>Louis II de Bourbon (1621–1686), a celebrated military commander.</note> was no fool in your opinion, and the Duchess of Longueville is cited as one of the wittiest women of her time. The Regent <note>Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who governed France during the King's childhood.</note> was a man who had few equals in every kind of intellect and knowledge. The Prince of Conti, who was elected King of Poland, was famous for his wit, and his verses are worth as much as those of La Fare and Saint-Aulaire <note>Refers to the poets Marquis de la Fare and the Marquis de Saint-Aulaire.</note>. The Duke of Burgundy <note>The father of Louis XV, known for his piety and studies under Fénelon.</note> was well-educated and very enlightened. The Duchess, daughter of Louis XIV, possessed infinite wit and wrote epigrams and couplets. The Duke of Maine is generally known only for his weakness, but no one had more charm of mind. His wife was a madwoman, but one who loved literature, knew poetry, and whose imagination was brilliant and inexhaustible. That is enough, I believe," he said; "and as I am no flatterer and fear anything that looks like it, I shall not speak of the living."

Everyone was astonished by this list and agreed with the truth of what he had said. He added: "Do they not say every day 'd'Argenson the Beast' (1) because he has an air of simple-heartedness and a middle-class tone? But I do not believe there have been many ministers so well-informed and so enlightened." I took a pen from the doctor's table and asked M. Duclos to dictate to me—

Duclos, meanwhile, was nodding his head. I left and tried to write down everything I had heard while it was still fresh in my mind. I had a valet, who possessed a fine hand, copy the part concerning the princes, and I gave it to Madame. But she said to me: "What! You are seeing Duclos? Do you wish to become a wit <term>bel esprit: a person of intellectual brilliance or wit, often a regular of the literary salons.</term>, my dear girl? That does not suit you." — "Indeed, I am far from it," I replied; and I told her how I had met him by chance at the doctor’s, where he would go to spend an hour whenever he came to Versailles. She told me: "The King knows that he is an honorable man."

## HISTORIOGRAPHER OF FRANCE <term>Historiographer: An official historian appointed by the King to record the history of his reign.</term>

### *Excerpts.*

*Page 28.* It remains for me to speak of two particular connections I still had at Versailles: one, based on simple convenience, with Quesnay, physician to Madame de Pompadour; the other, with Madame de Marchais and her close friend the Count d'Angiviller, a young man of great character. Let us begin with Quesnay, for he is the least interesting. Quesnay, lodged in very cramped quarters in the mezzanine <note>The original French term is *entresol*, a low-ceilinged floor between the main levels of the palace, where officials and high-ranking servants often lived.</note> of Madame de Pompadour, occupied himself from morning till night with nothing but political and agricultural economy. He believed he had reduced the system to calculations and axioms of irresistible evidence, and as he was forming a school <note>Quesnay was the founder of the "Physiocrats," a group of Enlightenment thinkers who believed that land and agriculture were the true sources of a nation's wealth.</note>, he was kind enough to take the trouble to explain his new doctrine to me in order to make me a disciple and a proselyte. I, who was thinking of making him a mediator with Madame de Pompadour, applied all my understanding to conceive these truths which he presented to me as self-evident, yet I saw in them only vagueness and obscurity. To make him believe that I understood what, in fact, I did not understand, was beyond my strength. But I listened to him with patient docility; and I left him with the hope of finally enlightening me and instilling his doctrine in me. That would have been enough to earn me his goodwill. I did more: I applauded a work that...

<meta>This page continues Marmontel’s account of his time at Versailles, specifically his relationship with the royal physician Quesnay and his maneuvering within the inner circle of Madame de Pompadour.</meta>

I found his work indeed estimable; for it aimed to make agriculture respectable in a country where it was too often looked down upon and to direct a host of fine minds toward this study. I even had an occasion to flatter him on this sensitive point, and it was he who offered it to me.

An Irishman named *Patullo*, having written a book (¹) in which he expanded upon the advantages of English agriculture over our own, had obtained through Quesnay, from Madame de Pompadour, permission to dedicate this book to her; however, he had written his dedicatory epistle poorly. Madame de Pompadour, after reading it, told him to approach me and to ask me on her behalf to carefully rewrite it. I found it easier to write him a new one; and in speaking there of the farmers, I attached to their condition such a poignant interest that Madame de Pompadour, upon reading this epistle, had tears in her eyes. Quesnay noticed this, and I cannot tell you how pleased he was with me. His way of serving my interests with the Marquise <note>Madame de Pompadour, the official chief mistress of King Louis XV and a powerful political figure.</note> was to drop remarks here and there that seemed to escape him naturally, yet which nevertheless left an impression.

Regarding his character, I will recall only one trait that will make it sufficiently known. He had been placed in his position by the old Duke of Villeroi and by a Countess d’Estrade, a friend and confidante of Madame d’Étiolles <note>Madame d'Étiolles was the name of Madame de Pompadour before she was granted her title.</note>, who—never believing she was warming a serpent in her bosom—had rescued her from poverty and brought her to court. Quesnay was therefore bound to Madame d’Estrade by gratitude when this intriguer abandoned her benefactress to devote herself to the Count d’Argenson and conspire with him against her.

It is difficult to conceive that a woman so wretched in every sense could, despite the ugliness of her soul and her face, have seduced a man of the character, wit, and age of Monsieur d’Argenson. But she possessed in his eyes the merit of sacrificing a person to whom she owed everything, and of being, for the love of him, the most ungrateful of creatures. Meanwhile Quesnay, unmoved by these hostile passions, was, on the one hand, the incorruptible servant of Madame de Pompadour and, on the other, the faithful debtor of Madame d’Estrade, who—

...vouched for him to M. d'Argenson; and although he went to see them sometimes without any secrecy, Madame de Pompadour felt no anxiety about it. For their part, they had as much confidence in him as if he had no ties to Madame de Pompadour.

Now, here is what Dubois, who had been his secretary, told me after the exile of M. d'Argenson. He shall speak for himself; his account is fresh in my mind, and you can imagine you are hearing him speak. "To supplant Madame de Pompadour," he told me, "M. d'Argenson and Madame d’Estrade had inspired in the King a desire for the favors of the young and beautiful Madame de Choiseul, wife of the *Menin* <term>Menin: one of six gentlemen chosen to be companions to the Dauphin, the heir to the throne</term>. The intrigue had progressed; it was reaching its climax. The rendezvous had been set; the young lady had gone there; she was there at the very moment when M. d'Argenson, Madame d’Estrade, Quesnay, and I were together in the minister’s office. We two were silent witnesses; but M. d'Argenson and Madame d’Estrade were very occupied and very anxious about what might have happened. After quite a long wait, Madame de Choiseul arrived, disheveled and in the state of disorder that was the mark of her triumph. Madame d’Estrade ran to meet her with open arms and asked if it was done. 'Yes, it is done,' she replied, 'I am loved, he is happy; she is to be dismissed; he has given me his word.' At these words, there was a great outburst of joy in the office. Quesnay alone remained unmoved. 'Doctor,' M. d'Argenson said to him, 'nothing changes for you, and we certainly hope that you will stay with us.' 'I, Monsieur the Count,' Quesnay replied coldly as he stood up, 'have been attached to Madame de Pompadour in her prosperity, and I shall be so in her disgrace'; and he left immediately. We were left petrified; but they did not suspect him. 'I know him,' said Madame d’Estrade; 'he is not the man to betray us.' And indeed, it was not through him that the secret was discovered and that the Marquise de Pompadour was delivered from her rival. This is the story from Dubois."

While storms were forming and dissipating beneath Quesnay's mezzanine <note>Quesnay lived in a small apartment on the *entresol* (mezzanine) level of the Palace of Versailles, directly above the King's private rooms.</note>, he scribbled his axioms and calculations of "rural economy" <note>Quesnay was the founder of the "Physiocrats," a group of early economists who believed land and agriculture were the only true sources of wealth.</note> as calm and as indifferent to these court movements as if he had been a hundred leagues away. Down there, they deliberated on peace, on war, on the choice of generals, and the dismissal of ministers; while we, in the mezzanine, reasoned about agriculture, calculated the *net product* <term>produit net: the surplus wealth created by agriculture after all costs of production are paid</term>, or sometimes dined gaily with Diderot, d’Alembert, Duclos, Helvétius, Turgot, and Buffon <note>This list includes the leading philosophers, scientists, and writers of the French Enlightenment.</note>; and Madame de Pompadour, unable to invite this group...

# A BRIEF NOTICE
## OF THE VARIOUS MODERN WRITINGS WHICH HAVE CONCURRED IN FRANCE TO FORM THE SCIENCE OF POLITICAL ECONOMY
### by DUPONT DE NEMOURS (1)

->(First part)<-

men united in society could be preferable to the researches of an abstract metaphysics, and even more constantly pleasant than reading little novels.

The success of the *Spirit of the Laws*, so well deserved due to the personal merit of its author, nevertheless persuaded many people who did not have the same merit that glory was not very expensive in the career path he had traveled. Some others glimpsed in how many respects it was still to be traveled; and Europe was flooded with a deluge of writings on legislation, on agriculture, on commerce, on manufactures, on population, etc.

Nothing proves better to what point we were far from having a science that decided these important objects than the strange diversity of opinions then debated among those who agitated these matters. Mr. Melon pleaded for luxury; Mr. Dutot pleaded against it; others held between the two. Some called for the *royal tithe*; this error of the great, the wise, the thrice good **VAUBAN** <note>Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban (1633–1707) was a famous military engineer under Louis XIV who, late in life, proposed a more equitable tax system to relieve the poor</note>, who did not know what the *net product* <term>net product: in Physiocratic theory, this is the surplus value produced by land after all costs of production (seeds, labor, etc.) have been paid</term> was and who had not thought that the costs of cultivation should never be subject to tax. Others demanded *taxes on consumption* <note>original: "droits sur les consommations"</note> and did not suspect that these taxes necessarily cost nations at least double what they brought in for sovereigns. The public, embarrassed by the crowd of arguments for and against, and of equal force, always found reason on the side of the one who spoke last ($^1$).

### THE YEARS 1754 AND 1755.

From the hands of these "madmen" full of wisdom there first emerged several writings in which one sees very useful and very judicious views shining through, though still spoiled by an almost equal number of very prejudicial errors. Such were the *Memoir on the Trade of Wheat*, by Mr. DU PIN; the *Remarks on the Advantages and Disadvantages of France and Great Britain, relative to Commerce*, by Mr. DANGEUIL; and the *Essay on the Nature of Commerce*, by Mr. CANTILLON. <note>Claude Jacques Herbert, Louis-Joseph Plumard de Dangeuil, and Richard Cantillon were foundational figures in early economics. However, even at this time, FRANÇOIS QUESNAY—whose works and important discoveries have raised his name so far above any titles and praises one could add to it—was led by his reflections on the state of cultivation and by his research into the character and power of *evidence* <note>In the philosophy of the time, "évidence" referred to a truth so clear and distinct that the mind cannot help but accept it; Quesnay sought to find these "self-evident" laws for society.</note> to examine, with the natural depth of his genius, whether one could arrive at a sufficiently large sequence of self-evident knowledge that it might sovereignly decide the rules of public administration most advantageous to the human race.

the necessity for farmers to be wealthy so that their cultivation may be successful and as profitable as it can be. He explains the extreme difference between the yields of land management that is conducted, directed, and funded by *wealthy farmers*, and those yields withdrawn from the labor of poor sharecroppers <note>French: *métayers*; farmers who give a portion of their crop as rent and often lack their own equipment</note> who do not have the necessary advances <term>avances: the initial capital or investment required to start a production cycle</term> to properly improve the estates entrusted to them. He shows that cultivators could only enrich themselves through the freedom and security of their persons, their labor, and their goods. He concludes that forced labor <term>corvées: a form of unpaid, mandatory labor tax</term>, the militias, the regulations that prescribed one type of crop rather than another, and the constraints and prohibitions in the trade of produce are public scourges. These, by discouraging wealthy people from engaging in agriculture, by diminishing the fortune of those who practice it, and by encouraging the sons of *farmers* to settle in the cities, expand *small-scale farming* and restrict *large-scale farming*, which would be infinitely more profitable. He demonstrates that all of humanity loses in this disastrous disorder; that the fate of agriculture decides that of society, because agriculture is the only *productive labor*, and that one cannot be compensated for its decay by the arts or by the trade of manufacturing and resale, which consist only of sterile labor that only the product of agriculture can pay and support.

Such was the first published work of **MR. QUESNAY** on economic matters, and we see that it contains two great truths quite unknown until his time by our political authors. One is that *agriculture is the* **SOLE** *source of wealth*. The other, that *to make agriculture prosper, it is not enough to have hands and good will; one must also have great operational wealth to employ there.*

In this same year, 1756, there appeared several other very estimable writings whose principles agreed greatly with those of the dissertation we have just discussed.

### YEAR 1757.

The foremost work in every respect to appear in 1757 was the entry *Grains* (political economy) in the *Encyclopédie*, by Mr. QUESNAY. One perceives in the dissertation bearing this title the progress of the author's discoveries and enlightenment. The entry *Farmers* <note>Referring to Quesnay's 1756 article "Fermiers"</note> presented several foundational truths of a great science. In the entry *Grains*, one sees this science fully formed and nearly complete. All the same truths the author had set forth the previous year are recalled here with great force and vigor, and developed with a clarity that shows they have become even more his own. They are linked here with new truths, no less important, which shed the greatest light upon one another. One of these truths, which could only be recognized by a stroke of genius, is the difference that exists between the average price of commodities for first-hand sellers <note>The farmers and landowners who produce the goods</note> and that for consumer-buyers. This difference is based on the fact that, in bad years, the cultivators and owners—who are the first-hand sellers—have only a small quantity of goods to sell at a high price; whereas in abundant years, they have a large amount to sell at a low price. Meanwhile, the consumer-buyers purchase an equal quantity every year, sometimes more expensively and sometimes more cheaply. Thus, the average price for the buyer’s expenditure is composed of EQUAL quantities at different prices, while the seller’s average is formed from the combination of UNEQUAL quantities with the same price differences—which clearly cannot produce the same results.

This difference, to the disadvantage of the first-hand sellers, is greater when there is more variety in prices. And there is more variety in prices when there is less freedom in trade. This is an unanswerable argument in favor of the freedom of trade in general and the grain trade in particular. It proves that this freedom—which ensures the preservation of grain from abundant years for bad years, and the alternating transport of surplus from countries that have much to those that lack it—equalizes prices between different districts and between different years. This equalization considerably increases

Another discovery, easier to make, which was right before everyone's eyes yet had attracted no one's attention—a truth found in the entry *Grains* <note>Quesnay’s seminal 1757 article for the *Encyclopédie*</note> that had always been ignored, even, as we have just seen, by the illustrious VAUBAN <note>Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban (1633–1707), a marshal of France known for his economic work *La Dîme royale*</note>, and even by the virtuous ABBÉ DE SAINT-PIERRE <note>Charles-Irénée Castel de Saint-Pierre (1658–1743), an early social reformer</note>—is the distinction between the *gross product* and the *net product* of cultivation. This brilliant distinction clarifies the benefits of high prices for produce, which yields a large surplus beyond the reimbursement of cultivation costs. When combined with the knowledge of the exclusive property agriculture possesses to produce wealth, one recognizes in it the entire *theory of taxation*. These two observations together show that commerce, manufacturing, the arts, trades, and finally work of every kind, should be exempt <note>The author uses "immunes," reflecting the Physiocratic belief that only land produces a surplus that can be taxed without stalling the economy</note>, and that even the reinvestments <note>Original: *reprises*—the capital a farmer must hold back to fund the next season's seeds, labor, and equipment</note> of agriculture should not be subject to tax. Taxation can only be levied on the net product without causing ruin, and must be proportional to that product.

The difference that nature has placed between *earning* and *producing*, which the author grasped so well, further enlightened him on the *illusion that modern politicians had created for nations regarding the balance of foreign trade in silver.* <note>A critique of Mercantilism, which measured a nation's wealth by its accumulation of gold and silver</note>

The essence of true gain among men—which does not consist in getting something for nothing, which is against the laws of nature:

->*Who sells even the blessings people believe she gives,*<-
<note>This poetic line emphasizes that in nature and economics, everything has a cost or a required investment; there are no "free" gifts</note>

—but which always consists in exchanges of equal value for equal value, reciprocally profitable to those who voluntarily decide on these exchanges, made him conceive the disadvantage nations face when harming one another. By doing so, they deprive those who would have naturally traded with them of the means to maintain that trade and pay for its returns.

One can see that the assembly of these truths, having entered the author’s mind through exact and scrupulous observation of facts and confirmed by calculation, already formed a body of science to which very little has been added since (¹).

We will not dwell at such length on the other works that we must include in this abbreviated notice: it is not that the *Reasoned Extract of all economic writings* <note>Original: *Extrait raisonné de tous les écrits économiques*</note> would not be a useful and interesting book; but for the very reason that it would be a *book*, we cannot include it in its entirety within this foreword. It simply seemed to us that we owed a few more details regarding the dissertations that opened and blazed the trail, and which, buried in a collection of twenty-two very expensive *folio* volumes, have not been able to find as many readers as they deserved.

What they will undoubtedly present as most singular is that, while all other moralists have started from the *natural right* of man to lead toward the rules of his actions, the author started from the calculated *interest* of men to arrive at the results strictly dictated by their *natural right*. Moral and political writers have often made the *justice* of some of the natural laws they developed very well felt; but they have always been at a loss to find the *physical sanction* <term>physical sanction: the inherent natural rewards or punishments—such as prosperity or famine—that naturally follow from following or violating economic laws, independent of human legislation</term> of these same laws. Mr. QUESNAY began by establishing their physical and imperious sanction, and it led him to recognize their *justice*. It is not surprising that his equally pure and luminous morality has made more rapid progress, since it presented more motives.

He had also composed for the *Encyclopédie* <note>The landmark 18th-century "Systematic Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts, and Crafts" edited by Diderot and d'Alembert</note> the entries: *interest of money*, *taxation*, and *men* (political economy). But when this dic—

> "Agriculture produces two kinds of wealth: namely, the annual product of the owners' income and the restitution of the costs of cultivation.
> 
> "The wealth employed for the costs of cultivation must be reserved for the cultivators and be exempt from all impositions.
> 
> "When the trade of local produce <note>Original: *denrées du cru*—raw agricultural goods produced on the land</note> is easy and free, manual labor is always infallibly ensured by the income from landed property.
> 
> "A nation that has little trade in its own local produce and which is reduced, in order to subsist, to a trade of industry <note>Referring to manufacturing and crafts as "industry," which the Physiocrats viewed as "sterile" or non-wealth-generating compared to agriculture</note>, is in a precarious and uncertain state.
> 
> "A nation that has a large territory and which lowers the price of its local produce to favor the manufacturing of manual labor, destroys itself on all sides.
> 
> "Worthlessness <note>Original: *non-valeur*—referring to low market prices</note> alongside abundance is not wealth. High prices alongside scarcity is misery. Abundance with (permanent) high prices is opulence.
> 
> "The advantages of foreign trade do not consist in the increase of pecuniary wealth <note>Meaning the accumulation of gold and silver</note>.
> 
> "One cannot know the advantage of trade and the state of wealth of each nation by the state of the balance of trade between various nations.
> 
> "A nation could undertake nothing against the trade of its neighbors without disturbing its own state and without harming itself, especially in the reciprocal trade it would have directly or indirectly established with them." (Original note.)

<meta>This page continues the discussion of François Quesnay's contributions to the *Encyclopédie*. ...dictionary <note>referring to the *Encyclopédie*, the massive Enlightenment project to catalog all human knowledge</note> ceased to be published publicly and under the protection of the government, Mr. QUESNAY did not feel he should continue to contribute to it. He kept his manuscripts, which are currently in our hands and which we certainly have no desire to withhold from our compatriots, who today know far better the value and utility of writings of this kind than they did in 1757.

One of the books that contributed most—both by itself and by its sequels—to bringing about such a happy revolution, appeared in that same year: it is *The Friend of Men, or Treatise on Population* <note>original: *l'Ami des hommes, ou Traité de la population*</note>, by the Marquis de MIRABEAU. This work, which appeared in three parts around the middle of the year 1757, published by *Hérissant* on rue Neuve Notre-Dame, is nevertheless not aligned with the principles of the science of political economy. It even contradicts them entirely, since the basis of his plan is to regard population as the source of wealth, and not wealth as the cause of population. <term>Physiocratic theory: unlike earlier thinkers who thought more people meant more wealth, Quesnay's school argued that agricultural productivity—wealth—must come first to support a population.</term>

But this error in the fundamental principles did not prevent the author from finding the truth in most of his results regarding the importance of agriculture, the necessity of free trade, the dangers of luxury, etc. In this work, he gave himself over entirely to the impulse of his own genius and the warmth of his brotherly heart; this engaging warmth made this *Treatise on Population* one of the most useful precursors to the science of political economy for a great many people. The sentiment with which it is imbued seized the souls of all its readers; it fixed their views, which were still wandering, toward agriculture. The title of the book (¹) became the name by which the author was known. This work, translated into so many languages and multiplied by so many editions, went seeking partisans and friends for him as far as the borders of Europe. And whatever efforts he has made since to fulfill his duty toward humanity, whatever writings he has published—some of which were even followed by events significant enough to mark an era—it is always by this name <note>The Friend of Men</note> that he is sought; and despite his own disavowal, it is by this work that he is known.

What is of an entirely different importance for those interested in the history of the science of political economy is that its inventor <note>Quesnay</note> judged from then on that *The Friend of Men* would become a worthy organ for this "science par excellence" and for the laws of the natural order; it is that he sought to know him; it is that from the first meeting, he did not mince words regarding his errors; it is that the docile soul of *The Friend of Men* recognized the truth, and that this illustrious man—then the object of everyone else's infatuation—became a student, loudly and stubbornly abjured his error, consecrated all the rest of his time and labor, and devoted his celebrity to the publication of the science discovered by QUESNAY. This is what he did in the subsequent parts of his work.

---

(¹) *The Friend of Men*. (Author's original note).

## YEAR 1758.

The first of these sequels appeared in 1758 under the title *The Friend of Men, Part Four* <note>original: *Quatrième partie de l'Ami des hommes*</note>. As with the first three parts, there are two original editions: one in a quarto volume and the other in two duodecimo volumes <note>standard book sizes of the 18th century; quarto is a larger desk volume, while duodecimo is a smaller, portable size</note> published by Hérissant, printer-bookseller in Paris, on rue Neuve Notre-Dame; there were also eight or ten pirated editions in the provinces, not counting translations and foreign editions.

At the head of this fourth part of *The Friend of Men*, one finds, instead of a preface, a *Dialogue, very lively and very cheerful, between the Superintendent d’O and the Friend of Men*. <note>François d'O was a notorious Superintendent of Finances under King Henri III, often associated with fiscal excess</note> The purpose of this dialogue is to show that all men are in a natural and necessary community of interests, and that even the most arbitrary and greedy authority would be obliged to conform to fixed, constant, and reasonable rules if it wished to make a profitable use of its power for its own sake.

This *dialogue* is followed by an *Introduction to the Memoir on Provincial Estates*. This *Introduction* is one of the finest pieces to have come from the pen of *the Friend of Men*. In it, he traces back to natural laws, which are the only fundamental laws of all societies, and distinguishes them from positive laws or regulations, which should only be emanations of the former, relative to circumstances. He shows that the bond of societies is *interest*, and that their base is *property* and respect for the rights of all. It is a great pity that in several places in this dissertation, so noble and so beautiful, the author was obliged to <unclear>sacrifice</unclear> certain specific principles, more in keeping with the current constitution of the state in which he lives than with the natural constitution, which is the most advantageous possible for societies.

The *Memoir on the Utility of Provincial Estates* <term>Provincial Estates: local assemblies in certain French provinces that had the right to negotiate taxes with the King, which the author preferred over direct royal administration</term> is, in this fourth part of *The Friend of Men*, only a second edition. We shall not provide a notice for it here because the title is sufficient to convey the objective of the work, and the details and discussion of the author’s reasons would lead us too far astray.

A *financier*, a self-styled *citizen*, attacked this memoir at the time. Instead of the *municipal sub-administration* to which *the Friend of Men* believed it useful to entrust the collection of taxes, this financier claimed that one should prefer to *work the provinces through finance* <note>a euphemism for the centralized and often predatory tax-farming system</note>. His claims, his expressions, and the very substance and wording of his work were equally pulverized by the *Responses to Objections against the Memoir on Provincial Estates*, which immediately follow that memoir. In these, *the Friend of Men* showed that he knew how to wage a good, frank, and rough war against those who undertook to "work" his friends.

The volume is concluded by some *interesting questions on population, agriculture, and commerce*, proposed to the academies and other learned societies of the provinces. These questions, which *the Friend of Men* felt he should add to his work, had been drafted by Messrs. QUESNAY and de MARIVELT.

Another very good work that appeared in 1758 is titled *Considerations on Commerce, and particularly on Companies, Societies, and Guilds*. It is a memoir that had been awarded a prize in

1757 by the *Royal Academy of Sciences and Belles-Lettres of Amiens* and composed by M. DE L'ISLE, under the supervision and with the advice of the illustrious M. DE GOURNAY, then Intendant of Commerce. <note>Jacques Claude Marie Vincent de Gournay (1712–1759) was a key figure in the development of economic liberalism and is often credited with the phrase "laissez-faire, laissez-passer."</note> One recognizes in it, as in everything that emanated from this worthy magistrate, excellent principles on the freedom of commerce. One finds there the most just and well-founded observations on the harm done to society by manufacturing regulations and the statutes of the <term>arts and trades</term> <note>referring to the restrictive guild system that controlled labor and production</note>, and the most singular examples of the damage caused by the inspectors who focus on enforcing these regulations—which are always useless when they are not dangerous and most often impossible to execute.

We do not know whether it is in this year or in the following that we should place the first edition of the *ECONOMIC TABLE* <note>Original: *TABLEAU ÉCONOMIQUE*</note>, along with its *EXPLANATION*, and the general *MAXIMS of economic government* which were joined to it under the title of *Extract from the Royal Economies of M. DE SULLY*: <note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, was the famous minister of King Henri IV; François Quesnay used his name to give historical weight to his new economic theories.</note> a very beautiful <term>quarto</term> <note>a book size where each sheet is folded twice to form four leaves</note> edition which was produced at the Palace of Versailles and of which copies can no longer be found except with the individuals to whom they were given. The author, who is, as we know, M. QUESNAY, has told us several times that this edition was from the month of December 1758 and that he had certain dates for it; *The Friend of Men* <note>The Marquis de Mirabeau</note>, his first disciple who was then intimately connected with him, assures us that it is only from the year 1759 and even that it <unclear>is</unclear> not from the beginning of that year, and that he also has certain dates for it.

We report this difference in account regarding such a modern fact, and from two men who should be so well-informed, only to show in passing how difficult it is to write history and how much one must generally rely on the dates it presents and on the small circumstances it reports. Fortunately, the history we are tracing here is that of enlightenment and its progress, where dates and periods are far less important than philosophical truths.

THE *ECONOMIC TABLE* is an arithmetic formula by which one can calculate with great speed, accuracy, and safety the effects of various disruptions that the distribution, circulation, and reproduction of wealth may experience, whether for good or for ill. Now, as one can perform almost no public act of government that does not influence wealth, the *Economic Table* provides a very prompt and clear means of very fairly estimating the value of all these operations by the precise extent of the profit or damage they must cause to humanity, to society, and to the various classes of men of which it is composed. This is why the invention of this formula has been regarded as the completion of the science of political economy.

There are two things to notice in the *Economic Table*: the formula itself, which depicts the circulation of wealth and which, according to the diversity of data, offers various results—advantageous, indifferent, or harmful; and the sum of truths that it was necessary to assemble, and whose connection had to be recognized and relationships weighed to invent it, and which must be grasped to understand it well. The formula is

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Economic Table" by François Quesnay, comparing its conceptual difficulty to arithmetic before moving into the publications of 1759, specifically the works of the Marquis de Mirabeau, known as "The Friend of Men."</meta>

very simple: like all operations of arithmetic, it can be very useful even to those who do not perfectly understand it. There are many people who perform divisions wonderfully and yet would be quite embarrassed to explain the logic of the process that provides them with undeniable results. The formula of the *Economic Table* <note>Original: *Tableau économique*, the first visual model of an economy, showing the flow of wealth between different social classes.</note> is easier to grasp superficially than that of division, because it speaks to the eyes and illustrates what it aims to convey. But the art of identifying, in different cases, the data to which one can apply this formula is much more difficult and much more complicated. It requires a prior and complete knowledge of almost all branches of the science of <term>political economy</term> <note>The study of how a country—the "body politic"—manages its resources and creates wealth.</note>. Very few people possess this knowledge; and that is why most have regarded the *Economic Table* as obscure and of little use. It is an excellent tool, which greatly advances the work, but its value can only be known by the masters who know how to wield it well.

In this first edition, the author presents the *Economic Table* of a nation in a state of prosperity. He explains the terms he uses in this table. He gives an example of how to calculate the total sum of a nation’s wealth when one knows the <term>net product</term> <note>The surplus wealth created by agriculture after all production costs have been paid; the "Physiocrats" believed only land could produce such a surplus.</note> of its territory and the state of its cultivation. The *Alleged Extract from the Royal Economies of M. de Sully* sets out in twenty-four maxims the conditions necessary to maintain a nation's state of prosperity. These maxims are accompanied by the most interesting notes, written with the greatest nobility, and where the warmth of patriotism and all the insights of a free and sublime philosophy shine. One sees that the importance of the subject and the utility that his maxims could provide elevated the author's soul. Such writings are very rare, and it is perhaps even rarer for them to be composed and printed within the palaces of kings. <note>Quesnay was the personal physician to King Louis XV's mistress, Madame de Pompadour, and operated a private printing press at the Palace of Versailles.</note>

### YEAR 1759.

The year 1759 first presents us with a very eloquent *Discourse*, addressed to the *Economic Society of Berne* by THE FRIEND OF MEN <note>Victor Riqueti, Marquis de Mirabeau (1715–1789), a leading economist who wrote under this pseudonym.</note>, regarding agriculture and the powerful reasons that must engage nations to respect it, favor it, and devote themselves to it preferentially; regarding the errors from which the administration of all states must protect itself under penalty of harming agriculture and, consequently, the reproduction of wealth which must nourish and make happy the people subject to its rule, and consequently under penalty of destroying its own power.

After this discourse, and under the common title of the *Fifth part of The Friend of Men*, one finds an extract from the most esteemed English book on the details of practical agriculture.

The *Sixth part of The Friend of Men* did not take long to follow the fifth. It is from the same year and includes a response to a book titled *Essay on Roadways* <note>Original: *Essai sur la voierie*</note>, whose author, a great supporter of the <term>corvées</term> <note>A system of unpaid, forced labor where peasants were required to work on public roads and infrastructure.</note>, had indulged in poor reasoning and ridiculous rants against what the *Friend of Men* had said in...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Physiocratic publications from the late 1750s, following the discussion of the "Economic Table." It specifically details the works of the Marquis de Mirabeau and his contemporaries regarding agricultural reform and free trade.</meta>

...his first work on this formidable method of road construction <note>This likely refers to the *corvée*, a system of forced labor used to build roads, which Mirabeau vehemently opposed.</note>. In this work, he defended the freedom of farmers using the strongest arguments and with the burning intensity of his character. It is in three or four places in this work that he happened to do something which perhaps belongs to him alone: to make his readers laugh and cry on the same page.

Under the title *Supplement to the Sixth Part of The Friend of Men*, and at the same time as the *Response to the Essay on Road Maintenance*, the *Second Explanation of the Economic Table* was printed; this is the first of those that **THE FRIEND OF MEN** <note>The Marquis de Mirabeau (1715–1789) was so famous for his book *L'Ami des hommes* that he was often referred to by that title rather than his name.</note> gave to the public. In this explanation, divided into fourteen sections, the author incorporated a large part of the notes and text from the Versailles edition mentioned above.

This same year offers us two other works that deserve a place in our record: the first is the *Essay on Land Improvement* by Mr. **PATTULLO**, a <term>duodecimo</term> <note>A small book size where the paper is folded to create 12 leaves (24 pages).</note> volume published in Paris by *Durand* on Rue du Foin. It is a sort of course on agriculture according to the English method, which concludes with extensive and very judicious reflections on the *freedom of the grain trade* <note>Original: *liberté du débit des grains*. The Physiocrats argued that removing trade barriers would stabilize prices and encourage production.</note>, which is the prerequisite for any improvement in cultivation, and without which it would be imprudent to attempt any, and impossible to do so successfully. In these reflections, the author recalls the calculation found under the entry *Grains* in the *Encyclopedia* regarding the difference between the seller's average price and the buyer's average price, and the advantage of price stability that can only be expected from free trade.

This decisive calculation is also represented in the other work we must discuss for this year, titled *Observations on the Freedom of the Grain Trade*, by Mr. **DE CHAMOUSSET**, a duodecimo pamphlet published by *Michel Lambert* on Rue de la Comédie and by *Humblot* on Rue du Foin. In this pamphlet, the author explains, with his natural simplicity, clarity, and modesty, most of the arguments found in the *Encyclopedia* under the entry *Grains* in favor of the free trade of this principal product of our land.

### THE YEAR 1760.

The year 1760 did not see a great number of writings published; but the only one it gave us can compensate for many others: it is the **THEORY OF TAXATION**, by **THE FRIEND OF MEN**. We will not go into any detail regarding this sublime work—which, to our knowledge, reached eighteen editions—and whose objective is to prove that all taxes, whatever they may be, ultimately fall upon the income of landowners; that some forms of taxation make them very burdensome to these owners; that there would be ways to replace them to the advantage of both the treasury and the nation, and that it is urgent to do so.

Apparently, it was then imprudent to disclose these truths, so essential to know for the good of the country, but which today are known to everyone. They brought upon the author a disgrace... <note>Following the publication of this book, Mirabeau was imprisoned in the Château de Vincennes for eight days and then exiled to his estate at Bignon for several months.</note>

(1) In the second part, especially, of the *Abridged Notice* (February 1769 issue of the <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>The *Éphémérides du citoyen* was the primary journal of the Physiocrats, a group of Enlightenment thinkers who believed that the wealth of nations derived solely from the value of "land agriculture."</note>), one sees how deeply this disgrace touched Quesnay and his disciples; indeed, under the heading *Year 1761*, one reads the following:
> “This year passed in silence. It was not, however, that the zeal of the citizen-philosophers who applied themselves to the study of the science of political economy had diminished; but after the misfortune that befell the **AUTHOR OF THE THEORY OF TAXATION** <note>The Marquis de Mirabeau was imprisoned in the Château de Vincennes for eight days in December 1760 and then exiled to his estate for his criticisms of the tax-farming system in this book.</note>, their respect for the government led them to believe this silence conformed to its views, the motives of which it was not their place to penetrate or judge. They only broke this silence after the permitted publication of several writings composed on the same subjects, by authors who had nothing in common with them but good intentions, proved to them that circumstances had changed and the moment for remaining silent had passed.”

And the expression of the author's grief is truly excessive in the report relating to *the year 1763*, where he says:
> “It was only toward the middle of this year that the explosion of a financial project <note>This likely refers to the royal declaration of 1763 regarding tax reforms and the cadastral survey.</note> where zeal had played a greater part than reflection, and the tolerance the government showed for other writings of the same kind, proved—after more than two and a half years of silence—that the administration would look kindly upon the efforts of citizens who applied themselves to the study of the science of political economy. Since that time, this science has been cultivated without interruption and with an ever-increasing activity, as has the number of studious men who have dedicated their labors to it.
>
> “When one reflects, however, upon this silence of two and a half years regarding matters most important to the happiness of the human race, it is impossible to ignore that the <term>progress of enlightenment</term> <note>Original: *progrès des lumières*. A core Enlightenment concept referring to the spread of reason and scientific knowledge to improve society.</note> was necessarily delayed by two and a half years. The result is that, since nothing can be remedied until a sufficient degree of enlightenment has been acquired, nations will inevitably remain for two and a half years longer the victims of the political disorders caused by ignorance of their true interests; for two and a half years longer, subjected to the destructive burden of <term>indirect taxes</term> <note>The Physiocrats argued that only a "single tax" on land was just; they viewed indirect taxes on goods and trade as economically ruinous.</note>, which are arbitrary and collected in advance; for two and a half years longer, oppressed and ruined by regulations on industry, by constraints on exchange and labor, and by reciprocal restrictions and prohibitions; for two and a half years longer, exposed to the atrocities of trade wars which never end except through the absolute exhaustion of both parties.
>
> “And when one considers that these *two and a half years more* can cause two million men to be slaughtered with weapons in hand; cause twenty million others to perish from hunger, cold, fatigue, and misery; make the existence of a hundred million others sad and unhappy; and prevent the birth of two hundred million children: one shudders: and one pities the fate of well-intentioned persons who, through reasons of state, out of regard for the circumstances surrounding them, or out of love for circumspection, prudence, and caution, allow themselves to be led into taking upon themselves the pronouncement of such terrible decrees.” A. D. <note>These initials refer to Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours (1739–1817), a prominent Physiocrat and the editor of the *Ephemerides*.</note>

# FARMERS

## (POLITICAL ECONOMY)

### Article by Mr. QUESNAY THE SON <note>Although signed "Quesnay the Son," this article was actually written by François Quesnay (1694–1774), the personal physician to King Louis XV and the founding father of the Physiocrats. He likely used his son’s name to maintain professional distance from his role at court.</note>

->Excerpt from the *Encyclopædia* (¹)<-

**FARMERS**, *Political economy*, are those who lease and turn to account the lands of the countryside, and who provide the wealth and resources most essential for the support of the State; thus, the employment of the *farmer* is a very important object in the kingdom and deserves great attention from the government.

If one considers agriculture in France only from a general perspective, one can only form vague and imperfect ideas of it. It is commonly seen that cultivation is only lacking in places where the land remains fallow; it is imagined that the labors of the poor cultivator are as advantageous as those of the rich *farmer*. The harvests that cover the land deceive us; our eyes, which scan them rapidly, assure us indeed that these lands are cultivated, but this glance does not inform us of the product of the harvests, nor of the state of cultivation, and even less of the profits that can be drawn from livestock and other necessary parts of agriculture; one cannot know these objects

---

<note>(1) The article appeared in Volume VI (1756) of the *Encyclopædia*; it was preceded, in this same Volume VI (also in 1756), by the purely philosophical article by the same author on *Evidence* <note>original: "Évidence," referring to Quesnay's theories on certain knowledge and natural law.</note>. In Volume V (1755) is found the well-known article *Economy* (moral and political) by J. J. Rousseau. It is not quite known how it happened that Quesnay—who until then had not yet given any public proof of his talents in this matter—suddenly took the place of Rousseau for questions of political economy. It is furthermore to be remarked that Quesnay signed his first two economic writings, the articles *Farmers* and *Grains*, as "Quesnay the son" and not with his own name. A. O.</note>

--- Page 188 ---
<meta>This page continues François Quesnay’s article "Farmers" from the Encyclopedia. Having established that superficial observations of the countryside are misleading, Quesnay now moves into a technical comparison between two systems of farming: the capital-intensive horse-based "Large-Scale Cultivation" and the labor-intensive ox-based "Small-Scale Cultivation."</meta>

except by a very extensive and thorough examination. The different ways of treating cultivated lands and the causes contributing to them determine agricultural output; it is these different types of cultivation that one must know well to judge the current state of agriculture in the kingdom.

Lands are commonly cultivated by *farmers* with horses, or by sharecroppers <note>original: "métayers." In this system, the landlord provides the capital (tools, animals) and the tenant provides the labor, splitting the harvest.</note> with oxen. People are prone to believe that the use of horses and the use of oxen are equally advantageous. Consult the cultivators themselves, and you will find them decided in favor of the type of cultivation that dominates in their own province. They would need to be equally informed about the advantages and disadvantages of both to evaluate and compare them; but such an examination is useless to them, for the causes that mandate cultivation with oxen do not permit cultivation with horses.

Only wealthy *farmers* can use horses to plow the land. A *farmer* who sets himself up with a four-horse plow team must incur considerable expenses before obtaining a first harvest: he cultivates for one year the land he is to sow with wheat; and after sowing, he only harvests in August of the following year; thus he waits nearly two years for the fruits of his labor and expenses. He has paid for the horses and other livestock necessary to him; he provides the seeds to sow the land, feeds the horses, and pays the wages and food for the servants. All these expenses, which he is obliged to advance for the first two years of cultivating an estate with one four-horse plow, are estimated at 10 or 12 thousand livres <note>The "livre tournois" was the currency of France until 1795. 10,000 livres was a massive sum, equivalent to the lifetime earnings of many laborers.</note>; and for two or three plows, 20 or 30 thousand livres.

In provinces where there is no *farmer* in a position to afford such establishments, landowners have no other resource for drawing some profit from their property than to have it cultivated with oxen by peasants who give them half the harvest. This sort of cultivation requires very little expense from the sharecropper; the owner provides him with the oxen and the seed; the oxen, after their work, find their food in the pastures; all the sharecropper's expenses are reduced to the tilling tools and the costs of his own food until the time of the first harvest—often even the owner is obliged to advance him these costs.

<vocab>agriculture, cultivation, farmers, sharecroppers, horses, oxen, plow, wheat, harvest, sharecropper, tilling, livres.</vocab>

<summary>Quesnay distinguishes between "large-scale" farming using horses, which requires significant upfront capital, and "small-scale" sharecropping using oxen, which is a fallback for regions lacking wealthy investment.</summary>
<keywords>Large-scale cultivation, sharecropping, agricultural capital, horse-drawn plowing, oxen, farming economics, François Quesnay</keywords>

<meta>This page continues François Quesnay’s technical comparison between two systems of farming: the capital-intensive horse-based "Large-Scale Cultivation" and the labor-intensive ox-based "Small-Scale Cultivation." Here, he discusses the financial arrangements of leasing and the physical limitations of using oxen.</meta>

<page-num>161</page-num>
Oncken, Works of Quesnay. 11

In some countries, the landowners, while burdened with all these expenses, do not share the harvests; the sharecroppers <note>original: "métayers." In this system, common in poorer regions, the landlord provided the tools and livestock while the tenant provided labor, usually splitting the crop 50/50.</note> pay them a cash income for the leasing of the lands and interest on the price of the livestock. But usually this income is very modest: however, many landowners who do not reside on their estates and who cannot be present for the sharing of the harvests prefer this arrangement.

Landowners who might take up the cultivation of their own lands themselves in provinces where one only farms with oxen would be compelled to follow the same custom, because they would find in these provinces neither sharecroppers nor drivers capable of managing and leading horses. They would have to bring them from distant regions, which is subject to many inconveniences; for if a driver leaves or falls ill, the work stops. These occurrences are very detrimental, especially during the busy seasons; furthermore, the master is too dependent on these servants whom he cannot easily replace when they wish to leave him, or when they serve poorly.

In all ages and in all countries, lands have been cultivated with oxen; this custom has been followed more or less according to what necessity required: for the causes that have bound men to this type of cultivation exist in all times and all countries; but they increase or decrease according to the power and the governance of nations.

The work of oxen is much slower than that of horses: moreover, oxen spend a great deal of time in the pastures to feed; this is why one usually employs twelve oxen, and sometimes as many as eighteen, in a domain that can be cultivated by four horses. There are some who leave the oxen for less time in the pasture and who feed them partly with dry forage: by this arrangement they get more work out of their oxen; but this practice is little followed.

It is a common belief that oxen have more strength than horses, and that they are more necessary for the cultivation of heavy soils which, it is said, horses could not plow; but this prejudice does not align with experience. In hauling, six oxen transport two or three thousand pounds in weight, whereas six horses transport six to seven thousand.

Oxen hold more firmly on mountains than horses; but they pull with less force. It seems that the

Haulage <term>charrois: the transport of heavy goods or agricultural produce by cart.</term> is handled better on bad roads by oxen than by horses; but because their load is less heavy, it sinks much less into soft ground. This has led to the belief that oxen pull more strongly than horses—who, in truth, do not find firm footing when the ground is not solid.

One can plow very light soils with two oxen; one can also plow them with two small horses. In soils with more substance, one puts four oxen to each plow, or else three horses.

Six oxen per plow are required in somewhat heavy soils: four good horses are sufficient for these same soils.

Eight oxen are used to plow strong <note>In historical agricultural texts, "strong" (fortes) refers to heavy, clay-rich, or compact soil that is difficult to turn.</note> soils: they are also plowed with four strong horses.

When many oxen are hitched to a plow, one or two small horses are added; but they serve for little more than guiding the oxen. These horses, constrained by the slowness of the oxen, pull very little; thus, this is only an additional expense.

A plow led by oxen plows, during the long days of the season, about three quarters <note>original: "quartiers." A quarter of an arpent.</note> of land; a plow drawn by horses plows about an arpent <term>arpent: an old French unit of area, roughly equivalent to an acre (approximately 0.85 to 1.3 acres depending on the region).</term> and a half. Thus, when four oxen are needed for one plow, twelve would be needed for three plows, which would plow about two arpents of land per day; whereas three plows, each led by three horses, would plow about four and a half arpents.

If one puts six oxen to each plow, twelve oxen drawing two plows would plow about an arpent and a half; but eight good horses leading two plows would plow about three arpents.

If eight oxen per plow are required, twenty-four oxen (working three plows) plow two arpents; whereas four strong horses being sufficient for one plow, twenty-four horses (working six plows) plow nine arpents. Thus, by reducing these various cases to an average state, one sees that horses plow three times as much land as oxen. Therefore, at least twelve oxen are needed where only four horses would be required.

The use of oxen only appears preferable to that of horses in mountainous countries or in ungrateful terrains where there are only small, scattered portions of arable land, because horses would lose too much time traveling to all...

Oxen that spend the night and part of the day in pastures provide no manure; they only produce it when they are fed during the winter in stables.

It follows from this that lands plowed with oxen produce much *less* than those cultivated with horses by wealthy *farmers*. Indeed, in the first case, good lands produce only about four septiers <term>septier: an old French measure of volume; for wheat in Paris, a septier was approximately 150 liters.</term> of wheat, Paris measure; and in the second, they produce seven or eight. This same difference in yield is found in the fodder that would serve to feed livestock and provide manure.

There is even another drawback that is no less harmful: the sharecroppers <term>métayers: poor tenants who provide only their labor, while the landlord provides the livestock and tools in exchange for half the crop.</term> who share the harvest with the owner use the oxen entrusted to them as much as they can to haul goods for their own profit, which interests them more than plowing the land; thus they neglect its cultivation so much that if the owner does not pay close attention, the greater part of the land remains fallow.

When lands remain fallow and become overgrown with brush, it is a great disadvantage in regions where one cultivates with oxen—that is to say, where one cultivates poorly—for the land there is at a very low price; so much so that an arpent of land that one would grub up <note>original: "esserterait."
