<meta>This page continues François Quesnay’s detailed economic comparison between using horses and oxen for agriculture. On the previous page, Quesnay argued that oxen-based farming is less efficient and produces less manure, thereby lowering soil fertility. Here, he begins a financial breakdown of the initial investment and long-term costs of livestock.</meta>

<page-num>164</page-num>

would buy an arpent <term>arpent: an old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre.</term> of land already under cultivation: thus, people prefer to acquire new land rather than incur these expenses; consequently, lands left fallow remain forever as common pasture <term>vaine pâture: the traditional right of villagers to graze livestock on fallow or harvested land; here it implies unproductive wasteland.</term>, which fundamentally degrades the owners' capital.

It is commonly believed that there is much more profit, relative to the expense, in plowing with oxen than with horses: this is what we must examine in detail.

We have observed that only four horses are needed to cultivate an estate where twelve oxen are employed.

Horses and oxen have different prices. The price of plow horses ranges from 60 *livres* <term>livre: the standard French currency of the time, which was later replaced by the franc.</term> to 400 *livres*; that of oxen is from 100 *livres* per pair up to 500 *livres* and more. However, assuming good teams, one should estimate each horse at 300 *livres* and a pair of large oxen at 400 *livres* to compare the purchase costs of each.

A horse used for plowing, kept as long as it can work, can serve for twelve years. However, practices vary greatly regarding how long oxen are kept for plowing; some replace them after four years, others after six, others after eight: thus, by reducing these different customs to a middle term, we will fix it at six years. After the oxen have worked at the plow, they are fattened for the butcher; but usually, it is not those who use them for plowing who fatten them; they sell them lean <note>In this context, "lean" (maigre) refers to livestock sold at a lower price before they have been bulked up for meat production.</note> to others who have pastures suitable for this fattening. Thus, fattening is a separate matter that must be distinguished from the service of the oxen. When oxen are sold lean after six years of work, they are about ten years old, and one loses approximately a quarter of the price they cost; when they are kept longer, the loss is even greater.

After this detail, it will be easy to understand the purchase costs for oxen and horses and to see whether there is a greater advantage in the purchase of one over the other.

These four horses can serve for twelve years: the interest on the 1200 *livres* they cost amounts in twelve years to . . . . . 720

There are some who employ oxen for only a few years—that is to say, until the most advantageous age for sale.

There are farmers who follow the same custom for plow horses and who sell them for more than they buy them. But in these cases, the oxen and horses are worked with caution <term>ménagement: moderate or careful use to avoid overworking the animals and preserving their resale value.</term>, and there is less advantage for the cultivation.

It is said that horses are more subject to accidents and diseases than oxen; it is granting much to agree that there is three times more risk in this regard for horses than for oxen: thus, by proportion, there is the same danger for twelve oxen as for four horses.

The general disaster caused by epidemic diseases in oxen is more dangerous than the specific illnesses of horses: one loses all the oxen, work ceases, and if one cannot promptly repair this loss, the lands remain uncultivated. Oxen, relative to the quantity required, cost twice as much to purchase as horses: thus the loss is more difficult...

Expenses are incurred for the shoeing and harness of horses that are not incurred for oxen: but only one driver is needed to plow with four horses, whereas several are required to plow with twelve oxen. These costs on both sides can be estimated as roughly the same.

But there is another factor to consider, which is feed: prejudice is in favor of oxen <note>It was a common belief in the 18th century that oxen were more economical because they ate grass rather than expensive grain.</note>. To dispel this, one must enter into the details of certain points of agriculture that need to be evaluated.

Lands cultivated with horses are rotated by thirds <term>rotation by thirds: also known as a three-field system.</term>: one third is sown with wheat, one third with oats and other grains sown after the winter <note>original: "grains de mars," or spring grains.</note>, and the other third is in fallow. Those cultivated with oxen are rotated by halves <term>rotation by halves: a two-field system where half the land rests every year.</term>: one half is sown with wheat and the other is in fallow. Little oats or other spring grains are sown because they are not needed for the feed of oxen; the same acre of land produces three wheat harvests in six years and remains alternately at rest for three years: whereas by horse cultivation the same acre of land produces only two wheat harvests in six years; but it also provides two harvests of spring grains and is at rest for only two years during the six.

The wheat harvest is more profitable because horses consume a portion of the spring grains for their feed: now, in six years, one has one more wheat harvest through cultivation with oxen than through cultivation with horses; from which it seems that the cultivation done with oxen is in this regard more advantageous than that which is done with horses. One must, however, remark that usually the field <note>original: "la sole," referring to the specific portion of land currently in the sowing phase of the rotation.</note> providing the harvest is not entirely sown with wheat; the slowness of the oxen's work often leads to putting more than a quarter of it into lesser grains, which require less plowing: from that point on, the entire advantage disappears.

Furthermore, it has been recognized that the same land which is only sown with wheat once every three years produces more, with equal cultivation, than if it bore wheat every two years; and one estimates the increase in what it produces at one-fifth more: thus, assuming that three harvests in six years produce twenty-four measures, two harvests in [six] <note>The text says "three years," but the context of the six-year comparison suggests this is a calculation for the two harvests occurring within the horse-rotation cycle.</note> years must produce twenty. The two harvests...

Oxen are also given a little bit of oats during times when work is pressing; thus, oxen consume roughly half of the oats that the sharecroppers harvest. They harvest three-quarters less than the *farmers* who cultivate with horses: therefore, only one-eighth remains for the sharecropper that is not consumed by the oxen; whereas a quarter can remain for the farmer that is not consumed by the horses. Thus, despite the heavy consumption of oats for the horses' food, there is more profit in this regard for the farmer who cultivates with horses than for the sharecropper who cultivates with oxen. It is not even preferred by owners who manage their own lands in regions where one only cultivates with oxen, because people blindly follow general custom. Only intelligent and educated men can protect themselves from common errors that are detrimental to their interests; but even then, to succeed, they must be in a position to advance the funds necessary for the purchase of herds and other livestock and to meet other expenses, for the establishment of a good system of cultivation is always very expensive.

Horses, through their labor, effectively provide their own food without reducing the profit that the cultivation must provide to the laborer.

This is not the case for ordinary cultivation done with oxen, for the harvests do not provide the food for these animals; they require pastures during the summer and hay during the winter. If there are laborers who give hay to horses, it is only in small quantities because it can be replaced by other fodder provided by the <term>spring grains: "grains de mars," crops like oats or barley sown in the spring</term>; furthermore, the amount of hay that twelve oxen consume during the winter and when pasture is lacking exceeds the small amount that four horses consume during the year. Thus, in this regard, there is still a saving on the feeding of horses; but there is, additionally, for oxen more than for horses, the expense of pastures.

This expense seems of little consequence, yet it deserves attention; for pastures suitable for feeding oxen used to plow the lands could likewise serve to raise or feed other livestock from which one could draw a real annual profit. This loss is even more significant when the pastures could be put under cultivation: it is only too well known how, under the pretext of preserving pastures for <term>plow oxen: "bœufs de labour"</term>, lands remain <term>fallow: "friche," uncultivated land</term> that could otherwise be farmed. Unfortunately, it is even in the interest of <term>sharecroppers: "métayers"</term> to cultivate as little land as they can, in order to have more time to perform <term>cartage: "charrois," transporting goods by wagon for hire</term> for their own profit. <note>Quesnay argues that sharecroppers prioritize their own side-businesses over the landlord's fields because they only receive a fraction of the harvest profit.</note> Furthermore, one must enclose the sown lands with hedges made of branches to protect them from the oxen roaming free in the pastures; farmers spend much time making these enclosures during a season when they should be occupied with plowing the land. All these causes contribute to making the expense of pasturing plow oxen very burdensome—an expense entirely avoided in regions where cultivation is done with horses. Thus, those who believe that the feeding of plow oxen costs less than that of horses are greatly mistaken.

A proprietor of an estate consisting of eight <term>domains: "domaines," individual farming units or manors</term> has about one hundred plow oxen, which cost him for their feeding at least 4,000 <term>livres: the primary currency of pre-revolutionary France</term> each year, the expense of each ox being estimated...

<meta>This page concludes the comparison between ox-based and horse-based farming, shifting from technical costs to a broader critique of the French agricultural economy. Quesnay argues that the reliance on oxen is a symptom of a deeper poverty among the peasantry, caused by systemic issues like taxation and urban migration.</meta>

<page-num>170</page-num>

But if one considers the true difference in the products of cultivation done with oxen versus that done with horses, one will perceive that there is a fifty percent loss on the product of lands cultivated with oxen. To this must be added the loss of income from lands that could be cultivated but are left <term>fallow: "en friche," land left unplowed and unplanted</term> for the grazing of oxen. Furthermore, it must be observed that in dry seasons when the pastures are parched, the oxen find little food and can hardly work at all: thus, the lack of fodder and manure, the meager amount of work, and the transport duties of the <term>sharecroppers: "métayers," farmers who give a portion of their crop as rent and usually lack the capital to own their own equipment</term> so limit the cultivation that the lands—even very extensive lands—produce very little income and often ruin both the sharecroppers and the owners.

It is claimed that seven-eighths of the lands in the kingdom are cultivated with oxen: this estimate can at least be accepted if one includes, under the same perspective, the lands poorly cultivated with horses by poor <term>farmers: "fermiers," specifically tenant farmers with enough capital to manage large plots</term> who cannot meet the expenses necessary for good cultivation. Thus, a portion of all these lands lies fallow and the other portion is almost fallow; this reveals an enormous degradation of agriculture in France due to the lack of *farmers*.

This disaster can be attributed to three causes: 1st, to the desertion of the children of laborers who are forced to take refuge in the large cities, where they take the wealth that their fathers once employed in the cultivation of the land; 2nd, to the <term>arbitrary taxes: "impositions arbitraires," such as the "taille," which were often increased if a farmer appeared to be prospering</term> which leave no security in the use of funds necessary for the expenses of agriculture; 3rd, to the restrictions to which people have found themselves subjected in the trade of grain.

It has been believed that policy regarded the indigence of the inhabitants of the countryside as a necessary needle to goad them into work: but there is no man who does not know that wealth is the great engine of agriculture and that much of it is needed to cultivate well. See the preceding article FARMER (<term>rural economy: "écon. rust."</term>). (¹)

However, one clearly exaggerates the scope of these relations by attributing to Quesnay a hand in the drafting of Le Roy's articles (among which are also the articles *Manure* and *Farm*).

<summary>Quesnay identifies the heavy reliance on ox-farming as a sign of French agricultural decline and lists three primary causes: urban migration, arbitrary taxation, and trade restrictions. He refutes the idea that keeping peasants poor encourages labor, arguing instead that capital investment is the true engine of prosperity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the economic analysis of French agriculture, transitioning from the comparative costs of livestock to a macro-level assessment of land usage and national productivity. It then shifts to a scholarly commentary regarding the collaboration between Quesnay and Charles-Georges Le Roy.</meta>

<page-num>171</page-num>

Those who possess wealth do not wish to be ruined; those who have none would work to no purpose, and men are not at all inspired to labor when they have no hope of improving their fortune; their activity is always proportional to their success. One cannot, therefore, attribute to political strategy views so contrary to the welfare of the State, so prejudicial to the sovereign, and so disadvantageous to the owners of the kingdom's property.

The territory of the kingdom contains approximately one hundred million <term>arpents: an old French unit of land measurement, roughly equivalent to an acre, though varying by region</term>. It is supposed that half of this consists of mountains, woods, meadows, vineyards, roads, barren lands, housing sites, gardens, grazing lands, or <term>artificial meadows: "prés artificiels," fields planted with specific forage crops like clover or alfalfa to improve soil and feed livestock</term>, ponds, and rivers; and that the remainder can be employed for the cultivation of grain.

It is estimated, therefore, that there are fifty million arpents of arable land in the kingdom; if one includes Lorraine, one may believe that this estimate is not forced. But, of these fifty million arpents, it is to be presumed that more than a quarter are neglected or <term>fallow: "en friche," land left unplowed and unplanted</term>.

There are, then, only about thirty-six million that are cultivated, of which six or seven million are managed by <term>large-scale cultivation: "grande culture," an intensive farming system using horse-drawn plows and significant capital investment</term> and about thirty million cultivated with oxen.

The seven million cultivated with horses are rotated by thirds: one third each year produces wheat and, in an average year, can yield about six <term>septiers: a pre-revolutionary measure of volume; for wheat, one septier was roughly 150 liters</term> per arpent, with the seed already deducted. This <term>field: "sole," a portion of land in a crop rotation system</term> will yield fourteen million septiers.

The thirty million managed by <term>small-scale cultivation: "petite culture," subsistence-level farming using oxen, often yielding far less than "grande culture"</term> are rotated by halves. The half that produces the harvest is not entirely sown—

In wheat, there is usually a quarter in <term>minor grains: "menus grains," such as oats, barley, or rye, often used for animal feed or the bread of the poor</term>; thus, every year there would only be about eleven million <term>arpents: an old French land measure roughly equivalent to an acre, though it varied by province</term> sown with wheat. Each arpent, in an <term>average year: "année commune," a standard measurement of productivity that accounts for both bumper crops and lean harvests</term>, can produce through this cultivation about three <term>septiers: an old French unit of volume for grain, roughly 150 liters or 4 bushels</term> of wheat, from which the seed must be deducted; thus the <term>sole: a specific section of land within a crop rotation system</term> will yield 28 million septiers.

The total product of both parts is 42 million.

It is estimated, according to <note>Nicolas-François Dupré de Saint-Maur (1695–1774), a French economist and demographer whose work on grain prices was foundational for 18th-century economic theory.</note> M. Dupré de Saint-Maur, that there are approximately sixteen million inhabitants in the kingdom. If every inhabitant consumed three septiers of wheat, the total consumption would be forty-eight million septiers: but out of sixteen million inhabitants, half die before the age of fifteen. Thus, out of sixteen million, there are only eight million who pass the age of 15, and their annual wheat consumption does not exceed twenty-four million septiers. Suppose another half of that for children under the age of 15, the total consumption will be thirty-six million septiers. M. Dupré de Saint-Maur estimates our wheat harvests, in an average year, at thirty-seven million septiers; from which it appears that there would be no surplus in our wheat harvests. But there are other grains and fruits which the peasants use for their food; moreover, I believe that by estimating the product of our harvests through the two types of cultivation of which we have just spoken, they can produce, in an average year, forty-two million septiers.

If the 50 million arpents of arable land (¹) that exist at the very least in the kingdom were all treated by <term>large-scale cultivation: "grande culture," an intensive farming system using horse-drawn plows and significant capital investment, which the author argues is far more productive than traditional methods</term>, each arpent of land, whether good or mediocre, would give, in an average year, at least five septiers, with the seed already set aside: the yield of one-third, each year, would be 85 million septiers of wheat; but there would be at least one-eighth of these lands employed in the cultivation of legumes, flax, hemp, etc., which require good soil and good cultivation; there would therefore be only about 14 million arpents per year which would bear wheat and whose yield would be 70 million septiers.

Thus the increase in harvest would be, each year, 26 million septiers.

These twenty-six million septiers would be surplus in the kingdom, since the current harvests are more than sufficient.

But it is not likely that such a large quantity could be sold at a good price. The English do not export more than a million each year; <note>The Barbary Coast (Barbarie) refers to the coastal regions of North Africa (modern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya), which were significant grain exporters to Europe in the 18th century.</note> Barbary does not export a million septiers. There are also about eight hundred thousand <term>tonneaux: a large cask or "tun" used as a unit of volume, roughly equivalent to 2,000 pounds of grain</term>, or seven million septiers, exported from Poland, which supplies the nations that buy it. These nations do not even pay very dearly for it, judging by the price at which the English sell it; but one can always conclude from this that we could not sell twenty-six million septiers of wheat to them, at least not at a price that could compensate the <term>laboureur: in this context, a "laboureur" refers to a wealthy tenant farmer who owned his own plow and teams, rather than a simple peasant laborer</term> for his expenses.

Therefore, we must look at the products of agriculture from other perspectives, brought to the most advantageous level.

The profits from livestock form the most considerable part of it. The cultivation of wheat requires many expenses. The sale of this grain is very unequal; if the farmer is forced to sell it at a low price or to keep it, he can only sustain himself by the profits he makes on livestock. But the cultivation of grain is nonetheless the foundation and essence of his status: it is only through it that he can feed many cattle; for it is not enough for livestock to have pastures during the summer, they need fodder during the winter, and most also need grain for their nourishment. It is the rich harvests that provide these: it is therefore from these two points of view that one must consider the management of agriculture.

In a kingdom like France, whose territory is so extensive and which would produce much more wheat than could be sold, one should only focus on the cultivation of good lands for the production of wheat; the very mediocre lands cultivated for wheat do not sufficiently compensate for the costs of such cultivation. We are not speaking here of the improvements of these lands; we are far from being able to afford those costs in France, where we cannot even, by a long shot, meet the expenses of simple agriculture. But these same lands can be more profitable if they are put to use through the cultivation of <term>minor grains: "menus grains," such as oats, barley, or rye, often used for animal feed or the bread of the poor</term>,

The vineyard owner apparently finds more advantage in cultivating vines; or else he requires less wealth to sustain this cultivation than to prepare lands to produce wheat. Each person considers his own <term>faculties: the financial means, resources, or capital available to an individual</term>; if one restricts by laws the customs established by invincible reasons, these laws are nothing but new obstacles opposed to agriculture: such legislation is all the more misplaced regarding vines, as it is not land that is lacking for the cultivation of wheat; it is the means to make them productive.

In England, much land is reserved for providing food for livestock. There is a prodigious quantity of livestock on this island; and the profit from it is so considerable that the product of wool alone is evaluated at more than one hundred and sixty million.

However, it must be admitted that in a very extensive kingdom, good lands should be preferred for the cultivation of wheat, because this cultivation is very expensive; the more ungrateful the lands are, the more they require expenditure and the less they can, by their own value, compensate the farmer.

Assuming, therefore, that we limited the cultivation of wheat in France to the good lands, this cultivation could be reduced to thirty million <term>arpents: an old French unit of land measurement, roughly equivalent to an acre</term>, of which ten would be sown each year in wheat, ten in oats, and ten in <term>fallow: land left unseeded for a season to restore its fertility</term>.

Ten million arpents of good, well-cultivated land, sown in wheat, would produce, in an average year, at least six <term>septiers: a historical measure of volume for grain, roughly 150 liters</term> per arpent, after the seed has been set aside; thus, the ten million arpents would yield sixty million septiers.

This quantity would exceed the product of our current wheat harvests by eighteen million septiers. If this surplus were sold abroad at only seventeen <term>livres: the primary currency of pre-revolutionary France</term> per septier—a low price due to the abundance—the eighteen million septiers would produce more than three hundred million livres; and there would still remain 20 or 30 million arpents of our land, not including vineyards, which would be used for other crops.

The increase in the harvest of oats and <term>small grains: lesser cereals like rye, barley, or buckwheat</term> that follow the wheat would be in the same proportion; it would serve, along with the product from the cultivation of mediocre lands, to increase the profit from livestock.

One could even presume that the wheat carried abroad would sell for about twenty livres per septier, the average price, provided that trade in wheat were free; for from the time of <note>reigned 1560–1574</note> Charles IX until the end of the reign of <note>reigned 1643–1715</note> Louis XIV, the average prices, calculated by decades, varied from 20 to 30 livres of our money today—that is to say, from about one-third to one-half the value of the <term>marc of silver: a historical unit of weight used for measuring precious metals</term>; a pound of wheat, which produces a pound of coarse bread, was worth about one <term>sou: a small coin, 1/20th of a livre</term>, which is two sous in our current money.

<meta>This page continues the economic analysis of wheat production. The previous page established that focusing on high-quality land could produce a significant surplus of grain (eighteen million septiers) which, if sold at seventeen livres, would generate three hundred million livres in revenue.</meta>

...culture, because the farmer is not forced to hoard his grain; he can always meet the necessary expenses for cultivation through the annual product of the harvests.

It is astonishing that in France, in recent times, wheat has fallen so far below its ordinary price and yet we so often experience <term>disettes: periods of scarcity or dearth, often leading to famine</term>. For more than 30 years, the common price of wheat has only reached 17 <term>livres: the primary currency of pre-revolutionary France</term>; in such cases, the "low price" of wheat is between eleven and thirteen livres. Scarcities occur easily following such low prices in a kingdom where there are so many poor <term>laboureurs: tenant farmers or independent cultivators who worked the land</term>; they cannot afford to wait for favorable times to sell their grain. Lacking a market, they are even forced to have part of their wheat consumed by livestock to extract some profit from it. These failures discourage them; the cultivation and the quantity of wheat decrease simultaneously, and scarcity ensues.

It is a very common custom among farmers, when wheat is at a low price, not to thresh the sheaves entirely, so that much grain remains in the fodder they give to the sheep. By this practice, they keep them fat during the winter and spring, and they derive more profit from the sale of these sheep than from the sale of the wheat. Thus, it is easy to understand, through this custom, why scarcities occur when bad years arrive.

It is estimated that, in an average year, harvests produce enough wheat for about two months more than a year's consumption. <note>The author is critiquing the optimistic "average year" statistics used by the government, which ignored the reality of poor storage and waste.</note> But the estimate of an average year is based on both good and bad harvests, and it assumes the preservation of the surplus grains produced by good harvests. This assumption being false, it follows that wheat must become very expensive when a bad harvest occurs, because the low price of wheat in previous years led the cultivator to use it for fattening livestock and caused him to neglect cultivation. Thus, it has been observed that abundant years—where wheat was at a low price and which are followed by a bad year—do not protect against scarcity. But the high price of wheat does not then compensate the poor farmer, because he has little to sell in bad years. The "average price" formed from the prices of several years is no rule for him; he does not share in this compensation, which exists only in calculations as far as he is concerned.

Thus, the total product of the wheat and the oats exceeds the costs by only 150 livres, a sum in which no provision has been made for his own food or the maintenance of himself and his family. He could only satisfy these essential needs through the yield of some livestock, and he would always remain poor and in danger of being ruined by losses: grains must therefore be at a higher price for him to be able to support himself and establish his children.

The <term>métayer: a sharecropper who provides labor while the landlord provides the land and capital</term> who cultivates with oxen commonly harvests only at a rate of five-to-one <note>meaning five seeds harvested for every one sown</note>; that is three and a third <term>septiers: a dry measure of volume, approximately 150 liters</term> per arpent: one-fifth must be deducted for seed. He splits this harvest in half with the landowner, who provides him with the oxen, the fallow lands, and the meadows to feed the oxen; [the landlord] exempts him from land rent and also provides him with some other livestock, the profit of which he shares. This sharecropper and his family cultivate the land themselves and avoid the cost of servants, a portion of the harvest costs, and the threshing costs: he spends little on the <term>harness-maker</term> and the <term>blacksmith</term>, etc. If this sharecropper cultivates thirty arpents of wheat each year, he commonly harvests for his share about thirty or thirty-five septiers, of which he consumes the greatest part for his food and that of his family: the remainder is used to pay his <term>taille: a direct land tax paid by commoners to the French crown</term>, the costs of laborers he cannot avoid, and the expenses he is forced to make for his needs and those of his family. He remains always very poor; and even when the land is mediocre, he can only sustain himself by the <term>charrois: cartage or transport services</term> he performs for his own profit. The <term>taille</term> imposed upon him is a small thing compared to that of the <term>farmer: in this period, a "fermier" was a wealthy tenant who paid a fixed cash rent, as opposed to the poorer sharecropping "métayer"</term>, because he harvests little and has no property of his own to secure the tax: his harvests being very weak, he has little fodder for the feeding of livestock during the winter: such that his...

The condition of the landowner is no more advantageous; he receives about 15 bushels per <term>arpent: a pre-metric unit of land area, roughly an acre</term>; instead of the two years' rent that a *tenant farmer* <note>original: "fermier" – in this context, a large-scale farmer with his own capital, distinguished from a poor laborer</note> would pay him, he loses the interest on the capital advances he provides to the <term>métayer: a sharecropper who provides labor while the landlord provides the land and livestock</term> for the oxen. If one aims to favor city dwellers, factory workers, and artisans through the low price of wheat, one desolates the *countryside*, which is the source of the *State's* true wealth: moreover, this plan fails. Bread is not man's only food; and it is still agriculture, when protected, that provides other foods in abundance.

The citizens, by buying a pound of bread for a few <term>liards: a small copper coin of very low value</term> more, would spend much less to satisfy their needs. *The regulatory administration <note>original: "la police" – referring to the government's grain-regulation policies</note> only has the power to decrease the price of wheat by preventing export*; but the price of other commodities is not similarly at its disposal, and it greatly harms the well-being of city dwellers by providing them with some slight savings on wheat while destroying agriculture. Butter, cheese, eggs, vegetables, etc., are at exorbitant prices, which proportionally increases the cost of clothing and other works of the artisans that the common people need. The high cost of these commodities increases the wages of workers. They abandon the countryside, or else they are reduced to feeding themselves on oats, barley, buckwheat, potatoes, and other cheap crops <note>original: "productions de vil prix"</note> that they cultivate themselves and which yield a harvest quickly. The cultivation of wheat requires too much time and labor: they cannot wait two years to obtain a harvest. This cultivation is reserved for the *tenant farmer* <note>original: "fermier" – a capitalist farmer who pays rent in cash and owns his equipment</note> who can afford the expenses, or for the sharecropper who is assisted by the landowner and who, moreover, is a weak resource for agriculture; but this is the only option for landowners who lack *tenant farmers*. The *tenant farmers* themselves can only profit through the superiority of their cultivation and the good quality of the lands they work; for they can only gain insofar as their harvests exceed their expenses. If, after the seeds and expenses are deducted, a *tenant farmer* has one <term>setier: a traditional French unit of volume, roughly 150 liters for grain</term> more per <term>arpent: a pre-metric unit of land area, approximately one acre</term>, that is where his advantage lies; for forty *arpents* sown with wheat then provide him a profit of forty *setiers*, which are worth about 600 livres; and if he cultivates so well that he can keep two *setiers* per *arpent* for himself, his profit is doubled. For this to happen, each *arpent* of land must produce seven to eight *setiers*; but he can only obtain this yield from good soil. When the lands he cultivates are partly good and partly poor, the profit can only be very mediocre.

The peasant who would undertake to cultivate wheat with only his own arms could not compensate himself for his labor; for he would cultivate so little that even if he had a few *setiers* of profit beyond his food and expenses, this advantage would not suffice for his needs. It is only from large harvests that one can draw any profit. This is why a *tenant farmer* who employs several plows and who cultivates good land profits much more than one who is limited to a single plow and who cultivates equally good land: and even in this latter case, the expenses are, in many respects, more considerable in proportion. But if he who is limited to a single plow lacks the wealth to expand his operation, he does well to restrict himself because he could not meet the expenses that a larger enterprise would require.

the profit and the principal from the purchase return to him; he can repay the sums he borrows: but the farmer can only withdraw the profit from the advances he has made for agriculture; the principal remains to sustain the same cultivation enterprise; thus, he cannot borrow it to repay it at fixed terms, and since his assets are in movable property <note>original: "mobilier" – meaning livestock, tools, and harvested crops rather than land itself</note>, those who might lend to him would not find enough security to place their money permanently. Those who are in a position to make these expenditures analyze the situation and do not expose their property to a certain loss. Grain is kept at a very low price in an age when all other commodities and labor have become very expensive. The farmer's expenses are thus increased by more than a third at the same time that his profits are diminished by a third; thus he suffers a double loss which diminishes his means and leaves him unable to sustain the costs of good cultivation: consequently, the status of the *tenant farmer* has almost ceased to exist; agriculture is abandoned to sharecroppers <note>original: "métayers" – poor farmers who do not own their equipment and must give half their harvest to the landlord</note>, to the great detriment of the State.

It is not simply good or bad harvests that regulate the price of grain; it is primarily freedom or constraint in the trade of this commodity that decides its value. If one wishes to restrict or hinder trade during times of good harvests, one disrupts the products of agriculture, weakens the State, diminishes the income of landowners, and encourages the laziness and arrogance of the domestic servants and laborers who ought to assist in agriculture; one ruins the farmers and depopulates the countryside. It would be a failure to recognize the advantages of France to prevent the export of grain for fear of running out, in a kingdom that can produce far more than could ever be sold abroad. The conduct of England in this regard proves, on the contrary, that there is no surer means to sustain agriculture, maintain abundance, and prevent famines than the sale of a portion of the harvests abroad. This nation has not experienced extraordinary high prices nor a collapse in value <note>original: "non-valeur" – a situation where the price of grain drops so low that it is not worth the cost of harvesting or selling</note> of grain since it encouraged and stimulated its export.

<meta>This page continues the economic analysis of French agriculture, specifically contrasting the inefficiency of small-scale farming using oxen ("petite culture") against the productivity of large-scale farming using horses ("grande culture"). Let us turn our eyes toward an object that is no less important than the cultivation of grain: I mean the profit from livestock in the current state of agriculture in France.

The 30 million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre, though it varied by region (usually between 0.85 and 1.3 acres).</note></term> managed under <term>small-scale farming<note>original: "petite culture" — a system of subsistence farming typically found in poorer regions, characterized by the use of oxen and a lack of significant capital investment.</note></term> can be divided into 375,000 estates, each with 80 arpents under cultivation. Assuming 12 oxen per estate, there are 4,500,000 oxen employed in the cultivation of these domains: small-scale farming thus occupies 4 or 5 million oxen for plowing the land. An ox is put to work at three or four years old; some keep them there for only three, four, five, or six years, but most retain them for seven, eight, or nine years. In this case, they are not sold to those who fatten them for the butcher until they are twelve or thirteen years old; by then, they are of poorer quality and sell for less than they were worth before being put to the plow. These oxen occupy pastures for a long time from which no profit is derived; whereas, if these pastures were used simply to raise oxen until they were ready to be fattened for the butcher, these oxen would be replaced every five or six years.

<column-break/>

...which constitutes the true strength of the State. Currently, according to Mr. <note>Nicolas-François Dupré de Saint-Maur (1695–1774), a French economist and statistician famous for his historical research on grain prices.</note> Dupré de Saint-Maur, about seven-eighths of the kingdom is cultivated with oxen; thus, only one-eighth of the land is cultivated by <term>farmers<note>original: "fermiers" — in the context of the Enlightenment "Physiocrat" economists, this refers specifically to wealthy, large-scale tenant farmers who used horses and modern equipment.</note></term>, whose number does not reach thirty thousand. This cannot provide even a thousand <term>militiamen<note>The "milice" was a form of compulsory military service for commoners. It was deeply loathed because it took able-bodied men away from the fields, and wealthy families often paid to avoid it.</note></term> who are sons of farmers. This small quantity is zero in our armies; but the four thousand who are terrified and abandon the countryside every time the militia is drawn are a great loss for the cultivation of the land. We shall speak here only of the <term>plowmen<note>original: "laboureurs" — in 18th-century France, this term did not mean a common laborer, but rather a prosperous peasant who owned his own plowing equipment.</note></term> who cultivate with horses, for (according to the author of this article) the others do not deserve the name. Now, there are about six or seven million arpents of land cultivated by horses, which represents the work of thirty thousand plows, at 120 arpents each. A large portion of the farmers have two plows; many have three. Thus, the number of farmers who cultivate with horses hardly reaches thirty thousand, especially if one does not confuse them with noble and privileged owners who practice the same style of cultivation. Half of these farmers do not have children of age to be drawn for the militia; for it is only eighteen or twenty years after their marriage that they can have a child of that age, and there are as many females as males. Thus, there cannot be ten thousand sons of farmers in a state to be drawn for the militia: a portion flee to the cities; those who remain exposed to the draw take their chances with the other peasants; there are thus not a thousand—perhaps not even five hundred—who actually fall to the militia. When the number of farmers increases as much as possible, the State should still protect them to support agriculture and in favor of the considerable contributions it would draw from them. <note>Note from the editors of the *Encyclopédie*.</note>

<meta>This page continues the economic analysis comparing different modes of agriculture in France. Through <term>large-scale farming<note>original: "grande culture" — a capital-intensive system of farming using horses and advanced crop rotation, which the Physiocrats argued was necessary for national wealth.</note></term>, horses leave the pastures free; they provide for their own food without diminishing the profit of the <term>farmer<note>original: "laboureur" — in this context, it refers to a wealthy tenant farmer who owns his own equipment, rather than a simple peasant laborer.</note></term>, who derives an even greater product from their labor than from that of oxen. Thus, by this mode of cultivation, one could put to use the pastures that are currently used at a total loss to feed the 4 or 5 million oxen that <term>small-scale farming<note>original: "petite culture" — a system of subsistence farming using oxen, prevalent in poorer regions of France due to a lack of capital for horses.</note></term> keeps at the plow. These oxen occupy, all together and for at least six years, pastures that could instead serve to raise another 4 or 5 million oxen for the <term>butcher<note>original: "boucherie" — refers to the livestock trade for meat consumption.</note></term>.

Oxen, before being put to <term>fattening<note>original: "engrais" — the practice of feeding livestock intensively to increase their weight and value before slaughter.</note></term> for the butcher, are sold at various prices according to their size: the average price can be reduced to 100 <term>livres<note>The livre was the currency of France until 1795; its value varied, but here it is used as a standard unit for economic calculation.</note></term>. Thus, the 4,500,000 extra oxen that would exist over six years would produce 450 million more every six years. Add a third more that the fattening would produce; the total would be 600 million which, divided by six years, would provide an annual profit of 100 million. We consider this product only in relation to the loss of pastures or fallow lands abandoned to the oxen kept at the plow; but most of these pastures could be returned to cultivation—or at least to a type of cultivation that would provide more food for livestock—and then the product would be much greater.

Flocks of sheep present another advantage that would be even more considerable through the increase in the production of wool and the annual sale of these animals. In the 375,000 estates cultivated by oxen, there is not even a third of the flocks that could be fed there if these lands were better cultivated and produced a greater quantity of fodder. Each of these estates, with its fallow lands, would feed a flock of 250 sheep; thus, an increase of two-thirds would be approximately 250,000 flocks, or 60 million sheep. Divided into ewes, lambs, and sheep proper, there would be 30 million ewes which would produce 30 million lambs, half of which would be male: these males would be kept to become the sheep sold for the butcher when they are two or three years old. The female lambs are sold, with the exception of a portion kept to renew the ewes. There would be 15 million female lambs: 10 million of them would be sold which, at 3 livres each, would produce 30 million.

There would be 15 million sheep succeeding each other every year: thus, there would be 15 million sheep for sale every year...

This wealth would spread to all inhabitants: it would provide them with better food, it would satisfy their needs, it would make them happy, it would increase the population, and it would grow the incomes of landowners and those of the State. The costs of cultivation would be hardly more considerable; only larger <term>funds<note>original: "fonds" — refers to the capital or investment required to start and maintain a farm.</note></term> would be needed to establish it; but these funds are lacking in the countryside because they have been drawn into the large cities. <meta>This page continues the author's argument for "large-scale farming" (using horses and capital) over "small-scale farming" (using oxen). The previous page ended by discussing how the restoration of large-scale farming would increase the production of livestock and animal products.</meta>

...much more profitable to individuals and much more advantageous to the State. These advantages, so essential to the happiness and prosperity of subjects, would procure another that contributes no less to the strength and wealth of the State; they would favor the propagation and preservation of men, especially the increase of inhabitants in the countryside. Wealthy <term>farmers<note>original: "fermiers" — specifically wealthy entrepreneurs who rented large tracts of land and invested capital in equipment and labor.</note></term> employ peasants whom the lure of money motivates to work: they become industrious, their earnings provide them with a level of comfort that keeps them in the provinces and enables them to feed their children, keep them near them, and establish them in their own province. The inhabitants of the countryside multiply, therefore, in proportion as wealth supports agriculture and agriculture increases wealth.

In the provinces where cultivation is done with <term>oxen<note>The author associates ox-driven plowing with "small-scale farming" (petite culture), which he views as inefficient and a sign of national poverty compared to horse-driven "large-scale farming" (grande culture).</note></term>, the farmer is poor and cannot employ the peasant: the latter, not being at all encouraged to work by the hope of gain, becomes lazy and languishes in misery; his only resource is to cultivate a small plot of land to obtain just enough to live on. But what is the food he obtains by this cultivation? Too poor to prepare the land to produce wheat and to wait for its harvest, he limits himself, as we have already said, to a cultivation that is less arduous and less time-consuming, which can provide a harvest in just a few months: barley, oats, <term>buckwheat<note>original: "blé noir" — literally "black wheat," a fast-growing crop often eaten by the poor.</note></term>, potatoes, <term>Turkish wheat<note>original: "blé de Turquie" — a common historical term for maize or corn.</note></term>, or other low-priced productions are the fruits of these labors; this is the nourishment he obtains and with which he raises his children. These foods, which barely sustain life while ruining the body, cause a portion of men to perish from childhood; those who resist such nourishment, who maintain their health and strength and who have intelligence, free themselves from this unhappy state by seeking refuge in the cities; the weakest and most inept remain in the countryside, where they are as useless to the State as they are a burden to themselves.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the economic structure of the countryside. He is transitioning from the technical benefits of large-scale farming (using horses) to the social and human benefits: how a wealthy agricultural system supports a thriving, healthy peasant population compared to the misery of the urban poor or the struggling sharecropper.</meta>

The inhabitants of the cities naively believe that it is the physical strength of the peasants that tills the soil and that agriculture only declines because there is a shortage of men in the countryside. People say we must drive out the schoolmasters who, through the instruction they give to the peasants, facilitate their <term>desertion<note>Refers to the migration of rural workers to the cities, which elites at the time feared would leave the fields empty.</note></term>. In this way, they imagine small-minded solutions, as ridiculous as they are disadvantageous. They view peasants as slaves of the State; rural life seems the hardest, most painful, and most contemptible because they destine the inhabitants of the countryside for tasks that are reserved for animals.

When the peasant plows the land himself, it is a proof of his misery and his uselessness. Four horses cultivate more than one hundred <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre.</note></term> of land; four men would not cultivate even eight. With the exception of the vine-grower and the gardener, who engage in this specific type of labor, peasants are employed by wealthy <term>farmers<note>original: "fermiers" — specifically wealthy entrepreneurs who rented large estates and invested capital in modern equipment and labor.</note></term> in other tasks that are more profitable for them and more useful to agriculture.

In wealthy provinces where cultivation is well-maintained, the peasants have many resources. They sow a few acres of land with wheat and other grains; the *farmers* for whom they work perform the plowing for them, and it is the wife and children who harvest the products. These small harvests, which provide a portion of their food, also produce fodder and manure for them. They grow flax, hemp, garden herbs, and vegetables of all kinds. They have livestock and poultry which provide them with good food and from which they earn a profit. Through their work during the harvest of the head farmer, they secure other earnings for the rest of the year. They are always employed in rural labor; they live without constraint and without worry. They despise the servitude of domestic servants, valets, and the slaves of other men. They do not envy the fate of the common people who inhabit the cities, who lodge at the very top of houses, and whose earnings are barely sufficient for their immediate needs. Being forced to live without any foresight and without any provision for future needs, the urban poor are continually exposed to languishing in <term>indigence<note>A state of extreme poverty.</note></term>.

Peasants only fall into misery and abandon the province when they are too disturbed by the <term>vexations<note>Historical term for harassment, often referring to arbitrary tax collection or bureaucratic abuses.</note></term> to which they are exposed, or when there are no *farmers* to provide them with work and the countryside is cultivated by poor <term>sharecroppers<note>original: "métayers" — subsistence farmers who lacked their own equipment and had to give a large portion of their crop to the landlord.</note></term> limited to small-scale cultivation, which they perform themselves very imperfectly. The portion that these sharecroppers receive from their...

<summary>The author argues that rural poverty is caused by a lack of wealthy capitalist farmers and excessive harassment, rather than a lack of manual labor or too much education. He paints a picture of the independent, healthy life of a rural laborer working under a wealthy farmer as far superior to the precarious life of the urban poor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that true national wealth is rooted in large-scale, capital-intensive agriculture rather than the subsistence labor of the poor. These poor cultivators, who are of so little use to the State, do not represent the true laborer—the wealthy <term>farmer<note>original: "fermier" — in this context, a wealthy entrepreneur who rented large estates, invested capital in modern equipment, and managed labor, as opposed to a subsistence peasant.</note></term> who cultivates on a large scale, who governs, who commands, and who increases expenses to multiply profits. This farmer, neglecting no method and no specific advantage, works for the common good; he usefully employs the inhabitants of the countryside; he can choose and wait for favorable times to sell his grain, or to buy and sell his livestock. It is the wealth of these *farmers* that fertilizes the land, multiplies the livestock, attracts and settles the rural population, and creates the strength and prosperity of the nation.

Manufactures and commerce, sustained by the disorders of <term>luxury<note>18th-century economic thinkers often viewed "luxury" as a social vice that diverted capital away from the "productive" work of agriculture and into "sterile" urban consumption.</note></term>, concentrate men and wealth in the great cities. This opposes the improvement of property, devastates the countryside, inspires contempt for agriculture, excessively increases private expenses, harms the support of families, prevents the growth of the population, and weakens the State.

The decline of empires has often closely followed a period of flourishing commerce. When a nation spends through luxury what it earns through commerce, the result is merely a movement of money without a real increase in wealth. It is the sale of surplus goods that enriches both the subjects and the sovereign. The productions of our lands must be the raw material for our manufactures and the object of our commerce; any other form of trade not built on these foundations is insecure. The more brilliant such trade appears in a kingdom, the more it excites the envy of neighboring nations and the more it is divided among them. A kingdom rich in fertile land cannot be imitated in its agriculture by another that lacks the same advantage. But to profit from this, one must remove the causes that lead people to abandon the countryside and that gather and hold wealth in the great cities. All the lords, all the wealthy, and all those who have rents or pensions sufficient to live comfortably settle in Paris or some other large city, where they spend almost all the income derived from the kingdom's lands. These expenses attract a multitude of merchants, artisans, servants, and laborers. This poor distribution of men and wealth is inevitable, but it has extended much too far; perhaps it was first encouraged by offering more protection to <term>citizens<note>original: "citoyens" — here referring specifically to inhabitants of the city (*cité*), as opposed to those living in the rural provinces.</note></term> than to the inhabitants of the countryside. <meta>This page continues the author’s critique of urban-centric economics, transitioning from a discussion on how commerce can weaken a state to how the government might restore the countryside by addressing rural flight and the complexities of taxation.</meta>

...people are attracted by self-interest and peace. If these advantages are provided to the countryside, it will be no less populated in proportion than the cities. Not all city dwellers are wealthy or comfortable. The countryside has its own riches and charms; people only abandon it to avoid the <term>harassment<note>original: "vexations" — This refers to the systemic abuses and heavy-handed tax collection methods that plagued French peasants in the 18th century.</note></term> to which they are exposed there; but the government can remedy these inconveniences. Commerce appears flourishing in the cities because they are filled with wealthy merchants. But what is the result of this, other than that almost all the money of the kingdom is employed in a trade that does not increase the nation's wealth at all? <term>Locke<note>The author refers to John Locke’s economic theories, which argued that internal trade merely moves money from one hand to another without increasing the total supply of gold or "real" value in the way production does.</note></term> compares it to a game where, after the players' gains and losses, the sum of money remains the same as it was before. Internal trade is necessary to provide for needs, to maintain luxury, and to facilitate consumption; but it contributes [little] to the strength and prosperity of the State. If a portion of the immense riches it retains, the use of which produces so little for the kingdom, were distributed to agriculture, it would produce far more real and substantial revenues. Agriculture is the **patrimony of the sovereign**: all its productions are visible; they can be appropriately subjected to taxes; pecuniary wealth <note>Money or liquid assets.</note> escapes the distribution of <term>subsidies<note>original: "subsides" — here meaning tax levies or government revenue.</note></term>, and the government can only seize it through means that are burdensome to the State.

However, the distribution of taxes on <term>laborers<note>original: "laboureurs" — in 18th-century French economic thought, this specifically refers to "wealthy" tenant farmers who owned equipment, as opposed to the "manouvriers" or poor peasants who had only their hands.</note></term> also presents great difficulties. <term>Arbitrary taxes<note>The "taille" was often assessed based on a local official's estimation of a farmer's wealth; if a farmer improved his land, his taxes might be raised arbitrarily, discouraging investment.</note></term> are too frightening and too unjust not to always powerfully oppose the restoration of agriculture. Proportional distribution is hardly possible; it does not seem that it can be regulated by the valuation and taxing of land: for the two kinds of agriculture we have discussed <note>Referring to "grande culture" (high-investment) and "petite culture" (subsistence) mentioned previously.</note> result in a great difference in the yields of lands of the same value; thus, as long as these two types of cultivation persist and vary, land cannot serve as a proportional measure for the assessment of the <term>taille<note>The "taille" was the primary direct land tax in pre-revolutionary France, from which the nobility and clergy were largely exempt.</note></term>. If land were taxed according to its current state, the system would become flawed as <term>large-scale farming<note>original: "grande culture".</note></term> expands; furthermore, there are provinces where the profit from livestock is much greater than the product of the harvests, and others where the harvest product exceeds the profit drawn from livestock; moreover, this diversity of circumstances is highly susceptible to change. It is therefore hardly possible to imagine any general plan to establish a proportional distribution of taxes.

<summary>The author argues that while internal trade merely redistributes existing money, agriculture creates "real" wealth that is visible and taxable for the benefit of the State. He identifies arbitrary taxation as the primary cause of rural depopulation and explains why creating a fair, proportional tax system is complicated by varying farming methods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s proposal for tax reform, moving from the general economic necessity of protecting agriculture to specific administrative measures meant to prevent tax collectors from unfairly assessing the wealth of rural workers.</meta>

But for the security of the farmer’s capital, it is less a matter of an exact <term>distribution<note>original: "répartition" — the process of dividing the total tax burden of a parish among its individual inhabitants.</note></term> than of establishing a check on the arbitrary estimation of the <term>plowman's<note>original: "laboureur" — in the 18th century, this specifically referred to a high-status peasant who owned a plow and a team of horses, distinguishing them from poorer manual laborers.</note></term> wealth. It would suffice to subject <term>taxes<note>original: "impositions" — specifically referring to the "taille," the main direct tax in pre-revolutionary France, from which the nobility and clergy were exempt.</note></term> to invariable and judicious rules that would ensure the payment of the tax while guaranteeing that the one who bears it is protected from the ill intentions or false conjectures of those who impose it. One should only be guided by visible assets; estimations of the secret wealth of individuals are deceptive, and such guesswork is always the pretext that authorizes the very abuses one wishes to avoid.

Visible assets are the common means for all plowmen to obtain the same profits; if there are men who are more industrious, more intelligent, and more thrifty, who derive a greater advantage from them, they deserve to enjoy the fruits of their savings and their talents in peace. It would therefore suffice to require the plowman to give the <term>collectors<note>original: "collecteurs" — these were usually local inhabitants appointed to collect taxes from their neighbors, a position often characterized by corruption or local feuds.</note></term> a faithful declaration every year of the quantity and nature of the goods of which he is the owner or *tenant farmer*, along with an account of his harvests, his livestock, etc., under penalty of being taxed arbitrarily if he is convicted of fraud. All the inhabitants of a village know exactly the visible riches of each person among them; fraudulent declarations would be easily noticed. The collectors would likewise be rigorously required to regulate the distribution of taxes relatively and proportionally to these declarations. As for simple <term>day laborers<note>original: "manouvriers" — unskilled rural laborers who owned no land or equipment and lived day-to-day.</note></term> and artisans, their status would serve as the rule for one and all, taking into account their young children and those who are fit to work. Although there would be some disproportion among these inhabitants, the smallness of the tax imposed on these types of workers in the villages would make the inconveniences negligible.

The taxes to be distributed among the merchants established in the villages are the most difficult to regulate; but their declaration regarding the extent and objects of their trade could be admitted or contested by the collectors; and in the latter case, it would be approved or reformed in an assembly of the inhabitants of the parish. The decision shaped by public knowledge would curb the fraud of the <term>taxpayer<note>original: "taillable" — a person subject to the "taille" tax.</note></term> and the abuses of arbitrary taxation by the collectors. Merchants are few in number in the villages; thus, these precautions could suffice in their regard.

We are considering here only the countryside, and especially in relation to the security of the plowman. As for the provincial cities that pay...

This proposal aims to protect productive farmers from the corruption of local tax collectors and ensure that industriousness is rewarded rather than taxed away.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the author’s proposal for a transparent tax system. It moves from the necessity of objective declarations to the practical implementation of a village-level "tariff" and the long-term benefits this would bring to the French economy.</meta>

the <term>taille<note>original: "taille" — the primary direct tax of the French Ancien Régime, from which the nobility and clergy were exempt, often criticized for its unpredictable and unfair assessment.</note></term>, it would be up to the communities themselves to establish the arrangements that suit them best to avoid arbitrary taxation.

Even if these rules do not overcome every obstacle, the remaining ones—and even those they might cause—would not be comparable to the danger of being exposed every year to the discretion of the collectors; everyone would willingly devote themselves to a tax regulated by law. This essential and much-desired advantage would dispel the excessive anxieties caused in the countryside by the arbitrary distribution of the <term>taille</term>.

It might be objected that requiring exact declarations to determine each farmer's tax could lead them to limit their crops and livestock to pay less, which would be a new obstacle to agricultural growth. But rest assured that the <term>plowman<note>original: "laboureur" — a prosperous peasant who owned his own equipment, a class the Physiocrats viewed as the primary drivers of economic wealth.</note></term> would not be so easily fooled; because his harvests, his cattle, and his other assets could no longer serve as a pretext to overburden him with taxes, he would then decide in favor of profit.

One might also say that this proportional distribution would be very complex and thus difficult for collectors unversed in calculation to execute. This would be the work of the <term>clerk<note>original: "l’écrivain" — a professional scribe or notary hired by the village to handle formal paperwork.</note></term> whom the collectors charge with drafting the <term>tax roll<note>original: "le rôle" — the official document listing the taxpayers and the amounts they were assessed.</note></term>. The community would first form a fundamental tariff, in accordance with the estimated value of the goods produced in the region; they could be assisted in this initial task by the <term>parish priest<note>original: "le curé"</note></term>, or by the <term>lord<note>original: "le seigneur"</note></term>, or by his <term>steward<note>original: "son régisseur"</note></term>, or by other capable and benevolent persons. Once this tariff is decided and accepted by the inhabitants, it would soon become familiar to every individual, as everyone would have an interest in knowing the share they must pay. Thus, in a short time, this proportional taxation would become very easy for them.

If the inhabitants of the countryside were delivered from the arbitrary imposition of the <term>taille</term>, they would live in the same security as the inhabitants of large cities. Many landowners would return to manage their estates themselves; the countryside would no longer be abandoned; wealth and population would be restored there. Thus, by removing all other causes detrimental to the progress of agriculture, the strength of the <term>kingdom<note>original: "le royaume"</note></term> would be gradually restored through the increase of the population and the growth of state revenues.

<summary>The author argues that a fixed, transparent tax "tariff" based on agricultural output would end the fear of arbitrary tax hikes, encouraging farmers to maximize production and prompting wealthy landowners to return to the countryside.</summary>

# GRAINS
## (POLITICAL ECONOMY)
### Article by MR. QUESNAY THE SON

->Excerpt from the *Encyclopédie* (¹)<-

The primary objects of commerce in France are <term>grains<note>original: "grains" — in this context, the term refers generally to cereal crops like wheat, rye, and barley, which formed the basis of the French economy and diet.</note></term>, wines and brandies, salt, hemp and flax, wool, and other products provided by livestock; the manufacturing of linens and common fabrics can greatly increase the value of hemp, flax, and wool, and provide a livelihood for many men who would be employed in such advantageous labors. But we see today that the production and trade of most of these commodities are almost annihilated in France. For a long time, luxury manufacturing has seduced the nation; we have neither the silk nor the wool suitable for making fine fabrics and fine cloths; we have devoted ourselves to an industry that was foreign to us; and a multitude of men have been employed in it at a time when the kingdom was depopulating and the countryside was becoming deserted. The price of our wheat was lowered so that manufacturing and labor would be cheaper than abroad: men and wealth have accumulated in the cities; agriculture, the most fertile and noble part of our commerce, the source of the kingdom's revenues, has not been seen as the primary foundation of—

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Quesnay contends that French economic policy has mistakenly prioritized urban manufacturing and luxury goods over the foundational wealth provided by agriculture.</meta>

...our wealth; <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "...has not been seen as the primary foundation of our wealth."</note> it seemed to interest only the farmer and the peasant; their labors were confined to the subsistence of the nation, which, by purchasing commodities, pays the expenses of cultivation; and it was believed that it was a commerce or a trade established on industry that was meant to bring gold and silver into the kingdom. The planting of vines was forbidden; the cultivation of <term>mulberry trees<note>original: "mûriers" — promoted by the state to foster a domestic silk industry, a move Quesnay critiques as a distraction from essential food production.</note></term> was recommended; the sale of agricultural products was halted and land income was diminished to favor manufactures that were detrimental to our own commerce.

France can produce all essential materials in abundance; it only needs to purchase luxury goods from abroad; mutual trade between nations is necessary to maintain commerce. But we have primarily focused on the manufacture and trade of goods that we could have obtained from abroad; and through an overly aggressive pursuit of competitive trade, we sought to harm our neighbors and deprive them of the profit they would have gained from us through the sale of their goods.

Through this policy, we have extinguished a reciprocal trade between them and us that was entirely to our advantage; they have banned the entry of our agricultural products, and we buy from them—via smuggling and at great expense—the raw materials we use in our factories. To earn a few million from manufacturing and selling fine fabrics, we have lost billions on the produce of our lands; and the nation, adorned in fabrics of gold and silver, believed it was enjoying a flourishing commerce.

These manufactures have plunged us into a disordered luxury that has spread somewhat among other nations and excited their emulation; we have perhaps surpassed them through our industry; but this advantage has been primarily sustained by our own consumption.

Consumption by the subjects is the source of the sovereign's revenue, and the sale of surplus abroad increases the wealth of the subjects. The prosperity of the State depends on the cooperation of these two advantages; but consumption driven by luxury is too restricted; it can only be sustained by opulence; those less favored by fortune can only indulge in it to their own detriment and to the disadvantage of the State.

The more enlightened ministry knows that consumption, which can provide great revenue to the sovereign and which creates the happiness—

The detailed examination we are about to enter into regarding the revenues that abundant harvests of *grain* can provide, and regarding freedom in the trade of this commodity, will sufficiently prove how much the production of primary necessities, their sale, and their consumption interest all the different ranks of the kingdom, and will allow one to judge what can be expected today from the government’s views on the restoration of agriculture.

We have already examined the state of agriculture in France, the two kinds of cultivation in use there—<term>large-scale cultivation<note>original: "grande culture" — referring to intensive farming using horses and advanced equipment, common in the more prosperous northern regions of 18th-century France.</note></term> or that which is done with horses, and <term>small-scale cultivation<note>original: "petite culture" — referring to traditional, less productive farming using oxen, which was more common in poorer provinces.</note></term> or that which is done with oxen—the difference in the products yielded by these two types of farming, the causes of the degradation of our agriculture, and the means to restore it. *See* FARMERS. One would therefore have to avoid an abundance of wheat in a kingdom where one should only harvest enough for the nation's subsistence. But in this case, shortages are inevitable because when the harvest yields wheat for three or four months more than the year's consumption, it is at such a low price that this surplus ruins the laborer; nonetheless, it is not enough for the following year's consumption if a bad harvest occurs; thus, it is only the ease of selling at a good price that can maintain both abundance and profit. <note>The author is describing the "paradox of plenty": without the ability to export surplus grain, a bumper crop causes prices to collapse, bankrupting farmers and leading to less planting—and thus famine—the following year.</note>

*State of large-scale grain cultivation.* <term>Large-scale cultivation<note>original: "grande culture" — farming characterized by the use of horse-drawn plows and significant capital investment, typical of the wealthy northern provinces.</note></term> is currently limited to approximately six million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of area, roughly equivalent to an acre (about 0.85 to 1.3 acres depending on the region).</note></term> of land, which mainly comprise the provinces of Normandy, Beauce, Île-de-France, Picardy, French Flanders, Hainaut, and a few others. One *arpent* of good land, well-managed through large-scale cultivation, can produce 8 <term>setiers<note>original: "septiers" — a measure of volume; the Paris setier for grain was roughly 150 liters, here specified as weighing 240 pounds.</note></term> or more, Paris measure, which is 240 pounds in weight: but all lands managed by this cultivation are not equally fertile; for this cultivation is practiced more due to a remnant of custom preserved in certain provinces than because of the quality of the land itself. Furthermore, a large portion of these lands is held by poor farmers unable to cultivate them well; this is why we have evaluated the average product of each *arpent* of land at only five *setiers*, after the seed has been set aside. We fix the *arpent* at 100 <term>perches<note>A unit of length; a "perch."</note></term> and the *perche* at 22 feet. (¹)

The six million *arpents* of land managed by this cultivation maintain every year a <term>shift<note>original: "sole" — a portion of land in a crop rotation system.</note></term> of two million *arpents* sown with wheat; a shift of two million *arpents* sown with oats and other <term>spring grains<note>original: "grains de mars" — cereals sown in the spring rather than the autumn.</note></term>, and a shift of two million *arpents* which are in <term>fallow<note>original: "jachères" — land left unplowed or unsown for a period to restore its fertility.</note></term> and which are being prepared to yield wheat the following year.

State of *small-scale farming* for *grains*. We noted in the article *Farmers*, already cited, that in provinces where there is a lack of <term>plowmen<note>original: "laboureurs" — in this context, it refers to wealthy independent farmers who owned their own teams of horses and equipment.</note></term> rich enough to cultivate the land with horses, the landowners or the farmers who manage the estates are obliged to have them cultivated by peasants to whom they provide oxen for plowing. We have seen that the costs required by this cultivation are no less substantial than those of cultivation done with horses; however, due to the lack of money in these provinces, it is the land itself that covers the costs. Land is left fallow for the grazing of the draft oxen; they are fed during the winter with hay produced by the meadows; and instead of paying wages to those who plow, they are granted half of the product provided by the harvest.

The oxen scattered across these pastures provide no <term>manure<note>original: "fumier"</note></term>; owners entrust few flocks to these <term>sharecroppers<note>original: "métayers" — tenant farmers who pay a portion of their crop as rent rather than a fixed cash sum.</note></term> or peasants charged with the cultivation of the land, which extremely diminishes the production of wool in France.
