and more fertile; but these advantages are not very profitable because the wheat, which is often held back within the province, has no market: and there is so little commerce that in several places in this province, as in many other regions, buying and selling are done only by barter or the exchange of the commodities themselves.

The small harvests that are gathered, which are mostly rye (1), provide little fodder and contribute little to the feeding of livestock; they can only be fed through pastures or land left <term>fallow<note>original: "en friche"</note></term>: this is why they are not spared. Furthermore, the <term>sharecroppers<note>original: "métayers"; farmers who rent land in exchange for a portion of the crop, often using equipment and livestock provided by the owner.</note></term>, who are always very poor, use the oxen provided by the owner as much as possible to perform <term>hauling jobs<note>original: "charrois"</note></term> for their own profit to earn some money. The owners are forced to tolerate this abuse to keep their sharecroppers; these men, who find more profit in hauling than in cultivation, greatly neglect the tilling of the land. When these sharecroppers leave land fallow for a long time and it becomes covered with thorns and bushes, it remains in this state because it would cost much more than its value to <term>clear and reclaim<note>original: "esserter et défricher"</note></term> it.

In these provinces, the peasants and laborers are not employed as they are in regions of <term>large-scale farming<note>original: "grande culture"; a more advanced agricultural system characterized by large capital investments and the use of horses rather than oxen.</note></term> by wealthy farmers who hire them for agricultural work and the management of livestock; the sharecroppers, being too poor, provide them with little work. These peasants subsist on poor bread made from <term>minor grains<note>original: "menus grains"; lower-value cereals such as millet or barley.</note></term> that they grow themselves, which require little cultivation and are of no profit to the State.

Wheat has little market for lack of consumption in these regions; for when the large cities are sufficiently supplied by neighboring provinces, wheat does not sell in those that are far away. <meta>This page continues the economic critique of the "small-scale farming" system (petite culture). It follows a discussion on how the lack of markets and the poverty of rural workers lead to the neglect of land and a reliance on subsistence-level bartering.</meta>

culture; the portion of the harvest intended for the <term>sharecropper<note>original: "métayer"; a farmer who works the land in exchange for a share of the produce, often living in poverty.</note></term> becomes barely sufficient to feed his family; and when the harvest is poor, he himself suffers from <term>scarcity<note>original: "disette"</note></term>: the owner must then make up the difference. This is why the yields obtained through this type of farming offer almost no resource in years of famine, because in bad years they barely suffice for the survival of the owner and the <term>tenant<note>original: "colon"; another term for the sharecropper or tiller of the soil.</note></term>. Thus, the high price of wheat in bad years does not compensate for the <term>lack of value<note>original: "non-valeur"; an economic term describing when a commodity's market price falls below its production cost, making it "worthless" to the producer.</note></term> of this commodity in good years; only a few wealthy owners, who can wait for favorable times to sell their harvested wheat, are able to profit from it.

Regarding this type of farming, one must therefore consider the value of wheat only in accordance with the ordinary price of good years; but the lack of market demand at that time in the provinces far from the capital keeps wheat at a very low price: thus, we must value it at only 12 <term>livres<note>The livre was the primary currency of France before the introduction of the franc.</note></term> per <term>setier<note>original: "septier"; a historical measure of volume for grain, roughly 150 liters.</note></term>, for both wheat and rye, in the provinces where the land is managed by <term>small-scale farming<note>original: "petite culture"</note></term>. Indeed, it is in these provinces that the price of wheat cannot support the financial costs of <term>large-scale farming<note>original: "grande culture"; a more advanced agricultural system characterized by capital investment and the use of horses.</note></term>; where the land is cultivated only at the expense of the land itself, and where one draws what product one can by making use of it with the least possible expense.

It is not because they plow with oxen that such a small product is drawn from the land; by this type of cultivation, by making the necessary investments, one could draw nearly as much product from the land as by cultivation done with horses; but these expenses could only be made by the owners; which they will not do as long as the trade in wheat is not free and as long as the lack of value in this commodity allows them to see only a certain loss.

It is estimated that there are about thirty million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of area, roughly equivalent to an acre.</note></term> of land managed by small-scale farming, each arpent, averaging the best and worst, producing in an ordinary year four times the seed, or thirty-two <term>bushels<note>original: "boisseaux"</note></term> not including the <term>tithe<note>original: "dîme"; a 10% tax paid to the church.</note></term>; from these thirty-two bushels, eight must be deducted for seed. There remain two setiers which are shared equally between the owner and the sharecropper. The latter is responsible for the <term>taille<note>A direct land tax paid to the French crown by commoners.</note></term> and some unavoidable costs.

Thirty million arpents of land managed by small-scale farming are divided into two <term>shifts<note>original: "soles"; parts of a field system used in crop rotation.</note></term> which produce wheat alternately.

It provides a statistical breakdown of the low yields and heavy tax burdens associated with small-scale agriculture in 18th-century France.</summary>

**The state of healthy grain cultivation.** Constraints on the grain trade, the lack of exportation, depopulation, the lack of wealth in the countryside, the arbitrary imposition of <term>subsidies<note>A general term for taxes or financial aids demanded by the state.</note></term>, the conscription of <term>militias</term>, and the excess of <term>corvées<note>Unpaid, forced labor required of peasants for public works, such as road building.</note></term> have reduced our harvests to this meager yield. Formerly, with a third more inhabitants who increased consumption, our agriculture provided a great quantity of grain to foreign nations; the English complained in 1621 that the French were bringing such considerable quantities of wheat into their country, and at such a low price, that their own nation could not compete in its own markets <note>original: (2)</note>; it was then sold in France for 18 livres in our current money: this was a low price for that century. <meta>This page transitions from the raw data of agricultural production to a theoretical analysis of economic growth, specifically contrasting current production levels with the era of Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, and arguing for the primacy of agricultural exports.</meta>

...they produced in those times at least 70 million <term>setiers<note>original: "septiers"; a traditional measure of volume for dry goods, roughly 150 liters.</note></term> of wheat; today they produce about 45 million. A population larger by one-third consumed 20 million more than our current consumption, and the kingdom still supplied foreign nations abundantly. This abundance was a happy result of the economic governance of <term>M. de Sully<note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully (1560–1641), the chief minister to King Henry IV. He is famous for the maxim: "Tillage and pasture are the two breasts from which France is fed."</note></term>. To provide revenue for the King and the nation, and to sustain the strength of the State, this great minister desired nothing but plowmen, vine-dressers, and shepherds.

The restoration of our farming also implies the growth of the population; the progress of both must go hand in hand. The price of *grains* must exceed the costs of cultivation; thus, domestic consumption and foreign sales must maintain a reliable profit on the price of *grains*. Selling abroad facilitates trade, revitalizes farming, and increases land revenue. Increasing revenue leads to greater spending, which favors the population because the increase in spending provides earnings for a greater number of men. The growth of the population expands consumption; consumption sustains the price of commodities, which multiply through farming in proportion to human needs—that is, in proportion to the population's growth. The principle of all this progress is therefore the export of <term>homegrown produce<note>original: "denrées du cru"; raw agricultural products harvested directly from the land.</note></term> because foreign sales increase revenue, the growth of revenue increases the population, the growth of the population increases consumption, and greater consumption increases farming, land revenue, and population more and more; for the increase in revenue increases the population, and the population increases the revenue.

But all these increases can only begin with the increase of revenue; this is the essential point, and the one most ignored, or at least most neglected, in France. In the employment of men, we have not even recognized the difference between the product of labor that only covers the <term>cost of hand-work<note>original: "main-d'œuvre"; basic manual labor expenses.</note></term> and the product of labor that pays for the hand-work while also generating revenue. In this state of inattention, industry has been preferred over agriculture, and the trade of manufactured works over the trade of homegrown produce; we have even supported manufacturing and a <term>luxury trade<note>original: "commerce de luxe"; the production of high-end goods. Physiocratic thinkers argued this was "sterile" because it didn't create new wealth from the earth like farming did.</note></term> to the detriment of land cultivation.

<summary>This page presents a Physiocratic argument that agricultural prosperity is the engine of national wealth and population growth, citing the historical success of Minister Sully. It criticizes the French government's preference for manufacturing and luxury trade over the foundational revenue of the land.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that agricultural prosperity is the foundation of national wealth. While the previous page praised the policies of the Duke of Sully, this section critiques the industrial focus of Jean-Baptiste Colbert and provides specific calculations for how France could maximize its wheat production by focusing on high-quality land and free trade.</meta>

However, it is evident that the government has no other means to make commerce flourish and to support and extend industry than to ensure the growth of revenues; for it is revenues that attract merchants and artisans and pay for their labor. We must therefore cultivate the base of the tree, and not limit our care to managing the branches; let us allow the branches to arrange and extend themselves in liberty, but let us not neglect the soil that provides the sap necessary for their growth and development. <term>M. Colbert<note>Jean-Baptiste Colbert (1619–1683), the influential Finance Minister under Louis XIV, famous for "Colbertism," which prioritized manufacturing and exports over agriculture.</note></term>, though entirely preoccupied with manufacturing, nevertheless believed it was necessary to reduce the <term>taille<note>original: "taille"; the primary direct land tax in pre-revolutionary France, which fell most heavily on the peasantry.</note></term> and make advances to farmers to revive a decaying agriculture. This he could not reconcile with the needs of the State; but he does not speak of the essential means, which consist of subjecting the *taille* to a regulated assessment and invariably establishing the freedom of the *grain trade*. Agriculture was neglected; the wars, which were continual, and the <term>militia<note>original: "milice"; local defense forces often raised by forcibly drafting peasants, which disrupted agricultural labor.</note></term>, which devastated the countryside, diminished the revenues of the kingdom. The <term>financiers<note>original: "traitants"; private tax-collectors who lent money to the Crown at high interest, often criticized as predatory.</note></term>, through treacherous aid, became the supporters of the State; the minister's foresight was limited to this unfortunate resource, the effects of which have been so fatal to France. (¹)

The cultivation of wheat is very expensive; we have much more land than we need for this cultivation. It should be restricted to good lands, where the yield would greatly exceed the costs of proper farming. Thirty million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre (0.8 to 1.3 acres depending on the region).</note></term> of good land would form an annual <term>planting block<note>original: "sole"; a section of land designated for a specific crop within a rotation system.</note></term> of 10 million arpents that would carry wheat. Good lands, well-cultivated, would produce at least, in an average year, six <term>setiers<note>original: "septiers"; a traditional unit of volume for grain, roughly 150 liters.</note></term> per arpent, after setting aside seed. Thus, the planting block of ten million arpents would yield, including the <term>tithe<note>original: "dîme"; a ten-percent tax on agricultural produce paid to the Church.</note></term>, at least 65 million setiers of wheat. <meta>This page continues François Quesnay's economic analysis, moving from a critique of historical figures like Colbert to specific calculations of agricultural productivity under a system of free trade. He compares the stability of the English grain market to the potential for the French market, arguing that modern techniques and livestock management are the keys to national wealth.</meta>

...internal consumption increasing and the freedom of the grain trade being fully restored, the price of each <term>setier<note>A historical French unit of volume for grain, varying by region but often around 150 liters in Paris.</note></term> of wheat, on average, can be estimated at 18 <term>livres<note>The standard currency of France before the introduction of the franc in 1795; it was roughly equivalent to the value of a pound of silver in much earlier times.</note></term>, give or take a little; it matters little; but at 18 livres the product would be 108 livres, not including the tithe.

To determine the common price of wheat more accurately, with export permitted, one must pay attention to the variations in crop yields and wheat prices according to those yields. One can judge the state of these variations in the case of export by following those that occur in England, where for many years they have only ranged from about 18 to 22 livres. It is easy to understand why these variations there are so small: agriculture has made very great progress in that kingdom; the harvests, however weak they may be, are always more than sufficient for the subsistence of the inhabitants. If our agriculture were in good condition, we would harvest in a bad year almost as much wheat as a good harvest provides us today: thus, without extraordinary accidents, one could not experience scarcity in a kingdom where even the smallest harvests, joined with what would necessarily remain from good years, would always be above the needs of the inhabitants. One can judge this by the presentation we are about to give of the variations in harvests produced by good cultivation according to the diversity of years. It will be noted there that a bad harvest from 10 million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre, though it varied by region.</note></term> yields 40 million setiers of wheat, without counting the harvest from the same number of arpents sown with <term>spring grains<note>original: "grains de mars"; crops like barley, oats, or peas sown in the spring rather than the autumn.</note></term>.

---

"...[he] manured [the land] very poorly because he sold his straw and fed little livestock. These lands yielded only three to four setiers of wheat per arpent in the best years; he was ruined, and was forced to hand over his farm to another more industrious cultivator. Everything has changed its face; no expense was spared; the lands, even better plowed than they were, have been covered with herds and manure: in two years they have been improved to the point of yielding ten setiers of wheat per arpent, and making one hope for even more in the future. This success will be repeated every time it is attempted. Let us multiply our herds, and we will almost double our harvests. May this persuasion strike farmers and owners alike! If it became general, if it were encouraged, we would soon see agriculture make rapid progress; we would owe it abundance along with all its effects." <note>Note from the original.</note>

(1) We set the price lower than in England, although French wheat is of better quality; but if we were to sell abroad, competition could lower the price on both sides. <note>original: "Note de l'original."</note>

(2) In the current large-scale cultivation in France, it was previously noted that the farmer loses in good years; here he gains, but he loses in bad ones; thus it is in his interest that there be much wheat: whereas in the other case abundance ruins the farmer, and he can only compensate himself slightly in bad years. <note>In a restricted market, a bumper crop causes prices to crash so low that farmers cannot cover their fixed costs, a phenomenon Quesnay sought to fix through free trade.</note> <note>original: "Note de l'original."</note>

(3) The common price for buyers would be one-fifth of 90 livres, which is 18 livres; this is approximately the ordinary common price of the sale of our wheat in recent times: thus exportation would not increase the price of wheat for buyers; it would increase it for farmers by 2 livres 4 sous per setier; on 65 million setiers, this would be a benefit of 160 million for agriculture, without the wheat increasing in price for the buyer. This is the advantage of exportation. Thus one should not be surprised by the progress of agriculture in England. <note>original: "Note de l'original."</note>

more or less expenditure on wine. But this more or less expenditure is an important object in relation to the income from vineyards and the inhabitants employed in cultivating them. This cultivation employs many men and can employ even more, which deserves great attention in relation to population; moreover, land used for vineyards yields a large product. The great object of government is to watch over the increase of income, for the good of the State and for the basis of taxation, for lands that produce much can sustain heavy taxation. Vineyards produce every year, so each <term>arpent<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre.</note></term> can provide for the <term>taille<note>A direct land tax paid by the peasantry and non-nobles to the French crown.</note></term> double what each arpent of land cultivated in wheat provides; which would produce for the king nearly as much as the <term>droits des aides<note>original: "droits des aides" — Indirect consumption taxes, primarily levied on wine and spirits.</note></term>, which ruin a trade essential to the kingdom and distress the winemakers through the rigors of the administration and the harassments of the clerks. In a system of good cultivation, a well-managed <term>taille</term> should be the primary source of the king's revenue. This is a matter that has not been deeply studied and is known only through the destructive abuses against which people have always protested and for which no remedy has yet been found. See **TAXES**. It appears that the author also holds somewhat to the common prejudice regarding industry. Industry provides subsistence to a multitude of men through the payment of wages; but it produces no revenue <note>The author reflects the Physiocratic view that only land creates "net product" or new wealth, while manufacturing merely "re-fashions" existing materials.</note>, and it can only be sustained by the incomes of the citizens who buy the works of the artisans. He defends the tax on industry for fear of annihilating it; but industry will always persist in a kingdom in proportion to income, regarding both necessary works and luxury works; taxation can only slightly increase the price. But this part interests foreign trade very little, which can only enrich us through the sale of our productions. The author is entirely decided in favor of well-ordered <term>General Farms<note>original: "fermes générales" — A system where the crown leased the right to collect taxes to private financiers, called "tax farmers."</note></term>; he finds there the king's revenues assured, interest for the lords under assumed names, honest fortunes for the farmers and sub-farmers, and salaries for the clerks; but he wants the financiers to have integrity. Another advantage he perceives in the [tax] farms is that they can increase without harming agriculture, industry, or commerce. It is at least true that in uncultivated kingdoms, this is perhaps the only way to draw revenue for the sovereign and interest for the lords; but in a State rich through its assets and through the trade of its productions, this burdensome means is not necessary and the lords sustain their expenses through the products of their lands. (Original Note.)

<meta>This page continues the argument that agriculture is the foundational source of all national wealth. The previous page ended while listing those who receive income from agricultural yields, concluding with the clergy.</meta>

clergy, and profits for farmers. It is these primary riches, perpetually renewed, which sustain all other classes in the kingdom, which provide activity to all other professions, which make commerce flourish, which encourage population growth, which animate industry, and which maintain the prosperity of the nation. But France is far from enjoying all those billions in revenue that we have glimpsed she might draw from herself. The annual consumption or expenditure of the nation is barely estimated at two billion. Now, expenditure is roughly equal to income, when merged with the costs of <term>labor<note>original: "main-d'œuvre" — In this context, it refers to the manual labor and manufacturing processes that transform raw materials.</note></term>, which provide subsistence to workers of all kinds and which are almost entirely paid for by the productions of the land; for, with the exception of fishing and salt, the profits of navigation themselves cannot be very considerable except through the trade of our home-grown produce.

Agriculture and commerce are continually viewed as the two resources of our wealth; yet commerce, like labor, is but a branch of agriculture: but labor is much more extensive and much more significant than commerce. These two sectors only subsist through agriculture. It is agriculture that provides the raw materials for labor and commerce, and which pays for both; yet these two branches return their gains to agriculture, which renews the riches that are spent and consumed each year. Indeed, without the products of our lands, without the income and expenditures of landowners and farmers, from where would the profit of commerce and the wages of labor arise? The distinction between commerce and agriculture is an abstraction that presents only an imperfect idea and seduces authors writing on this matter—even those who direct it—and who attribute to productive commerce that domestic trade which produces nothing, which serves the nation, and which is paid for by the nation.

One cannot too greatly admire the superiority of the views of <term>M. de Sully<note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully (1560–1641), the Superintendent of Finances under Henri IV, famous for the quote "Pasturage and tillage are the two breasts from which France is fed."</note></term>; this great minister had grasped the true principles of the economic government of the kingdom, by basing the king's wealth, the power of the State, and the happiness of the people upon the income from land—that is to say, upon agriculture and the foreign trade of its productions; he used to say that without the export of grain, the subjects would soon be without money and the sovereign without revenue. The alleged advantages of manufactures of all kinds did not— <note>The sentence continues on the following page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the interdependence of agriculture and industry, specifically focusing on how livestock and forage crops act as the engine for grain productivity and national wealth.</meta>

...did not seduce him: he only protected those of wool fabrics because he had recognized that the abundance of harvests depended on the sale of wool, which favors the multiplication of the herds necessary to fertilize the lands.

Good harvests produce much forage for the feeding of livestock; the thirty million <term>arpents<note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre, though it varied by region.</note></term> of mediocre lands would also be partly destined for this use. The author of *Artificial Meadows* <note>original: "Prairies artificielles" — A reference to the practice of sowing specific forage crops like clover or alfalfa rather than relying on natural grass, a key innovation of the Agricultural Revolution.</note> decides very judiciously that one needs roughly the same quantity of arpents of artificial meadows as there are lands sown with wheat each year. Thus, for thirty million arpents, ten million arpents of artificial meadows would be needed to feed the livestock, which would provide enough manure to supply a good fertilizer for the lands that must be sown with wheat each year. This practice is well understood, for if one obtains, through the fertilizing of the land, one <term>septier<note>A measure of volume for grain. A "setier" of Paris was roughly 150 liters.</note></term> of wheat more per each arpent, the profit is nearly doubled. An arpent of wheat that yields five septiers at 15 <term>livres<note>The primary currency of France before the introduction of the franc.</note></term> per septier gives, after all expenses are deducted, 20 livres of income; but one more septier would almost double the income of an arpent by itself; for if an arpent gives six septiers, the income is 35 livres, and if it yielded seven, the income would be 50 livres, or 3/5 more income than in the first case; income is not calculated simply by the product, but by the ratio of the product to the costs. Now, the increase in costs is in livestock, which also have their own product; thus the profits of an imperfect cultivation are not comparable to those of a good cultivation.

Thus we see that the fortune of the farmer in a position to bear the costs of good cultivation depends on the product of one or two more septiers per arpent of land; and although he shares the value for the <term>taille<note>A direct land tax paid by the French peasantry and non-nobles to the Crown.</note></term> and for the <term>fermage<note>The annual rent paid by a tenant farmer to the landowner.</note></term>, his gain is much more considerable, and the better portion is always for him; for he harvests forage in proportion, with which he feeds livestock that increase his profit.

He can only obtain this advantage by means of livestock; but he would also gain much on the product of these same cattle. It is true that a farmer limited to the use of a single <term>plow<note>original: "charrue" — Here used to describe the scale of a farm; a "one-plow" farm was a small-scale operation.</note></term> cannot claim a considerable gain; it is only those who are rich enough to form larger establishments who can withdraw a good profit and, through the expenditures they can make, bring the lands to their highest value.

<meta>This page continues the economic argument from page 217, transitioning from the technical requirements of forage and livestock to the organizational efficiency of large-scale farming versus small-scale cultivation, citing Richard Cantillon to explain the origins of urban centers.</meta>

He who operates only one <term>plow<note>In this context, "charrue" (plow) refers to a unit of land manageable by one plow-team, roughly 80 to 120 arpents depending on the region.</note></term> must draw from this small enterprise all the necessary expenses for the subsistence and maintenance of his family; he must even spend more in proportion for the various requirements of his undertaking. Having only one plow, he can only have, for example, a small flock of sheep, which costs him no less for the shepherd than what a larger flock would cost—a flock that would produce a much greater profit. A small enterprise and a large enterprise therefore require, in many respects, expenses that are not in the same proportion to the gain on either side. Thus, the <term>prosperous farmers<note>original: "riches laboureurs." In 18th-century France, a "laboureur" was not a simple peasant but a wealthy tenant farmer who owned his own plows and draft animals, acting as an agricultural entrepreneur.</note></term> who operate several plows cultivate much more advantageously for themselves and for the State than those who are limited to a single plow; for there is a saving of men, less expense, and a greater product. Now, the labor and work of men are only profitable to the State insofar as their products renew and increase the wealth of the nation. The lands must not nourish only those who cultivate them; they must provide the State with the greater part of its <term>subsidies<note>In this period, "subsides" referred to the taxes or revenues collected for the public treasury.</note></term>, produce tithes for the clergy, revenues for the owners, profits for the farmers, and gains for those they employ in cultivation. The revenues of the king, the clergy, and the owners—as well as the gains of the farmer and those he employs—turn into expenditures which are distributed among all the other <term>estates<note>original: "états" — referring to the various social classes or professions within the kingdom.</note></term> and all the other professions. An author(1) recognized these fundamental truths when he said: "that the gathering of several rich landowners who reside in the same place is sufficient to form what is called *a city*, where merchants, manufacturers, artisans, laborers, and servants gather in proportion to the revenues that the owners spend there: in which case the size of a city is naturally proportioned to the number of landowners, or rather to the product of the lands belonging to them. A capital city is formed in the same manner as a provincial city, with the difference that the great landowners of the entire State reside in the capital."

Lands cultivated in small parcels by small farmers require more men and expenses, and the profits are much more limited. Now, men and expenses must not be squandered on labors that would be more profitable to the State if they were executed with fewer men and less cost. This bad— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Ce mau-," which likely begins the word "mauvais" (bad/poor).</note>

(1) Cantillon, *Essay on Trade*, chapters 5, 6. <note>original: "Essai sur le commerce." A reference to Richard Cantillon's seminal work, "Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en Général," which heavily influenced the Physiocratic school of economics.</note> (Note from the original.)

<summary>This page argues that large-scale farming is more efficient and beneficial for national wealth than small-scale farming due to economies of scale. It explains that the concentration of agricultural surplus and landowner spending is what fundamentally creates and sustains cities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the economic argument regarding agricultural efficiency. While the previous page focused on the physical costs and benefits of operating multiple plows, this page transitions to the role of the farmer as an entrepreneur and the broader impact of agricultural wealth on the State's population and stability.</meta>

the misuse of labor for the cultivation of land would be detrimental, even in a very populous kingdom; for the more populated it is, the more necessary it is to draw a great product from the earth. However, it would be even more disadvantageous in a kingdom that was not sufficiently populated, for then it would be necessary to be more attentive to distributing men to the tasks most necessary and most profitable to the nation. The advantages of agriculture therefore depend greatly on the consolidation of land into large farms, brought to their highest value by wealthy farmers.

The only cultivation carried out solely through human labor is that of the vineyard; it could occupy a larger number of men in France if the sale of wines were encouraged and if the population increased. This cultivation and the trade of wines and brandies are too restricted; it is, however, an object that deserves no less attention than the cultivation of *grains* <note>original: "grains." In the 18th century, the "grain" trade was a central political and economic issue, as bread was the primary food source for the population.</note>.

We do not view the wealthy farmer here as a laborer who plows the land himself; he is an entrepreneur who manages and brings value to his enterprise through his intelligence and his wealth. Agriculture led by wealthy cultivators is a very respectable and very lucrative profession, reserved for free men in a position to make the <term>advances<note>In Physiocratic economic theory, "advances" (avances) refer to the upfront capital investment required for equipment, livestock, seeds, and wages before a harvest can be sold.</note></term> for the considerable costs required by the cultivation of the land, and which employs the peasants and always procures for them a suitable and assured gain. These, according to the idea of <term>M. de Sully<note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully (1560–1641), was the chief minister to King Henry IV. He is famous for his focus on agricultural development as the foundation of French prosperity.</note></term>, are the <term>true farmers or the true financiers<note>original: "vrais fermiers ou les vrais financiers." This is a provocative play on words: "financiers" usually referred to tax collectors, but the author argues that farmers are the ones who actually create the nation's financial health.</note></term> who must be established and supported in a kingdom possessing a large territory; for it is from their wealth that the subsistence of the nation must be born, along with public comfort, the revenues of the sovereign, those of the owners, of the clergy, a large expenditure distributed to all professions, a numerous population, and the strength and prosperity of the State.

It is large revenues that produce large expenditures; it is large expenditures that increase the population, because they extend trade and labor and provide gains to a great number of men. Those who only view the advantages of a large population as a means to maintain large armies judge the strength of a State poorly. If it becomes too high, he can no longer afford the costs of cultivation, and the property is degraded. Taxation must always fall upon the capital value of the land and never upon the process of cultivation; and it should only fall upon the capital value relative to its worth and the state of cultivation, which is determined by the farm rent.

If the *taille* were equal to one-third of these 1,950 livres, it would amount to 650 livres which, paid by five sharecroppers in equal portions, would be 131 livres each.

These sharecroppers together have half the grain, which is to say 3,000 livres; thus, the share for each is 600 livres. A lower-investment farming system usually relying on oxen and sharecropping, common in central and southern France.</note></term> where the lands are leased and where the owners have a revenue decided by the rent. <meta>This page continues the economic argument that taxation (the taille) must be calculated differently for sharecropping systems than for fixed-lease tenant farming. There are cases where the lands are so good that the <term>sharecropper<note>Original: "métayer." A farmer who works the land for an owner in exchange for a portion of the harvest rather than paying a fixed cash rent.</note></term> receives only one-third of the farm's produce as his share: even in these cases, that third is as advantageous to him as half of the product of a farm where the lands are less fertile. Thus, the <term>taille<note>Original: "taille." Therefore, by taxing the sharecroppers at one-sixth or one-fifth of their share of the farm's grain product in cases where the harvest is split by halves, one would have a general and very simple rule for establishing a proportional tax. This tax would increase to the benefit of the King as agriculture progressed through free trade in grain and the security of a fixed tax rate.

A less efficient farming system using oxen, common in poorer regions with less investment capital.</note></term>, because the yields of the former are far more substantial than those of the latter.

This small imperfection does not disturb the social order; on the contrary, it pushes back against the contempt that the "petty bourgeoisie" affects toward the most commendable and essential class. What advantage, then, could one claim to gain from the arbitrary imposition of the tax to repress men whom the ministry has an interest in protecting? Would it be to expose them to the injustice of a few individuals who could only harm them to the detriment of the State's welfare?

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the grain trade, specifically addressing how domestic movement of goods is insufficient compared to a robust export market. Thus, this expedient, far from increasing consumption in the kingdom, would decrease it even further. One must facilitate sales everywhere through export and domestic consumption which, along with foreign sales, maintains the price of commodities. But these advantages can only be expected from the general trade of grain, from population, and from the prosperity of the inhabitants, which would always provide a market and the consumption necessary to support commodity prices.

To better understand the advantages of the trade in ***grain*** with foreign countries, it is necessary to make some fundamental observations on trade in general and mainly on the trade of <term>manufactured goods</term> <note>original: "marchandises de main-d'œuvre"; literally goods produced by hand-labor/industry.</note>, and on the trade of raw produce; for as for the <term>transit trade</term> <note>original: "commerce de trafic"; the business of buying goods from one country to resell them to another without processing them.</note>, which consists only in buying to resell, it is only the employment of some small States that have no other resources than to be merchants. And this sort of trade with foreigners deserves no attention in a great kingdom; thus we will limit ourselves to comparing the advantages of the two other types of trade to know which interests us most.

## MAXIMS OF ECONOMIC GOVERNMENT.

I. *Industrial labor does not multiply wealth.* Agricultural labor covers costs, pays for the labor of cultivation, provides gains for the farmers, and, furthermore, it produces the revenue from <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "biens-fonds"; real estate or land. In this economic school, only land produces a "net product" or surplus above the costs of production.</note>. Those who buy manufactured works pay for the costs, the workmanship, and the profit of the merchants; but these works produce no revenue beyond that.

Thus, all spending on manufactured works is drawn only from the revenue of landed property; for labor that produces no revenue can only exist through the wealth of those who pay for it.

Compare the gain of the workers who manufacture industrial goods to that of the workers whom the farmer employs in the cultivation of the land; you will find that the gain, on both sides, is limited to the subsistence of these workers; that this gain is not an increase in wealth; and that the value of manufactured works...

<meta>This page continues the "Maxims of Economic Government," specifically detailing Maxim I regarding the sterile nature of industrial labor and beginning Maxim II regarding how industry interacts with national population and wealth.</meta>

is proportioned to the very value of the <term>subsistence</term> <note>Basic needs, primarily food, required for a worker to live and continue working.</note> that the workers and the merchants consume. Thus, the artisan destroys as much in subsistence as he produces by his work.

There is therefore no multiplication of wealth in the production of industrial works, since the value of these works only increases by the price of the subsistence that the workers consume. The large fortunes of merchants should not be viewed otherwise; they are the results of large commercial enterprises that gather together gains similar to those of small merchants; just as large-scale construction projects form great fortunes through the small profits gathered from the labor of a great number of workers. All these entrepreneurs only make fortunes because others are spending. Thus, there is no increase in wealth <note>The author argues that industry merely "transforms" existing wealth (food and raw materials) into a different form (goods), whereas agriculture "creates" new wealth from the earth.</note>.

It is the source of human subsistence that is the principle of wealth. It is <term>industry</term> <note>In this context, "industry" refers to the manual skill and labor used to process raw materials, rather than large-scale factories.</note> that prepares it for human use. The landowners, to enjoy this wealth, pay for industrial labor; and through this, their income becomes common to all men.

Men therefore multiply in proportion to the revenue of <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "biens-fonds"; fixed assets in the form of land and the buildings on it.</note>. Some give birth to this wealth through <term>cultivation</term> <note>original: "culture"; meaning agriculture or farming.</note>, others prepare it for enjoyment; those who enjoy it pay both the former and the latter.

There must therefore be landed property, men, and wealth, to have wealth and men. Thus, a State that was populated only by merchants and artisans could only subsist through the revenues of the landed property of foreigners.

II. *Industrial labor contributes to population and the increase of wealth.* If a nation earns a million from foreigners through its <term>labor</term> <note>original: "main-d'œuvre"; literally "hand-work."</note> on goods manufactured at home, and if it also sells a million worth of its own raw produce to foreigners, both of these products are equally an increase in wealth for the nation and are equally advantageous, provided it has more people than the income from the kingdom's soil can maintain; for then a portion of these men can only subsist through the manufactured goods that the nation sells abroad.

In this case, a nation draws from the soil and from men all the product it can draw; but it gains much more on the

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Maxims of Economic Government," specifically comparing the economic value of raw agricultural goods versus manufactured goods. sale of a million in goods of its own growth than on the sale of a million in manufactured goods, because it only gains on the latter the price of the artisan’s labor, whereas it gains on the former the price of the labor of cultivation and the price of the raw materials produced by the soil. Thus, given equal sums drawn from the sale of these different goods, trade in raw produce is always, proportionally, much more advantageous.

III. *Industrial labor that occupies men to the detriment of the cultivation of landed property harms the population and the growth of wealth.* If a nation that sells a million in manufactured goods and a million in goods of its own growth to foreign countries does not have enough men occupied in improving <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "bien-fonds"; this refers to fixed assets, specifically land and the permanent structures on it.</note>, it loses greatly on the employment of men attached to the manufacturing of goods it sells abroad; because men can then only devote themselves to this work at the expense of the land’s revenue, and the product of the labor of men who cultivate the earth can be double or triple that of the manufacturing of goods.

IV. *The wealth of the farmers gives rise to the wealth of cultivation.* The product of cultivation labor can be zero or nearly zero for the State when the farmer cannot afford the costs of good cultivation. A poor man who draws from the earth, through his labor, only low-value foodstuffs, such as potatoes, <term>buckwheat</term> <note>original: "blé noir"; a crop often associated with poor soil and subsistence living in this period.</note>, chestnuts, etc., who feeds himself on them, who buys nothing and sells nothing, works only for himself alone; he lives in misery; he and the land he cultivates return nothing to the State.

Such is the effect of <term>indigence</term> <note>Extreme poverty or destitution.</note> in the provinces where there are no <term>farmers</term> <note>original: "laboureurs"; in 18th-century economic theory, a "laboureur" was not just a worker, but a wealthy tenant farmer who possessed the capital—horses, plows, and seed—to manage a large farm.</note> in a position to employ peasants, and where these peasants, being too poor, can only obtain for themselves poor food and poor clothing.

Thus, the employment of men in cultivation can be fruitless in a kingdom where they do not have the wealth necessary to prepare the land to bear rich harvests. But the revenues of landed property are always assured in a kingdom well-populated with wealthy farmers.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of economic maxims, specifically addressing the balance between agricultural production (the "raw produce") and industrial manufacturing. It follows the argument that wealth is primarily generated by land and that industry should ideally serve to consume and add value to local agricultural surpluses.</meta>

industrial labor. A nation that, through the fertility of its soil and the difficulty of transport, would annually have a surabundance of foodstuffs that it could not sell to its neighbors, and which could sell them manufactured goods easy to transport, would have an interest in attracting to its territory many manufacturers and artisans who would consume the country's produce, who would sell their work abroad, and who would increase the nation's wealth through their earnings and their consumption.

But then, this arrangement is not easy because manufacturers and artisans only gather in a country in proportion to the actual revenues of the nation; that is to say, in proportion to the number of landowners or merchants who can buy their works at roughly the same price they would sell them elsewhere, and who would provide them with sales as they manufactured them; which is hardly possible in a nation that does not itself have the sales for its own produce and where the <term>lack of value</term> <note>original: "non-valeur"; in 18th-century economics, this refers to a situation where commodities have no market value or cannot be sold for a profit due to lack of demand or high transport costs.</note> of these same produce does not currently produce enough revenue to establish factories and manual labor.

Such a project can only be carried out very slowly. Several nations that have attempted it have even experienced the impossibility of succeeding.

This is the only case, however, where the government could usefully concern itself with the progress of industry in a fertile kingdom.

For, when the <term>trade in raw produce</term> <note>original: "commerce du cru"; this refers specifically to the trade of agricultural goods grown locally.</note> is easy and free, manual labor is always infallibly ensured by the revenues of <term>landed property</term>.

VI. *A nation that has a large trade in produce of its own growth can always maintain, at least for itself, a large trade in manufactured goods. For it can always pay, in proportion to the revenues of its landed property, the workers who manufacture the handiwork it needs.*

Thus, trade in industrial works belongs as surely to this nation as trade in the produce of its own growth.

VII. *A nation that has little trade in produce of its own growth, and which is reduced to a trade in industry to subsist, is in a precarious and uncertain state. For its trade can be taken from it by other rival nations who would devote themselves to this same trade with more success.*

Moreover, this nation is always tributary and dependent on those who sell it essential raw materials. It is reduced to a rigorous economy, because it has no revenue to

### VIII. *A large domestic trade in manufactured goods can only subsist through the revenue of landed estates.*

One must examine, in a kingdom, the proportion between foreign trade and domestic trade of industrial works; for if the domestic trade in <term>manufactured goods</term> <note>original: "marchandises de main-d'œuvre"; literally "goods of hand-labor."</note> were, for example, three million and the foreign trade were one million, three-quarters of all this trade in manufactured goods would be paid for by the revenue of the nation’s landed estates, since foreigners would only pay for one quarter of it.

In this case, the revenue from landed estates would be the principal wealth of the kingdom. Therefore, the primary object of government would be to see to the maintenance and the increase of the revenue of these landed estates.

The means to achieve this consist of the freedom of trade and the preservation of the wealth of the <term>cultivators</term>. <note>In 18th-century economic theory, "cultivators" refers to the entrepreneurial farmers who manage land and invest capital, rather than simple laborers.</note> Without these conditions, revenue, population, and the products of industry are all annihilated.

Agriculture produces two kinds of wealth, namely: the annual product of the owners' revenue and the reimbursement of the costs of cultivation.

The revenue must be spent so as to be distributed annually to all citizens and to contribute to the subsidies of the State.

The wealth employed for the costs of cultivation must be reserved for the cultivators and be exempt from all impositions; for, if it is taken away, agriculture is destroyed, the earnings of the inhabitants of the countryside are suppressed, and the source of the State’s revenue is cut off at its spring.

### IX. *A nation that has a large territory and which lowers the price of its own produce to favor the manufacturing of manual labor, destroys itself on all sides.*

For, if the cultivator is not compensated for the great expenses that cultivation requires, and if he does not make a profit, agriculture perishes; the nation loses the revenue from its landed estates; the labor of manufacturing decreases, because such work can no longer be paid for by the owners of the landed estates; the country becomes depopulated through misery and the desertion of manufacturers, artisans, laborers, and peasants, who can only subsist in proportion to the earnings provided to them by the nation's revenue.

### X. *The advantages of foreign trade do not consist in the increase of pecuniary wealth.*

The increase in wealth provided by a nation's <term>foreign trade</term> <note>original: "commerce extérieur"; the author is arguing against the common belief of the time that the goal of trade was simply to hoard gold.</note> may not be an increase in <term>pecuniary wealth</term> <note>original: "richesses pécuniaires"; this refers to money in the form of gold and silver coin (specie).</note>, because foreign trade can be conducted with foreign countries through the exchange of other goods that are consumed by that nation. But it is nonetheless a wealth for this same nation that it enjoys and which it could, through thrift, convert into pecuniary wealth for other uses.

Moreover, <term>commodities</term> <note>original: "denrées"; essential goods, usually agricultural products like food or raw materials.</note>, viewed as merchandise, are both pecuniary wealth and <term>real wealth</term> <note>original: "richesses réelles"; to the Physiocrats, "real" wealth consisted of the actual goods that satisfy human needs, rather than the money used to trade them.</note> all at once. A <term>farmer</term> <note>original: "laboureur"; in this context, not a simple peasant but an entrepreneurial farmer who manages land and owns equipment.</note> who sells his wheat to a merchant is paid in money; with this money, he pays the owner, the <term>taille</term> <note>A direct land tax in pre-revolutionary France, often weighing heavily on the agricultural class.</note>, his servants, his workers, and buys the goods he needs. The merchant who sells the wheat abroad and buys another good from them, or who trades with them by exchange, resells the imported good upon his return, and with the money he receives, he repurchases wheat.

Wheat, viewed as merchandise, is therefore pecuniary wealth for the sellers and real wealth for the buyers.

Thus, commodities that can be sold must always be regarded indifferently in a State as pecuniary wealth and as real wealth, which the subjects can use as they see fit.

The wealth of a nation is not determined by the mass of pecuniary wealth. The latter can increase or decrease without being noticed, for it is always effective in a State by its quantity or by the speed of its <term>circulation</term>, based on the abundance and value of the commodities. Spain, which enjoys the treasures of Peru <note>A reference to the massive influx of silver and gold from the Americas, which led to high inflation (the Price Revolution) and economic decline in Spain despite its abundance of precious metals.</note>, is always exhausted by its needs. England sustains its opulence by its real wealth; the <term>paper</term> <note>original: "papier"; referring to bank notes or credit instruments, which the author argues are stable only when backed by a productive economy.</note>, which represents money there, has a value secured by trade and by the revenues of the nation's assets.

It is therefore not the greater or lesser amount of pecuniary wealth...

*XI. One cannot know the advantage of trade or the state of a nation’s wealth simply by looking at the state of the balance of trade between various nations.* For some nations may be richer in men and <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "biens-fonds"; fixed assets like land and buildings, which the Physiocrats believed were the only true source of wealth.</note> than others; and the latter may have less internal trade, consume less, and have more external trade than the former.

Trade in manufactured goods is also deceptive because the price of <term>raw materials</term> <note>original: "matières premières"</note> is confused within the final product, whereas it ought to be distinguished from the cost of the manufacturing labor.

*XII. It is enough to have the foundation in real wealth.

*XIII. ### XIV.
In *reciprocal* trade, those nations that sell the *most necessary or most useful goods* have the advantage over those that sell *luxury goods*. A nation that is secured by its <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "biens-fonds"; fixed assets like land, which the author views as the source of all real wealth.</note> through a trade in its own produce—and consequently also by an internal trade in <term>manufactured goods</term> <note>original: "marchandises de main-d’œuvre"; literally "labor goods," referring to items produced by artisans rather than extracted from the earth.</note>—is independent of other nations. It only trades with them to maintain, facilitate, and extend its foreign trade; and it must, as much as possible, to preserve its independence and its advantage in reciprocal trade, only obtain luxury goods from them and sell them goods necessary for the needs of life.

They <note>Referring to the foreign nations buying the essentials.</note> will believe that, due to the real value of these different goods, this reciprocal trade is more favorable to them. But the advantage is always with the nation that sells the most useful and necessary goods.

For then its trade is established upon the needs of others; it only sells them its surplus, and its purchases only concern its <term>opulence</term> <note>The author uses "opulence" here to mean discretionary wealth—the ability to buy things one does not strictly need to survive.</note>. These others have more interest in selling to it than it has a need to buy, and it can more easily cut back on luxury than others can save on what is necessary.

It should even be noted that States which devote themselves to luxury manufacturing experience unfortunate <term>vicissitudes</term> <note>Sudden changes or shifts in fortune.</note>. For when times are hard, the luxury trade languishes, and the workers find themselves without bread and without employment.

France could, if trade were free, produce an abundance of <term>essential commodities</term> <note>original: "denrées de premier besoin"; the basic food and raw materials required for survival.</note> that would suffice for both large-scale consumption and extensive foreign trade, and which could support a large trade in manufactured goods within the kingdom.

But the state of its population does not allow it to employ many men in luxury works; and it is even in its interest, to facilitate the foreign trade of its own produce, to maintain a reciprocal trade with foreign nations through the purchase of luxury goods.

It is also essential not to subject the trade of provincial commodities to temporary and arbitrary bans and permissions, which ruin the countryside under the deceptive pretext of ensuring plenty in the cities. Cities survive through the spending of the property owners who live in them; thus, by destroying the income from <term>landed property</term> <note>original: "biens-fonds"; the primary source of wealth in Physiocratic theory, consisting of land and its improvements.</note>, one neither favors the cities nor procures the well-being of the State.

The management of the nation's revenues must not be left to the discretion or the authority of subordinate and local administration.

One must not limit the export of grain to specific provinces because they exhaust themselves before other provinces can restock them; and the inhabitants may be exposed, for a few months, to a shortage that is rightly attributed to exportation.

But when the freedom to export is general, the withdrawal of grain is not noticeable because merchants draw from all parts of the kingdom, and especially from provinces where grain is at a low price.

Then, there are no longer any provinces where commodities are in a state of <term>non-value</term> <note>original: "non-valeur"; refers to goods that cannot be sold at a price covering the cost of production, effectively making them worthless to the producer.</note>. Agriculture revives everywhere in proportion to the market demand.

The progress of trade and agriculture go hand in hand; and exportation never carries away anything but a surplus, which would not exist without it, and which always maintains abundance and increases the kingdom's revenues.

This increase in revenue increases the population and consumption because spending increases and provides gains that attract men.

Through such progress, a kingdom can reach a high degree of strength and prosperity in a short time. Thus, by very simple means, a sovereign can make, within his own States, conquests much more advantageous than those he would undertake against his neighbors. Progress is rapid; under <note>Henri IV (r. 1589–1610) was often cited by 18th-century economists as a model of a king who restored French prosperity through agricultural support.</note> Henri IV, the exhausted kingdom, burdened with debt, soon became a land of abundance and wealth. *See* **TAXATION**.

*Observations on the necessity of wealth for the cultivation of grain.*

It must never be forgotten that the state of prosperity to which we might aspire would be less the fruit of the laborer's toil than the product of the wealth he could employ in the cultivation of the land. It is manure that procures rich harvests; it is livestock that produces manure; it is money that provides livestock and supplies the men to manage them. We have seen, through the preceding details, that the costs for thirty million <term>arpents</term> <note>An old French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre, though it varied by region.</note> of land managed by <term>small-scale cultivation</term> <note>original: "petite culture"; a system of farming characterized by low capital, the use of oxen, and subsistence-level yields.</note> are only 285 million; and that those one would incur for 30 million arpents well-managed by <term>large-scale cultivation</term> <note>original: "grande culture"; a capital-intensive farming system using horses, more fertilizer, and modern tools to produce a high surplus.</note> would be 710 million. However, in the first case, the product is only 390 million; and in the second, it would be 1,378,000,000. Greater expenses would produce even greater profits; the additional expenditure and manpower required by good cultivation for the purchase and management of livestock provide, for their part, a product that is hardly less considerable than that of the harvests.

Poor cultivation, however, requires a great deal of work; but, because the cultivator cannot make the necessary expenditures, his labors are fruitless; he succumbs, and foolish <term>bourgeois</term> <note>Here referring to city-dwellers or middle-class observers who do not understand the realities of rural economy.</note> attribute his failures to laziness. They believe, no doubt, that it is enough to plow, to "torment the earth" to force it to bear good harvests; one applauds oneself when saying to a poor man who is not busy: *Go plow the land.* It is horses and oxen, and not men, who should plow the land. It is herds that must fertilize it; without these aids, the land poorly rewards the labors of the cultivators. Does one not know, moreover, that the land makes no advances; that it, on the contrary, makes one wait a long time for the harvest? What then could be the fate of this indigent man to whom one says: *Go plow the land?* Can he cultivate on his own account? Will he find work with farmers if they are poor? These farmers, powerless to meet the costs of good cultivation and unable to pay the wages of servants and laborers, cannot employ the peasants. The land, without fertilizer and nearly uncultivated, can only leave both one and the other to languish in misery.

It must further be observed that all the inhabitants of the kingdom must benefit from the advantages of good cultivation for it to be sustained and produce great revenues for the sovereign. It is by inc—

<meta>This page continues the economic argument regarding the circulation of wealth. While the previous page focused on the capital costs of "large-scale" versus "small-scale" cultivation, this section explains how taxing the farmer directly—rather than the surplus income—destroys the economic cycle that supports all social classes.</meta>

...by increasing the incomes of landowners and the profits of farmers, it provides gains to all other <term>estates</term> <note>original: "états"; referring to the various social classes or orders of society, such as the clergy, nobility, and commoners.</note> and maintains the consumption and spending that, in turn, sustain the system itself. But, if the <term>sovereign's</term> <note>The King or the central government.</note> taxes are placed directly upon the cultivator himself, and if they strip away his profits, cultivation withers and the incomes of landowners decrease. This results in an inevitable tightening of spending which impacts wage-earners, merchants, workers, and domestic servants: the general system of spending, labor, profit, and consumption is disrupted; the State weakens; and taxation becomes increasingly destructive. A kingdom can therefore only be flourishing and formidable through productions that are renewed or reborn continually, springing from the very wealth of a numerous and active people whose industry is supported and encouraged by the government.

It has been imagined that the disruption the government might cause to the fortunes of individuals is a matter of indifference to the State because, it is said, if some become rich at the expense of others, the wealth still exists within the kingdom. This idea is false and absurd; for the riches of a State do not sustain themselves on their own; they are only preserved and increased insofar as they are renewed by being employed with intelligence. If the farmer is ruined by the <term>financier</term> <note>In the 18th century, "financiers" were often private individuals who handled the King’s finances or "farmed" the taxes, often seen by economists of the time as parasitic figures who drained capital away from productive agriculture.</note>, the revenues of the kingdom are annihilated, commerce and industry languish, and the laborer lacks work. The sovereign, the landowners, and the clergy are deprived of income; spending and gains are abolished. Riches, locked away in the coffers of the financier, are unproductive; or, if they are lent out at interest, they become a burden upon the State. The government must therefore be very careful to preserve, for all productive professions, the wealth that is necessary for them to produce and increase the riches of the kingdom.

Finally, one must recognize that the products of the earth are not wealth in and of themselves; they are only wealth insofar as they are necessary to men and insofar as they can be traded. They are, therefore, wealth only in proportion to their consumption and the number of people who require them. No man living in society applies his labor to every single one of his needs; rather, by selling what his own labor produces, he procures what he lacks. Thus, everything becomes tradable, and everything becomes wealth through the mutual traffic between men—

men, and that it is these very needs themselves that establish wealth; thus, the more men there are in a kingdom whose territory is vast and fertile, the more wealth there is. *Observation on the price of grain.* Income multiplies spending, and spending attracts men who seek profit; foreigners leave their homelands to come share in the comfort of an opulent nation, and their arrival increases its wealth even further by sustaining, through consumption, a good price for agricultural products and by encouraging, through that good price, an abundance of these products: for not only does a good price favor the progress of agriculture, but it is in the good price itself that the wealth it procures consists. The value of a <term>setier</term> <note>A "setier" was a traditional French unit of volume; for grain in Paris, it was roughly 150 liters.</note> of wheat, considered as wealth, consists only in its price: thus, the more expensive and abundant the wheat, wine, wool, and livestock are, the more wealth there is in the State. *Worthlessness alongside abundance is not wealth; high prices with scarcity is misery; abundance with high prices is opulence.* I mean a permanent state of high prices and abundance; for a temporary high price would not provide a general distribution of wealth to the entire nation, nor would it increase the income of the landowners or the revenues of the king; it would only be advantageous to a few individuals who happened to have commodities to sell at a high price.

Commodities can therefore only be wealth for a nation through abundance and a good price constantly maintained by good cultivation, by high consumption, and by foreign trade: one must even recognize that, for an entire nation, abundance and a good price that is current abroad is great wealth, especially if this wealth consists of agricultural products; for this is a wealth of property tied to the specific territory that can produce it: thus, through its abundance and its high price, it is always to the advantage of the nation that possesses the most and sells to others. For the more a kingdom can procure for itself wealth in money, the more powerful it is and the more its facul—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between high agricultural prices and national wealth, concluding a point about the resources available to the sovereign.</meta>

...of individuals are expanded, because money is the only wealth that can be applied to all uses and determines the strength of nations relative to one another.

Nations are poor wherever the country's products most necessary for life are at a low price; these products are the most precious and marketable assets; they can only fall into worthlessness through a lack of population and foreign trade. In these cases, the source of pecuniary <note>original: "pécuniaires" — relating to or consisting of money.</note> wealth is lost in countries deprived of the advantages of trade, where men, strictly reduced to the goods necessary for existence, cannot obtain what they need to satisfy other needs of life and the security of their homeland: such are our provinces where <term>commodities</term> <note>original: "denrées" — specifically agricultural produce intended for consumption or sale.</note> are at a low price, those lands of abundance and poverty where forced labor and excessive saving are not even resources for obtaining money. When commodities are expensive and when incomes and gains increase proportionally, one can, through economic arrangements, diversify spending, pay debts, make acquisitions, establish children, and so on. It is in the possibility of these arrangements that the comfort resulting from the "good price" of commodities consists. This is why the towns and provinces of a kingdom where commodities are expensive are more inhabited than those where all commodities are at too low a price, because this low price stifles income, cuts spending, destroys trade, and suppresses the gains of all other professions, as well as the labor and wages of artisans and laborers; furthermore, it annihilates the king's revenues, because the greater part of trade for consumption is done by exchanging goods and does not contribute to the circulation of money; this provides the king with no duties on the consumption of food in these provinces and very little on the income from property.

When trade is free, the high price of commodities necessarily has its limits, fixed by the prices of the commodities of other nations that extend their trade everywhere. It is not the same for worthlessness or high prices caused by the lack of freedom of trade; they follow one another in turn and irregularly; both are very disadvantageous and almost always depend on a vice of government.

<meta>This page continues the argument for maintaining a "good price" for agricultural products, specifically refuting the idea that low grain prices benefit the working class or the national economy.</meta>

totaling three <term>setiers</term> <note>An old French unit of volume for grain; in Paris, it was roughly 150 liters, though it varied by region.</note> of wheat: if, due to a healthy market price, he bought each setier four livres more, this price would increase his daily expenditure by at most one sou; his wage would also increase proportionally, and this increase would be a small matter for those paying it, compared to the wealth resulting from the good price of wheat. Thus, the advantages of a good price for wheat are not at all destroyed by the increase in workers' wages; for then this increase is far from approaching the increase in the profits of farmers, the income of landowners, the product of <term>tithes</term> <note>original: "dîmes" — a ten-percent tax on agricultural produce paid to the Church.</note>, and the revenues of the king. It is also easy to see that these advantages would not have increased the labor costs of the manufactures by even one-twentieth, perhaps not even one-fortieth—those same industries that imprudently decided to forbid the exportation of our grain and caused the State an immense loss. It is, moreover, a great disadvantage to accustom the people to buying wheat at too low a price; they become less industrious, they feed themselves on bread at little cost and become lazy and arrogant; farmers find it difficult to hire workers and servants; thus, they are very poorly served in years of abundance. It is important that the common people earn more and that they be driven by the need to earn. In the last century, when wheat was sold for much more, the people were accustomed to it: they earned proportionally; they must have been more industrious and more comfortable.

Thus, we do not mean here, by the word *dearness* <note>original: "cherté" — in this context, it refers to a high but stable and profitable market price, rather than a scarcity-driven spike.</note>, a price that could ever be excessive, but only a price common between us and foreign nations; for, under the assumption of free foreign trade, the price will always be regulated by the competition of the trade in commodities of neighboring nations.

Those who do not consider the distribution of a State's wealth in its full extent may object that dearness is only advantageous for sellers and that it impoverishes those who buy; that it thus decreases the wealth of some as much as it increases that of others. Dearness, according to these ideas, cannot therefore be, in any case, an increase in wealth in the State.

<meta>This page continues the argument that high grain prices do not harm the economy but rather stimulate it by allowing workers to charge more for their labor, thereby increasing the overall flow of wealth within the State.</meta>

...the gains? Do not the manual laborer, the craftsman, the manufacturer, etc., charge for their time and their work in proportion to what their subsistence costs them? The more revenue there is in a State, the more trade, manufacturing, the arts, crafts, and other professions become necessary and lucrative.

But this prosperity can only be maintained through the <term>good price</term> <note>original: "bon prix" — a central concept in Physiocratic economic theory, referring to a price high enough to provide a profit to the farmer after all costs are covered, thereby stimulating the economy.</note> of our commodities: for when the government halts the sale of the land’s produce and when it causes its prices to drop, it opposes abundance and diminishes the wealth of the nation in proportion to the drop in the price of commodities that are converted into money.

This state of a good price and abundance existed in the kingdom as long as *our grains were an object of trade*, cultivation was protected, and the population was numerous. But the restriction of the trade in <term>grain</term> <note>original: "blés" — while specifically meaning wheat, it was often used generically for all bread-making cereals.</note>, the method of taxing subsidies, the poor <unclear>employment</unclear> of men and wealth in the manufacturing of luxury goods, continual wars, and other causes of depopulation and poverty have destroyed these advantages; and the State loses annually more than three-quarters of the product it derived a century ago from the cultivation of grain, not including the other losses that necessarily result from this enormous degradation of agriculture and population.
